title: Buffalo Bills defense steps up in victory over Los Angeles Chargers
summary: For two games, the Buffalo Bills’ offense looked unstoppable. Their defense, on the other hand, looked extremely porous, allowing 31 points in each of the team’s first two victories. That the offense was able to score 36 and 41 pints, respectively, in those games is really the only reason why we haven’t seen more concern […]
full_text: For two games, the Buffalo Bills’ offense looked unstoppable. Their defense, on the other hand, looked extremely porous, allowing 31 points in each of the team’s first two victories. That the offense was able to score 36 and 41 pints, respectively, in those games is really the only reason why we haven’t seen more concern about the team’s defensive output overall. We’ve seen some criticism of the defense, both on this site and elsewhere, and that criticism has been warranted. “The Bills won’t be able to win shootouts every week,” those critics declared, and they were proven right perhaps even earlier than they expected to be. The Bills weathered three first half turnovers on Sunday against the Los Angeles Chargers, somehow entering halftime in a 10-10 tie. With two more turnovers in the second half contributing to a 13-10 Chargers lead midway through the fourth quarter, it was fair to wonder whether or not this was Buffalo’s day to drop an ugly game. However, the offense woke up in that final quarter, scoring a pair of touchdowns just four minutes apart to turn that 13-10 deficit into a 24-13 lead with just over three minutes to play. The Bills were only in a position for those touchdowns to matter because of the continued tough play of their defensive unit on Sunday. Buffalo’s offensive woes placed the defense in adverse situations time and again, and the stop unit weathered the storm. Three of Buffalo’s five turnovers came inside their own territory, but the defense stood tough. Buffalo’s first turnover—on the game’s first play from scrimmage, no less—came on a James Cook fumble that Los Angeles recovered at the Buffalo 47-yard line. That turnover directly led to a touchdown. Buffalo’s seconds turnover came on an interception at the Bills’ 43-yard line, as safety Genesis Smith jumped a route and intercepted Josh Allen. That gifted the Chargers great field position, which they converted into a Cameron Dicker field goal and a 10-0 advantage. Buffalo’s fifth turnover should have been the back-breaker. Allen was sacked, and on his way down, he fumbled at the Bills’ 28-yard line. The Chargers could have thrown three incomplete passes and been in great shape for a 45-yard field goal. They could have run the clock down and added a game-icing touchdown. Instead, they did the one thing that they couldn’t do: they gave the ball right back to Buffalo without scoring. On third down and five from Buffalo’s 23-yard line, Justin Herbert tried to force a pass up the seam to Marquez Valdes-Scantling. C.J. Gardner-Johnson jumped the route, intercepted the pass, and returned it to the Buffalo 43-yard line. From there on, Buffalo’s offense ran 19 plays for 103 yards and two touchdowns over the course of their next two drives. Buffalo’s defensive effort throughout the day was outstanding. They held the Chargers to just one touchdown despite gifting them five extra possessions via turnovers. While they allowed some longer drives in the early going, allowing Los Angeles to march 47 yards for a touchdown on their first possession, they held the Chargers out of the end zone on each of their three longest drives. Los Angeles had a 63-yard drive end in a missed field goal, and then had a pair of 69-yard drives end in made field goals for Cameron Dicker. This was a continuation of a trend that has shown itself this year, as Buffalo’s defense has stepped up in the biggest moments thus far. Even on Sunday, the Bills’ defense bowed its neck and gave the offense a chance to redeem itself in that fourth quarter. After Allen’s fumble, the Chargers ran eight plays on their next two drives. They gained a total of seventeen yards, threw one interception, and turned over the ball on downs. Those two turnovers directly led to Buffalo’s 14 second-half points, which gave them the margin needed to win the game. Yes, there were still warts on defense. Some ugly penalties extended drives that should have ended. There’s also the necessary caveat that the Chargers aren’t exactly an offensive juggernaut, as they have totaled just 44 points this season and average just 309 yards per game. That average is way up from their first two weeks thanks to the 348 total yards they gained on Sunday. Has Buffalo’s defense been perfect this year? No, it hasn’t been. However, after looking like it could be a huge liability through two games, Sunday’s effort was another step in the right direction for defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s charges. While they won’t play struggling offenses like Los Angeles every week, the Buffalo defense continued its trend of stepping up for the team in the biggest moments. And, at least for one week, the offense can thank the defense for covering its mistakes rather than the reverse being true.
author: Sean Murphy

title: Should Buffalo Bills be worried about James Cook’s fumbles?
summary: On the first play from scrimmage in Week 3 against the Chargers, Buffalo Bills running back James Cook had his second fumble of the season. Should the Bills be seriously concerned about his recent fumbling issues? I wanted to investigate whether or not fumbles are fluky. To do so, I conducted a study using 25 […]
full_text: On the first play from scrimmage in Week 3 against the Chargers, Buffalo Bills running back James Cook had his second fumble of the season. Should the Bills be seriously concerned about his recent fumbling issues? I wanted to investigate whether or not fumbles are fluky. To do so, I conducted a study using 25 years of nflverse play-by-play data. So we’re talking from the beginning of the 2001 season through last year, in the regular season. What I found was this; for running backs, the league-wide fumble rate in this enormous sample was right around 1.01 fumbles per 100 touches. And the year-to-year correlation coefficient for fumble rates of all the qualifying running backs in the study (100-plus touches in a given season) was only 0.197 . That’s darn close to a 0.0 coefficient, which indicates zero relationship, or more straightforwardly, complete randomness. Fumble rate year-to-year is largely very noisy. One season is not very predictive of the next. However, that’s not where my study ended. From the most fumble-prone to the least-fumble prone, I wanted to gather the fumble rates of all running backs in one season then track fumble rates the following season. Essentially, this was the regression-to-the-mean test. Here are the results: Year 1 fumble rate / 100 touches Same RBs in Year 2 Change Lowest 20% of RBs (least fumble-prone) 0.08% 0.83% +0.75 21-40% 0.58% 0.81% +0.23 41-60% 0.91% 1.02% +0.11 61-80% 1.34% 1.07% -0.27 81-100% (most fumble-prone) 2.17% 1.24% -0.93 Clearly, regression to the mean is very real here. The most fumble-prone running backs in Year 1 nearly cut their fumble rates in half the next season, while the least fumble-prone running backs in Year 1saw a 10-fold increase in their fumble rate the following season. But the 1.24% fumble rate from the originally most fumble-prone group was still higher than 0.83% from the initially least fumble-prone collection of runners. That means that, yes, the more fumble-prone backs do tend to continue to fumble a bit more than the least fumble-prone runners, but over time, the difference in their fumble rates gets smaller. Heck, even just check the difference in range from the Year 1 rates to the Year 2 rates for the whole sample. It’s significantly tighter and less spread out in the second season. In his NFL career, counting the postseason, Cook’s fumble rate is 1.25 per 100 touches. Since the beginning of 2025, when the fumbles have felt more frequent, his fumble rate has jumped to 2.01 per 100 touches. Before the 2025 campaign — in the first three seasons as a member of the Bills — Cook’s fumble rate was 0.80 . He does have eight fumbles in his last 14 games (counting playoffs), which sounds the alarm bells for many. And I get it. That’s a high rate (would place in the top 20% of the study). We can’t totally dismiss it as random. But historical fumbling data is quite favorable to Buffalo’s star. Running backs with high fumbling rates — like Cook since the start of 2025 — have enjoyed major regression to the mean eventually. Now, do I know exactly when that regression will begin for Cook, when he’ll start fumbling less? No. But I’m going to lean on 25 years of data to predict it will start happening. Great news for Cook, and the Bills offense ahead of Week 4’s contest against the Patriots.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Did Josh Allen injure his knee in fourth quarter vs. Chargers?
summary: Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen took a sizable hit directly to his knee in the fourth quarter in the Week 3 win over the Chargers, and it’s left some to believe he could actually be injured. While there’s yet to be any official report on the matter, a handful of Twitter/X doctors have given their […]
full_text: Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen took a sizable hit directly to his knee in the fourth quarter in the Week 3 win over the Chargers, and it’s left some to believe he could actually be injured. While there’s yet to be any official report on the matter, a handful of Twitter/X doctors have given their own diagnosis of the potential knee injury. #billsmafia Josh Allen LEFT knee Took helmet to knee at 9:46 in 4th. Grimaced. Did have one more designed run next drive Limping postgame, leaning onto right leg, painful back-step in locker room Contusion most likely vs MCL/meniscus pic.twitter.com/fQBpop63N8 — Thigh Doctor (@ThighDoctor) September 27, 2026 If you watch the second video above, you certainly can see Allen favoring his left knee in the locker room after the game. Then there was this from Jesse Morse, M.D. on Twitter as part of the swirling speculation: Josh Allen Left knee injury Most likely: MCL sprain +/- bone bruise If grade 1 sprain – likely plays Week 4 If grade 2 sprain – could miss 1-3 weeks + ⬇️ in designed runs If grade 2 + mensicus – 3+ weeks If ACL involved – gets complicated, s/e If bad meniscal tear – think… pic.twitter.com/ywvCJ7mhvH — Jesse Morse, M.D. (@DrJesseMorse) September 27, 2026 David Chao, @ProFootballDoc on Twitter/X who runs Sports Injury Central, also chimed in on what may have happened to Allen’s knee on that hit, and gave a reasonably positive educated guess, stating the following: “We went back and looked at all the film…Allen does take a hit on the outside of his left knee, but we feel he’s more hurt than injured.” Chao followed by saying, “thankfully his foot was not planting. I do not see a significant MCL-type injury.” Here’s the full video: The latest injury analysis on Bills QB Josh Allen from @ProFootballDoc Full details on the site! #billsmafia pic.twitter.com/ovsBX2eYHR — Sports Injury Central (@SICscore) September 28, 2026 Of course, it is worth noting that Allen stayed in the game and finished that drive with a one-yard tush push touchdown to give Buffalo its first lead of the game, 17-13. Joe Brady will speak to the media today, and I’m assuming one of the first questions he’ll be asked is about the status of Allen’s knee, although I don’t necessarily expect the head coach to have any definitive answers less than 24 hours removed from the game. We’ll undoubtedly stay on this development all week.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Takeaways from Buffalo Bills ugly Week 3 win over Chargers
summary: After two gorgeous wins to open the season, the Buffalo Bills proved they can win ugly in a five-turnover victory over the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 3. The 24-16 win came after Buffalo trailed 10-0 in the first half, and these were my takeaways from the contest that got the Bills to 3-0. Buffalo’s […]
full_text: After two gorgeous wins to open the season, the Buffalo Bills proved they can win ugly in a five-turnover victory over the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 3. The 24-16 win came after Buffalo trailed 10-0 in the first half, and these were my takeaways from the contest that got the Bills to 3-0. Buffalo’s defense was damn good, in a modern NFL type of way These were the Chargers drive results after building a 1o-0 lead that came after three Bills turnovers in the first 16 minutes of the game: Missed field goal Punt End of half Field goal Punt Interception Turnover on downs Field goal I don’t care about the yardage allowed on each of those drives. In today’s NFL that is stingy defense. And even if we count the missed field goal as a make, that would’ve been nine points on Los Angeles’ final eight drives. A 1.12 yards-per-drive rate is very pedestrian for any offense. After allowing 31 points in consecutive weeks to begin the season, surrendering 16 points in a contest in which the offense committed five turnovers is downright sensational. And, heck, it absolutely felt like Justin Herbert was on his game yesterday. But he did ultimately finish with a 6.6 yards-per-attempt average — 7.0 is the benchmark for solid albeit unspectacular quarterback efficiency. For perspective, Jared Goff averaged 8.6 yards per attempt in Week 2, and C.J. Stroud’s YPA was 7.2 in Week 1. If Buffalo’s offense drove the Bills to victories in the opening two weeks, its defense saved the day in Week 3, which should serve as another reminder football is the ultimate team game. No, 348 yards of total offense allowed is not representative of suffocating defense, yet in today’s NFL, it was a strong, situation-based effort from the Bills defense in this win. Chargers took away away middle of the field In Week 3, beyond the line of scrimmage and over the middle, Allen was 7-of-13 for 84 yards with two interceptions, a far cry from the 20-of-29 for 316 yards with four touchdowns and no picks in the first two games on over-the-middle throws. Clearly, the Chargers realized Allen both loves the middle of the field and is excellent throwing passes in that area of the field, so they regularly inserted a “robber” safety, free to roam there, especially at the intermediate level. Rookie Genesis Smith was that robber on Allen’s first interception, jumping an in-breaking route over the middle intended for DJ Moore. But it wasn’t just that throw. Khalil Shakir, who normally feasts over the middle, only caught one pass for six yards and was targeted on one of the Chargers five pass breakups in this game. This is not to suggest Los Angeles unlocked the secret to limiting Allen through the air. He’s more than capable of ripping throws outside the numbers on a regular basis to dice secondaries that way. But like I wrote earlier last week, it appeared the Bills game plan was centered around the Chargers being vulnerable at safety with Elijah Molden out, and it actually was Los Angeles’ safeties who made some significant plays in this game. Imagine that. The Chargers had one of the more unique pass-rush plans I’ve seen In this contest, Los Angeles started its defensive ends exceptionally wide — almost as if they were blitzing corners. That wrinkle did two things — first and foremost, it kept Allen in the pocket far more frequently than he’s accustomed to. Secondly, it forced the Bills tackles to block on an island with plenty of space around them. Dion Dawkins and Spencer Brown are fine island blockers, but the unique approach from those extra-wide rushers seemed to throw off the blockers’ timing. They were deep into their vertical pass-protection sets, and Khalil Mack and Akheem Mesidor/Tuli Tuipulotu were still steps away from them, charging ahead at full speed. That disrupted timing for Buffalo’s talented tackles, and gave Mack and Co. flat angles to get to Allen. The Chargers pressured Buffalo’s quarterback on 38.7% of his drop backs despite only blitzing 22.6% of the time. Couple those creative pass-rush looks with Los Angeles’ prioritizing the elimination of Allen’s easy outlets between the numbers, and you get an awkward-looking superstar for a large portion of this contest. Was there something to Josh Allen not running as much early? From the Dawson Knox (failed) tush push to a few instances in the first half that appeared to be easy-access running opportunities than Allen stunningly passed up, at the half, I wondered if Allen was a little dinged OR if it was suggested to him to stay away from taking big hits as a runner after the NFL saw a litany of starting quarterback suffer injuries in Week 2. Fortunately for the Bills — and the quarterback’s natural tendencies — there was plenty more scrambling and designed-run opportunities in the second half. It all appeared back to normal. But in those opening two stanzas, things were different. Can’t discount the Chargers defensive game plan — which was damn good, I alluded to above — keeping him contained as well. The sample size is plenty big enough… I don’t expect Allen to become timid as a runner. But it probably is something to monitor for at least into Week 4’s game against the Patriots. The value of James Cook (and Ty Johnson) In a game like that one, where the opponents’ defensive game plan and execution are incredible, it’s quite the luxury to have the reigning rushing champion and one of the league’s best third-down backs at your disposal. For as much as I’m an advocate for Allen being the center of every tactical plan each week, Cook’s presence cannot be ignored. Toting the rock 24 times for 154 yards with a score against that run defense? Magnificent. Hats off the big boys up front too. And how about Johnson? Four catches for 50 yards, none bigger than his 29-yarder on a 4th down with the Bills trailing by three in the fourth quarter. The importance of his return to the field cannot be overstated.

title: Bills vs. Chargers game analysis: Buffalo overcomes real adversity
summary: It wasn’t the prettiest day (starting with the new alternate uniforms, ugh) but the Buffalo Bills got the job done and beat the Los Angeles Chargers, 24-16. The Bills are 3-0 now, and 2-0 at their new home. I had a lot of thoughts running through my mind while this one played out live. Here […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 27: Khalil Mack #52 of the Los Angeles Chargers hits Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills as he throws during the first quarter of the game at Highmark Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images It wasn’t the prettiest day (starting with the new alternate uniforms, ugh) but the Buffalo Bills got the job done and beat the Los Angeles Chargers, 24-16. The Bills are 3-0 now, and 2-0 at their new home. I had a lot of thoughts running through my mind while this one played out live. Here are my notes from the game, written as it happened. 1st Half James Cook fumble issues are becoming a real problem. First defensive campaign also didn’t look good. Players were way too often out of position, pre and post-snap. Chargers are getting pressure rushing just four. Far from ideal from Bills’ OL, especially the interior. I don’t know what Josh Allen thought on that INT — he started his read on the other side of the field, but when he got to DJ Moore, the safety was sitting there, just waiting for the pass, and Josh still threw it. Weird. How could he not see the safety there? Hoped Moore would run an in instead of a post? Penalties on D are a huge issue in this 1st qtr. 2nd qtr, and Josh forcing it deep to DJ Moore vs double team (maybe thought he had a free play? DL jumped early), another INT. How that ball didn’t touch the ground. Rookie Genesis Smith starts his career with 2 INTs so far. That’s why I always will prefer to give young talented players an opportunity instead of insisting with a guy like Damar Hamlin, who has shown his limitations often. Cameron Dicker missing a field goal from inside the 50 isn’t very c’mon. Momentum builder? Rough game for Josh so far. Huge missed opportunity in the red zone. Overthrew DJ when he had a one-on-one opportunity on the ground vs Tony Jefferson. C.J. Gardner-Johnson hurt himself trying a big hit on Keaton Mitchell. Missed tackle also allowed a 1st down when a more conservative wrap-up would have avoided the gain and the injury. CJGJ has been very underachieving after all the hype during camp. Pass rush finally getting the job done with a sack by Greg Rousseau. Bills will get the ball back with a chance to tie. Can’t ask for more than that with the way they’ve played on offense. 3 TOs and still can tie? Sign me up. 2-minute drill and DJ Moore is so important. WRs not winning, and he’s the one Josh trusts. Big play to Keon Coleman for 20+ yards and almost a TD. Great to see Josh recovering inside the game and even better to see Keon staying ready to contribute. TD Bills , Josh with the Tush Push. Unstoppable. Half-Time, 10-10. With the way the Bills started the game? It’s a win. 2nd Half Christian Benford getting torched by Tre’ Harris to start the 2nd half. Slow start for Buffalo’s CB1 continues, this time not against a top-tier WR in the league. 3rd and 15, pressure got to Justin Herbert ; secondary gotta do better. Dee Alford out of position there. CJGJ INT in the end zone , nullified by Benford’s penalty. Oof. New Highmark and Bills Mafia are certainly impacting the game here. 2 OL penalties, just 3 points for the Chargers here — another win. Another great chance of taking the lead, another missed opportunity. A big play by Dalton Kincaid quickly became another blunder — opportunistic Chargers D forces another fumble. 4th Bills TO in the game. Benford hurt, non-contact injury. Davison Igbinosun with a great play in man coverage next. Deone Walker’s length created an INT opportunity , Alford couldn’t capitalize, but the D again did its job. Rookie Akheem Mesidor dominates Dion Dawkins and sacks Allen. Chargers’ defense created problems for the Bills’ offense the entire afternoon, being able to contain the run from light boxes and getting to the QB with just 3 and 4 rushers. Josh’s been uncomfortable all game , no easy completions, no lanes to run, pocket closing in on him with few rushers. Something to check on all 22 , but it looked like one of those games where Josh refused to take the check-downs, and the Chargers D took away the deeper routes with split safeties. 2nd sack in a row for the Chargers , and it’s a fumble. When the Bills needed it the most, CJGJ made a huge play at the goal line. Big-time INT and once again, the D keeps the team in the game. It’s not always pretty, but this D has done its part in all 3 games so far. Start of 4th qtr and Joe Brady tries something different — less under center, more shotgun, quick passes and even a QB run on 1st down. Previous plan wasn’t working, it was time. Bills survive a 4th and 7 at the middle of the field , scores a TD on an Allen magical play, loses the TD due to a penalty. It’s the start of a festival of holding penalties by the Bills OL. Chargers DB holds Coleman and saves the Bills from a 3rd and 27. 1st down Buffalo. What a crazy game, does anybody want to win it? Under center run game works with Cook for a couple of plays , and Josh Allen scores on another Tush Push. Only Chargers TO becomes a Bills TD, the difference in this game. Bills had 5, and LA couldn’t always capitalize. The defense stops the Chargers at the middle of the field the following drive. Deone Walker and Bradley Chubb sack Herbert on 2nd down. Chargers’ offense can’t get the job done. It’s time for the offense to close the game out. Cook is finding lanes. How in the world is it not a foul? Josh took a knee and gave up on the play; Tuli Tuipulotu punched it out after the play was clearly dead. Another DJ Moore catch , this time on a crossing route and setting up a potential game-winning TD. What an addition. James Cook TD at the goal line. 3:13 left. Ball game. Bills D allows the Chargers to drive downfield , bends but doesn’t break. Allow an FG as we reach the 2-minute warning. Chargers will need an onside kick. Keon Coleman recovers the onside kick. He obviously doesn’t have a big role on O right now, but it’s been positive how he’s been ready to contribute any time his number is called. Shows maturity, previously a concern. Where’s the crowd of “you can’t win a game with 4 turnovers”? That’s what I talk about, you clearly can, as long as you take advantage of opportunities to get out of the field on defense and hold the opponent to FGs mostly, and in striking range. Bills’ defense could do it for the offense today, and the team was rewarded with a win, even though it was far from the best offensive performance. Last week the team had a dominant performance , but it wasn’t always shown on the scoreboard. Today was the opposite — despite a lackluster performance, they were able to stay in it and win at the end. They won’t be able to play well every game, just find a way to win. 1-0. Go Bills. Catch up on all this and more with the latest edition of Leading the Charge!

title: Buffalo Bills QB Josh Allen ties Marshawn Lynch in rushing TDs
summary: Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen has spent the past few years chasing running backs up the NFL’s all-time rushing touchdown list. On Sunday, he caught one Bills Mafia knows pretty well.  Allen ran for two touchdowns against the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 3, giving him 85 for his career and tying former Bills running back […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 27: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills runs through left guard for a 1-yard touchdown against the Los Angeles Chargers during the second quarter of the game at Highmark Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen has spent the past few years chasing running backs up the NFL’s all-time rushing touchdown list. On Sunday, he caught one Bills Mafia knows pretty well. Allen ran for two touchdowns against the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 3, giving him 85 for his career and tying former Bills running back Marshawn Lynch for 17th place in NFL history. Allen’s first rushing touchdown of the game, a one-yard run in the second quarter, broke his tie with Pro Football Hall of Fame running back Jim Taylor, who finished his career with 83. Allen entered the game tied with Taylor after scoring twice against the Detroit Lions in Week 2. JOSH. ALLEN. 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/kerB8XhOr9 — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) September 27, 2026 Then came No. 85. GUESS WHO?! 😏 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/pbasZtwopG — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) September 27, 2026 Allen took another one in from the one-yard line in the fourth quarter, pulling him even with Lynch, who scored 85 rushing touchdowns during a 12-year NFL career that began in Buffalo. Lynch spent parts of four seasons with the Bills after Buffalo selected him 12th overall in the 2007 NFL Draft before going on to spend the bulk of his career with the Seattle Seahawks. And there are some pretty big names suddenly within Allen’s reach. Priest Holmes is next with 86 rushing touchdowns, followed by Eric Dickerson and Curtis Martin at 90 and Jerome Bettis and Franco Harris at 91. Allen has averaged just under 10 rushing touchdowns per season over his career, but that number has jumped to nearly 14 per season over the past three years. If Allen keeps anything close to that recent pace, Dickerson, Martin, Bettis, and Harris are all well within reach this season. And with six rushing touchdowns through the first three games, even Barry Sanders’ 99 doesn’t look quite as far away as it did when the season started. Of course, keeping up a two-rushing-touchdowns-per-game pace would be absurd. But this is Josh Allen, and we have been doing this long enough to know better than to completely rule out absurd.
author: Rachel Auberger

title: Buffalo Bills’ defense stole spotlight in Week 3 win
summary: The Buffalo Bills improved to 3-0 thanks to an impressive defensive effort, the kind of work so many people had been waiting to see out of new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s group. In total, Buffalo’s defense allowed the Chargers just one trip to pay dirt and a trio of field goals all while navigating some […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 27: DeWayne Carter #90 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates after winning the game against the Los Angeles Chargers at Highmark Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills improved to 3-0 thanks to an impressive defensive effort, the kind of work so many people had been waiting to see out of new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s group. In total, Buffalo’s defense allowed the Chargers just one trip to pay dirt and a trio of field goals all while navigating some very difficult situations on the heels of five turnovers. It was an ugly day for the Bills’ offense, clearly caught in a dangerous Los Angeles defensive trap. Buffalo’s defense wasn’t listening to any bit of that trap-game narrative, playing the type of football that allowed quarterback Josh Allen and company the time needed to clear their heads and claw back to a game-tying touchdown just before halftime. In truth, the first half could have gone much worse if not for the defense’s effort holding up against short fields. Winning is difficult in the NFL, and the Bills probably don’t walk off the field undefeated without that defensive effort. Once again, outside linebacker Greg Rousseau roared to the rescue late in action of each half. He leads the league in sacks, claiming another pair in Week 3 for a total of six on the season. Rousseau looks like a gladiator unleashed in Leonhard’s system, finally freed from the cages of Buffalo’s prior 4-3 system. Through the first two games, it seemed pretty clear that the Bills’ path to success would require offensive perfection, fireworks on every drive. Then the Chargers’ stout defense came to town ready to change the narrative. Allen appeared off all day, unable to build any sustained success as a passer. Los Angeles’ defense did well in taking the short passing option away early, and convincing Allen it was unwise to scramble for yards even with a lot of green grass in front of him. It’s true that Los Angeles’ offense was at times its own worst enemy, with plenty of miscues and mistakes. That shouldn’t take away from what the defense accomplished against quarterback Justin Herbert, limiting him to a 76.3 rating while going 20-0f-34 for 226 yards with a touchdown and interception. Herbert rarely looked locked-in, a testament to the defensive backfield in the game’s biggest moments — which really rallied to action following cornerback Christian Benford’s toe injury. Buffalo didn’t claim its first lead until there was 7:35 left in regulation. It was only possible because the Bills’ defense forced field-goal tries on four drives, one of which went astray for kicker Cameron Dicker. Late in the fourth, the Chargers decided to go for it on fourth down, but Buffalo’s defense was ready and gave its offense the short field needed to run toward victory. Now, perhaps, the Bills’ defense will be able run to the spotlight.

title: Buffalo Bills’ Joe Brady makes NFL history with 3-0 start
summary: Joe Brady is three games into his NFL head-coaching career, and he still hasn’t lost one.  The Buffalo Bills beat the Los Angeles Chargers 24-16 on Sunday, improving to 3-0 under Brady and putting their new head coach in some pretty exclusive company in the process.  At 37 years old, Brady became the fifth-youngest head coach in NFL history to begin […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Head coach Joe Brady of the Buffalo Bills communicates during an NFL football game between the Detroit Lions and the Buffalo Billsat Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, New York, USA, on Thursday, September 17, 2026 (Photo by Amy Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images Joe Brady is three games into his NFL head-coaching career, and he still hasn’t lost one. The Buffalo Bills beat the Los Angeles Chargers 24-16 on Sunday, improving to 3-0 under Brady and putting their new head coach in some pretty exclusive company in the process. At 37 years old, Brady became the fifth-youngest head coach in NFL history to begin his career with three straight wins. Only Josh McDaniels, John Madden, Bill Cowher, and Mike Tomlin were younger when they started 3-0. McDaniels and Madden were both 33 when they reached the mark, while Cowher and Tomlin were 35. Brady had already made a little franchise history one week earlier. Buffalo’s win over Detroit made him the first head coach in Bills history to win each of his first two regular-season games at the helm. Sunday’s win pushed the streak to three and moved the accomplishment beyond the Buffalo record book. Brady turned 37 on Wednesday, making him the youngest active head coach in the NFL. According to Bills PR, he is also the second-youngest head coach or manager across the NFL, MLB, NBA, and NHL, behind only 34-year-old Washington Nationals manager Blake Butera. Bills HC Joe Brady turns 37 today. Brady is the youngest active HC in the NFL and is the second-youngest coach across the MLB/NBA/NFL/NHL, behind only Washington Nationals' manager Blake Butera (34 years old). pic.twitter.com/aJdPRmBxiZ — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) September 23, 2026 Brady took over as Buffalo’s head coach after spending the previous two-plus seasons running the Bills’ offense, first as interim offensive coordinator during the 2023 season and then in the permanent role. Now, three games into his first head-coaching job, Brady has three wins. That means his usual postgame message needs another update. 3-0.
author: Rachel Auberger

title: Buffalo Bills stock report: horns up/horns down vs. Los Angeles Chargers
summary: The Buffalo Bills fought hard against the Los Angeles Chargers, weathering a first half period of horrendous play before settling into what was ultimately a very competitive football game. After falling into a 10-0 hole early on, the Bills were able to tie it up at 10 before the end of the first half. A […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 27: C.J. Gardner-Johnson #22 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates after a play during the third quarter of the game against the Los Angeles Chargers at Highmark Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills fought hard against the Los Angeles Chargers, weathering a first half period of horrendous play before settling into what was ultimately a very competitive football game. After falling into a 10-0 hole early on, the Bills were able to tie it up at 10 before the end of the first half. A series of miscues throughout the game prevented Buffalo from gaining any sort of momentum, however, until the fourth quarter. The Bills added two second half turnovers to the three they committed in the first half, limiting any positive progress that the team made on offense. Eventually, the Buffalo offense fought through that early malaise, doing just enough to pull out an ugly, hard-fought win over a motivated Chargers team desperate to avoid an 0-3 start. While Buffalo trailed into the fourth quarter, the Bills ultimately prevailed, digging deep for a 24-13 win and a 3-0 start to the 2026 NFL season. The Bills aren’t going to put much of today’s game on any highlight reels, but an ugly win is always better than a pretty loss. There were plenty of ups and downs today, and we’ve done the best we can to reflect the roller coaster ride in our stock report for this one. _____________________________________________________________________________ Horns Down: Offensive Preparedness It was a sloppy first quarter, and that’s putting it kindly. On Buffalo’s first offensive play, James Cook lost a fumble, negating the advantage given to the Bills by Greg Dortch’s excellent opening kickoff return. It also gifted the Chargers a short field, which they took advantage of in the form of a short passing touchdown to running back Keaton Mitchell. After a punt on their second possession, the Bills third possession came to a quick end when Josh Allen misread the Chargers’ defensive coverage and threw an interception directly into the hands of safety Genesis Smith, which led to a Chargers field goal and a 10-0 first quarter lead. A holding penalty on Alec Anderson and some poor blocking from Connor McGovern and O’Cyrus Torrence also had Buffalo on the ropes early. It was a horrendous starts for a Buffalo offense that had been exceptional in its first two outings. Horns Down: First Half Josh Allen With Allen, turnovers tend to come in bunches or not at all. Unfortunately, that trend continued, as Allen threw his first interception on a bad read. Then, on the ensuing possession, Allen made another boneheaded decision, throwing into triple coverage deep down field in an attempt to let DJ Moore make a play. Granted, it took an absolute fluke play for Genesis Smith to come down with his second interception of the day, but the decision to throw the ball was not a great one. After two nearly flawless games to open the year, Allen played about as poorly as he could have to start the game. It wasn’t pretty, but he cleaned it up as the day went on, eventually leading the Bills on long scoring drives that gave Buffalo the victory. Allen completed 16-of-26 passes for 204 yards. He also rushed eight times for 22 yards and two scores. His three turnovers were an issue, but the Bills were able to do enough to overcome them. Horns Up: Special Teams Greg Dortch looked good on kickoff returns, averaging nearly 31 yards per try. Sam Franklin Jr. was a demon on kick coverage, notching two tackles and sticking his nose in plenty of tough spots. Tyler Bass hit all three of his PATs and his lone field goal try, a 28-yard boot. Tommy Doman Jr. drilled a 51-yard punt. Overall, the special teams unit led by special teams coach Jeff Rodgers has been a positive for the team. Horns Up: Greg Rousseau Groot has been incredible this season, and he made his presence known early in today’s game. He made a few solid run stuffs on plays to the outside, and he also brought a first-half drive to an end by notching Buffalo’s first sack on Justin Herbert. That was Rousseau’s fifth sack of the season, continuing what has been an outstanding start to the year for Buffalo’s 2021 first-round pick. Rousseau’s career high for sacks in a season is eight; at this pace, he’s going to race by that before the Bills’ bye in Week Seven. He added another sack in the second half to give him six on the year, and he notched eight tackles, including four tackles for loss, in today’s win. Horns Up: DJ Moore Playing through a painful shoulder injury isn’t an easy task, but Moore was huge for the Bills in the first half. We already talked about the bad Allen force on what turned out to be an unlucky interception (a play where Allen might have thought he had a free play with a Chargers player offside), but Moore was able to find space and move the chains for Allen and the offense on the team’s first touchdown drive. Moore converted two huge third downs on that two-minute drive, catching a 13-yard pass on third-and-four before the two minute warning, and then another 10-yard pass to convert a third-and-seven on the other side of the two minute warning. Moore added one other grab on the drive, which ended with a one-yard Josh Allen plunge. Moore looked good throughout the afternoon, catching six passes for 67 yards on a team-high ten targets. Horns Down: Christian Benford I feel like a broken record hammering the same point over and over, but Benford has played poorly all season. He’s losing in coverage when the team plays man, finding himself in trail position far too often. He also committed a huge holding penalty (that was, if you’re asking a biased Bills fan like myself, not a foul) to negate what would have been a big interception from C.J. Gardner-Johnson. Granted, the Bills defense held the Chargers to a field goal, but the difference between holding the team to three points or no points at all is huge in the grand scheme of a Sunday. I think it’s fair to wonder whether Benford is miscast in new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s defense. He went down with an injury late in the third quarter, and it was announced that he was questionable to return with a toe injury. I hope I’m overreacting to a poor stretch of play, but Benford needs to be better overall. Horns Up: Davison Igbinosun The rookie looked excellent in relief of Benford, notching a pass breakup on the second play after No. 47 left with his injury. He also was strong in run support, totaling six tackles on the afternoon, most of which came near the line of scrimmage. There was speculation that Igbinosun was drafted to provide competition for second-year man Maxwell Hairston, but today, he proved to be a more-than-capable replacement for Benford. Horns Up: James Cook Yes, he had that one negative play to start the game. However, as the afternoon wore on, the Chargers run defense had few answers for him. Cook continually found big chunks on the ground, and he was able to get out some tough yards between the tackles, as well. Buffalo’s offensive line settled as the day wore on, especially in run blocking, which gave Cook plenty of room to operate. He totaled 21 carries for 141 yards and a big-time touchdown in the fourth quarter to ice the game. Horns Up: C.J. Gardner-Johnson The veteran had an interception overturned by a questionable penalty on Christian Benford, but then he made up for it later, ending a potentially back-breaking Chargers drive by intercepting Justin Herbert in the end zone on a third down early in the fourth quarter. Gardner-Johnson’s long return put the Buffalo offense in great position, and it could have been even better had a facemask penalty been called as he was tackled. Overall, Gardner-Johnson was a bright spot in the secondary, which was a positive sign after two weeks of middling play from the veteran. Gardner-Johnson had five tackles…

title: The Optimist: Ouch Town. Population us, bro.
summary: Sometimes in the NFL, a team comes together so completely that they look like they are playing a different sport than their opponents. Coaching decisions are logical and devastating. Complementary football means offense, defense, and special teams work together to smother any possibility of competition. Sometimes in the NFL, the exact opposite of that happens. […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - SEPTEMBER 27: Jalen Coker #18 of the Carolina Panthers walks off the field prior to the game against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field on September 27, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sometimes in the NFL, a team comes together so completely that they look like they are playing a different sport than their opponents. Coaching decisions are logical and devastating. Complementary football means offense, defense, and special teams work together to smother any possibility of competition. Sometimes in the NFL, the exact opposite of that happens. Sometimes, you see both types of performances in back-to-back weeks. Welcome to your 2026 Carolina Panthers. You can place blame for yesterday’s loss squarely on the shoulders of the coaches, of Bryce Young, and of most everybody else on the Panthers. The defense started the game unable to tackle and ended it unable to cover. The offense could get no push in the running game while the coaches stuck to running off the right side for no to limited game. The officials were hugely inconsistent and frequently impactful. Oh, yeah, and right now we’re waiting on injury updates for Damien Lewis, Jalen Coker, Jaycee Horn, and Mike Jackson. We’ll take this in parts and try to find some hope in there somewhere. The injury bug is biting hard This is the real kicker for this team. Injuries happen to every team, but threatening to remove LG1, WR2, CB1, and CB2, from a team already missing LT1, RT1, however you would designate Brady Christensen, RB2, RB3, S1, ILB1, OLB2, and DT2 is beyond the pale. That is Lewis, Coker, Horn, Jackson, Ikem Ekwonu, Taylor Moton, the aforementioned Christensen, Jonathon Brooks, Trevor Ettiene, Nick Scott, Devin Lloyd, Nic Scourton, and Tershawn Wharton for those of you following along at home. Each of those players is out for varying lengths of time, with only Scourton definitively out for the season. It is only Week 3 and ten projected or actual starters have missed significant time, including the same time for much of the last half of the game yesterday. Tha’s effectively half of the team’s best talent, plus a handful of their best depth, that was unavailable to contest the end of the Browns game. We will eagerly await news this week on Horn, Jackson, Lewis, and Coker before judging just how devastating a loss Week 3 really was. Who is Bryce Young? Young seems poised to be a quarterback who can succeed when everything is going well. We have seen too much good football from him to say he can’t play at all. As the most pressured quarterback in the league, his strengths and weaknesses have so far been laid bare and are his to refute in the coming weeks. He is good against zone coverage and pretty awful against man. That gets magnified when under pressure. He can be accurate pushing the ball downfield when he has time. He can be wildly erratic and throw incredibly weak passes when forced to work off platform. The good news is that few teams have the personnel to do man blitzes or get pressure with just four and hold up against the likes of Tetairoa McMillan and, I guess, Brycen Tremayne and Darren Waller. Young isn’t fully “cooked” after one bad game just as he wasn’t “Him” after two reasonably good ones. As always, these things require nuance. What happened on fourth down? The Panthers clearly thought they had a winning gameplan against the Browns and that gave them the confidence to be reckless. They ended the day 0-3 on fourth down. Two of those failed conversions gave the Browns excellent field position that they managed to turn into ten points. Both teams struggled on the field. The decision to be that aggressive in the first half was a coaching error that gave the Browns an unearned leg up and, more than anything, led to yesterday’s loss. What’s next? The team I saw yesterday loses next Sunday to the Detroit Lions before retreating to lick their many, many wounds during their early bye week. Of course, they’ve surprised us before. My current hope for the Panthers is that they can continue to build on Young’s strengths this season, continue to get healthier instead of more injured, and return to playing some entertaining football. Yes, injuries will mount as the season continues, but the Panthers also have the opportunity to return a lot of offensive lineman across the season with relatively fresh legs. That could improve the protection that Young enjoys as the season goes on and lead to more games like we saw at the opening of the season. It won’t be every game. Young may not prove to be the answer long term given his frequently limited play, but we may yet have some fun. The team could even still turn out to be good. There is too much football left to play and too many injuries left to clear up to condemn the season after three games. Plus, you can’t condemn a team that is once again leading its division with a losing record. That’s right ladies and gentlemen, your 1-2 Carolina Panthers are still in sole possession of first place in the NFC South for at least another week. Huzzah.

title: Panthers 18 Browns 21: The offense comes crashing down
summary: Bryce Young and the offense regressed from Weeks 1 and 2 while injuries mounted in the Carolina Panthers loss to the Cleveland Browns. First Quarter The Panthers got the ball first but weren’t able to do anything with it. A couple of penalties stalled momentum, though Bryce Young was able to find Brycen Tremayne on […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - SEPTEMBER 27: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers warms up prior to the game against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field on September 27, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images Bryce Young and the offense regressed from Weeks 1 and 2 while injuries mounted in the Carolina Panthers loss to the Cleveland Browns. First Quarter The Panthers got the ball first but weren’t able to do anything with it. A couple of penalties stalled momentum, though Bryce Young was able to find Brycen Tremayne on a slant after one of them to pick up a long first down. Sam Martin’s punt and a Browns penalty backed the home team inside their ten yard line to start their first drive. The Panthers defense had a couple almost big plays. Tre’von Moehrig almost had a sack, but DeShaun Watson slipped away. Will Lee almost had a pick six, but he couldn’t quite real it in. The defense was able to get off the field and force a punt. The Panthers offense had another ineffective drive and punted it right back. The Browns put together a few good plays and drove into Carolina territory as the first quarter came to a close. Second Quarter The drive lasted for seemingly forever as the teams kept trading penalties. The Browns picked up a fourth down conversion but ended up getting backed back up by their penalties. They eventually punted it away again. Young was able to get Coker involved for the first time and moved the offense across midfield despite a run game that continued to be entirely ineffective. The Panthers were also faced with a 4th and 3, but they couldn’t pick it up. Young was sacked and picked up a little knock in the process. The Browns were able to capitalize on the good field position and work into field goal range with just a couple of first downs. They kicked a field goal for the game’s first points. The Panthers answered with more of the same. They ran the ball three straight times to set up 4th and 1. They went for it again. Young faced quick pressure after play action and was unable to push the ball out to a wide open Tommy Tremble. It fell incomplete for another turnover on downs. The Browns gashed the defense with a few long runs and quickly worked into the red zone. The defense stopped three plays, but Todd Monken elected to go for it on 4th down inside the five. Watson was given ample time to find Harold Fannin wide open in the back of the end zone since no one on the defense elected to run with him. Carolina got the ball back with a minute to and a half left needing to put something on the board. They picked up their first third down conversion on an out to Tetairoa McMillan. A questionable roughing the passer helped the offense move along. Hubbard picked up a huge chunk of yards on a checkdown and the Browns continued adding penalties to help. Young was sacked on third and goal after not throwing to an open Tommy Tremble in the flat, and the Panthers were forced to kick a field goal to make it 10-3 going into the half. Third Quarter The Panthers were called for a procedure penalty on the opening kickoff of the second half. Despite Malachi Corley taking a shot on the first return, the Browns elected to force a rekick. On the rekick, Corley got popped again, this time by Thomas Incoom, and the ball came out. Incoom also pounced on the ball to set the Panthers up in Browns territory. They couldn’t take advantage though. On 3rd and 2, Young dirted a ball to a wide open John Metchie, forcing another field goal attempt. The defense answered the bell and forced a three and out after a Princely Umanmielen sack in which he very blatantly got Watson by the face mask, but it somehow wasn’t called. Unfortunately the offense did nothing once again and punted. The Browns again did the same. A couple of passes to Darren Waller moved the Panthers into field goal range, but the drive stalled after Young chucked a couple of wild deep balls near no one in particular. Ryan Fitzgerald connected from 53 yards for his third field goal of the game to make it a 10-9 game. Fourth Quarter Watson’s play had been deteriorating throughout the game, and the fans started voicing their displeasure. He missed a couple of throws as his offense went three and out again. After the punt, AJ Dillon picked up a couple of nice gains to give the Panthers a first down. A few plays later, Young found Tremayne deep down the left sideline for a leaping catch and 31 yard gain. He converted another third down with a deep out to John Metchie. That was enough to get into comfortable field goal range, which was important because that was the only way the Panthers could score. Fitzgerald made his fourth field goal of the game to make it 12-10. Watson found Denzel Boston wide open for his first catch of the game, and that moved the Browns into Panthers territory. Trevis Gipson notched a sack to slow down the drive a couple plays later, and that forced Cleveland into a field goal attempt of their own. Andre Smyzt knocked it through to make it 13-12. Young found Mitchell Evans for a good gain to start the drive, then Chuba Hubbard ripped off a couple nice runs to work the Panthers deep into Browns territory. Young found Tremble for another modest gain, then found Metchie wide open in the end zone to put the Panthers back ahead. They went for two to try to make it a seven point game, but Hubbard fumbled the ball at the goal line. Watson broke contain to gain a bunch of yards on scramble. The defense made a point to contain him better, and Watson had a hard time finding receivers. He took a shot to the end zone, where Will Lee made a great play to break up the pass. Akayleb Evans caught the ricochet in the end zone for what should have been an interception. Unfortunately, back where Watson released the ball, Bobby Okereke got called for roughing the passer since he caught Watson in the head with his arms while trying to knock down the pass. A few plays later, Watson was finally able to break contain again, which bought him time to find Harold Fannin in the end zone for a go ahead touchdown. He found Denzel Boston on a quick slant to pick up the two point conversion. Young took over needing another game winning drive, and it wasn’t in the cards. He threw an incomplete pass and then a checkdown for no yards. After a third down sack, Young hesitated to throw a deep ball and instead threw a checkdown to Waller on 4th and 18. He was tackled short, obviously, and the ball was given back to the Browns to close out the game. But…Browns are gonna Browns. They could have milked almost all of the clock, but they were called for an illegal formation on one of their runs, which stopped the clock and gave the Panthers a free first down. The defense stuffed the run attempts, including on fourth down, and got the ball back. Young hit Tremayne for one big gain, but that was all the offense could muster. He got hit on the arm on a third down pass attempt, and the ball fluttered in the air for an easy interception. Overall Outlook Young regressed massively from the first two weeks of the season. The Browns pressured him, and he looked tremendously flustered for most of the game. His footwork was erratic, and some of the decisions he made didn’t make any sense. He seemed lost and unsure on just about every play. To add injury to insult, the Panthers lost a number of key players in a game that they were already shorthanded for. Jalen Coker, Jaycee Horn, and Mike Jackson all left the game and didn’t return. Stay tuned later this week for the injury report, because there’s going to be lots to keep an eye on there. The Panthers have a week to figure this out. They’ll be on prime time next week as they host the Detroit Lions on Sunday Night Football.

summary: Well, the prop master (self-titled, of course) took a brutal beating last week. After our typical 2-1 outcome in week 1, we followed that up with a 0-3 burger in week 2. That drops our season record to 2-4 and puts us below .500 for the first time in over two seasons. But we look […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 20: Kyle Monangai #25 of the Chicago Bears runs the ball against the Minnesota Vikings during the third quarter of the game at Soldier Field on September 20, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images Well, the prop master (self-titled, of course) took a brutal beating last week. After our typical 2-1 outcome in week 1, we followed that up with a 0-3 burger in week 2. That drops our season record to 2-4 and puts us below .500 for the first time in over two seasons. But we look to have a better week in week three. The Bears play tonight on Monday Night Football as they welcome the Philadelphia Eagles. Here are three props we like this week. Odds courtesy of FanDuel. Kyle Monangai OVER 38.5 Rushing Yards -113 The Chicago Bears are going to have Case Keenum run the offense this week, and I think the one thing we know is that Ben Johnson is going to focus on getting the run game going and try to take some of the pressure off Keenum. The Eagles have given up some yards on the ground this year, and Monangai diced them up last year. I don’t think Monangai runs for 130 again, but I think he can definitely clear 40 yards. Kalif Raymond OVER 23.5 Receiving Yards -113 Raymond has easily cleared this number in the first two games. While it’s a wild card to know where Keenum is going to go with the ball, I think Keenum knows what a “coach’s best friend” Raymond is, and since Keenum is practically a coach himself, he will look for Raymond a few times to secure the ball when they need to move the chains. He can go to Raymond short and let him work with the ball in his hands, and I think there’s no reason he isn’t up over 40 yards again. Dontayvion Wicks OVER 41.5 Receiving Yards -113 The Bears offense is certainly more of a question this week, so it’s worth looking over on the other side of the aisle for any intriguing plays and Wicks is one for me. Wicks has cleared 70 yards in each of the first two games of the season, and I certainly don’t trust the Bears secondary to be sticky in better conditions. Last week, the secondary play improved, but I’m going to need to see it on a clean field and in good conditions to truly believe in it. I think the conditions slowed down the Vikings’ passing attack more than the Bears did. Wicks feels like a guy that will slip behind Tyrique Stevenson once or twice for a decent gain and comfortably clear 41.5 this evening.

title: Chicago Bears vs. Philadelphia Eagles Game Picks and Predictions
summary: Monday night at Soldier Field is the kind of spotlight the Bears were looking forward to, as this ascending team could gain further credibility with Caleb Williams at the helm and lead the Bears to another victory over the Eagles. But that was before the injury. With Caleb lost to a hamstring injury and exactly […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - NOVEMBER 28: Kyle Monangai #25 of the Chicago Bears runs the ball during an NFL football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on November 28, 2025 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Monday night at Soldier Field is the kind of spotlight the Bears were looking forward to, as this ascending team could gain further credibility with Caleb Williams at the helm and lead the Bears to another victory over the Eagles. But that was before the injury. With Caleb lost to a hamstring injury and exactly which backup QB, Case Keenum or Tyson Bagent, will be the starter still in doubt, the 2-0 Eagles roll in as 3½- to 4½-point favorites. That said, Chicago’s identity is still that league-leading ground game, and it gashed Philadelphia for 281 yards last November. Whoever takes the snaps at quarterback, the Bears will lean even harder on D’Andre Swift and the offensive line. The defense needs to do just enough to keep the Bears in the game. What follows are our score pick, winner, and projected stat lines for a prime-time rematch, Monday at 7:15 p.m. CST on ESPN and ABC. Lester : Bears win a close one, 23-21. Chicago gets back to its ground-and-pound identity, and they establish the run, while the quarterbacking, whoever it may be, is under 200 yards but efficient with several schemed-up short completions. The Eagles try to pick on rookie Malik Muhammad, but he rises to the moment with an interception. Tory Taylor has his banana ball floating around, and he keeps Philly’s returners off balance. Josh : I think the Eagles pull this one out and it’s ugly. Call it 21-27, with a lot of opportunities left on the board. Sam : It’s a tough one. But when it’s likely the third QB who’s playing, it’s hard to win a football game. The Bears keep pace with a strong ground game, but ultimately fall short: Eagles 23, Bears 20. GOOCH : I think the Bears go back to the formula that let them dominate the Eagles last year. They stuff the ball down their throat. Keenum is efficient – even throws for a TD. But the Guy and Swift both score touchdowns, and the Bears rush for 200 yards. Booker notches a sack against Hurts, who also throws a pick to JJ. Bears 27 – Eagles 17. Superfans: If QB1 was playing, this would have been a 47 to 12 Bears victory. If QB2 was playing, we’d be looking at a 30 to 10 win. But with QB3 likely starting, our beloved Bears will be in for a much, much, much closer contest. They’ll need to rally around 38-year-old Case Keenum, get the running game rocking, and have the defense step it up. So let’s call it, Bears 27, Eagles 4. Kyle Monangai and D’Andre Swift combine for 312 yards from scrimmage, Darnell Wright has a TD catch, and the defense intercepts Philly 3 times. Who do you think is going to win, and what will be the score? Tell us that and more in the comments below!

title: Chicago Bears Injury Update on Caleb Williams and Tyson Bagent
summary: We got some good news and some bad news regarding the Chicago Bears quarterbacks today, so let’s get the bad news out of the way first. ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported that Williams’ hamstring is more severe than initially thought, writing that it’s a “Grade 2 hamstring injury that doctors say could sideline him for three […]
full_text: Jul 23, 2025; Lake Forest, IL, USA; Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) chats with quarterback Tyson Bagent (17) during training camp at Halas Hall. Mandatory Credit: Kamil Krzaczynski-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect We got some good news and some bad news regarding the Chicago Bears quarterbacks today, so let’s get the bad news out of the way first. ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported that Williams’ hamstring is more severe than initially thought, writing that it’s a “Grade 2 hamstring injury that doctors say could sideline him for three to four weeks.” Williams has been ruled out of tomorrow night’s game against the Philadelphia Eagles. In Week 4, the Bears host the New York Jets; Week 5, they are on the road against the Green Bay Packers; and Week 6, they travel to play the Atlanta Falcons (10/18). In Week 7, the Bears play on short rest as they host the New England Patriots on Thursday Night Football (10/22). Schefter added, “This doesn’t mean that Williams, whom the Bears have touted as a quick healer, couldn’t return sooner than that timeline. It just means that doctors believe this type of injury normally takes three to four weeks of recovery, and that is the doctors’ best estimation of how long it could take Williams to recover.” The Bears did receive some good news today as Tyson Bagent cleared concussion protocol and no longer has an injury designation for the game. On the FOX Pregame show, Jay Glazer reported that Bagent will be the backup quarterback with Case Keenum starting. “They couldn’t make him the starter because he wasn’t involved too much in the game plan,” Glazer said . Bagent was away from the facility earlier in the week, but practiced yesterday and was presumably present for today’s walk-through.

title: 3 things we learned from the Bengals’ sloppy loss to the Steelers
summary: Let’s be honest. Deep down, we all knew this was entirely possible. The Pittsburgh Steelers (2-1) were a wounded animal coming into Sunday, while the Bengals (2-1) were riding high on top of the AFC North. Now they have the exact same records. Here’s what we learned from a sloppy Bengals performance in Pittsburgh. There […]
full_text: Sep 27, 2026; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA; Pittsburgh Steelers defensive tackle Cameron Heyward (97) sacks Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow (9) during the fourth quarterv at Acrisure Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Barry Reeger-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Let’s be honest. Deep down, we all knew this was entirely possible. The Pittsburgh Steelers (2-1) were a wounded animal coming into Sunday, while the Bengals (2-1) were riding high on top of the AFC North. Now they have the exact same records. Here’s what we learned from a sloppy Bengals performance in Pittsburgh. There are some serious coaching issues You can put the blame for the muffed punt directly on Ke’Shawn Williams if you want. But it’s not clear why he was entrusted with that role to begin with (especially when Cincinnati previously had a perfectly reliable returner in Charlie Jones on the roster). But then there was also a roughing the punter penalty on Cedric Johnson, when going for a block wasn’t necessary. And the Bengals committed another six penalties, bringing their season total to 25. Cincinnati’s offense looked stronger than it had all season, but even that fell apart to a familiar theme (an o-line breakdown) on the most important play of the game. Zac Taylor has a serious problem with finishing close games and is now 6-51 when trailing after the third quarter. It’s not easy to come from behind in the NFL, but this seems alarming. The Bengals are 6-51 when trailing after three quarters in the Zac Taylor era. h/t @ByJayMorrison pic.twitter.com/5M3D3Ly7Sx — Chatterbox Sports (@CBoxSports) September 27, 2026 Relying on the heroics of Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, and Tee Higgins isn’t a real plan. Something needs to change quickly if this team wants to content for a Super Bowl. Dexter Lawrence can’t single-handedly fix the defense Though it honestly felt like that his first two weeks on the Bengals. The big nose tackle had yet another stellar game, this time finally getting official credit for a couple of sacks. Watching Darnell Washington FINALLY be utilized today as a legitimate playmaker was so refreshing to see. Teams are SCARED to tackle him: pic.twitter.com/i8ozTCfRRq — Logan Arblaster (@ArblasterLogan) September 27, 2026 But the overall tackling was back to 2023 and 2024 levels for major stretches of the game, with Jaylen Warren, Darnell Washington, and Roman Wilson all getting receptions of 30 or more yards and Warren also ripping off a 35 yard run. There is no clear favorite in the AFC North Yes, it’s just three weeks, but, to put things in perspective, the Bengals are now tied with the Cleveland Browns for the best record in the division (and, of course, the Steelers and the Baltimore Ravens). At least three of the teams are serious threats to contend for the division title, but, more importantly, all four will absolutely feel like they can win against any of the other three. The Steelers came into the Week 3 matchup against the Bengals with Aaron Rodgers looking like he was already mentally checked out. Meanwhile, Warren hadn’t even reached 50 rushing yards in his first two games. All of a sudden, both looked like stars on Sunday, which is largely because of Mike McCarthy’s game plan, but also the adrenaline boost Steelers players get when they go up against their hated rivals. In case there was any doubt, Cincinnati cannot take any opponent, especially an AFC North one, lightly.

title: Tee Higgins defends Joe Burrow after late fumble seals Bengals’ first loss of the season to Steelers
summary: One of the worst things to come out of Sunday’s loss at Pittsburgh is that the conversation about Joe Burrow not being clutch is likely going to be reignited. With a chance to lead a game-winning drive, or at the very least a game-tying drive, Joe Burrow fumbled with less than a minute remaining, with […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 27: Quarterback Joe Burrow #9 of the Cincinnati Bengals warms up prior to an NFL football game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Jeff Dean/Getty Images) | Getty Images One of the worst things to come out of Sunday’s loss at Pittsburgh is that the conversation about Joe Burrow not being clutch is likely going to be reignited. With a chance to lead a game-winning drive, or at the very least a game-tying drive, Joe Burrow fumbled with less than a minute remaining, with the Bengals in field-goal range. The Bengals had a 1st & 10 at the Steelers’ 38-yard line with 53 seconds left. Burrow was trying to make a play while being pressured, but Steelers defensive tackle Derrick Harmon got a hold of him. Harmon not only sacked him, but Burrow lost the ball, and Steelers defensive tackle Sebastian Joseph-Day recovered it to seal the game. After the game, Bengals wide receiver Tee Higgins vehemently defended his quarterback after another instance where he had a chance to lead the Bengals to a game-winning or game-tying drive but didn’t. “S—t. How many yards did Joe throw for? I think they did pretty damn good. Obviously like I said, man, it's football. Sometimes players f—k up too. So, you know, it's just ball.” Tee Higgins on the last play sack that ended the Bengals hopes. pic.twitter.com/hRyF0FyXvG — Mike Petraglia (@Trags) September 27, 2026 The conversation about Burrow being clutch has been around for several years. In 2021, he absolutely was, with five game-winning drives. In 2022, he led several game-winning and game-sealing drives as the Bengals won 10 straight games en route to the AFC Championship Game. Over the last three years, Burrow has had opportunities to lead game-winning, game-tying, or game-sealing drives. At times he has. Other times, he has not. Is it all on Burrow? No. Sunday, the Steelers’ defensive line finally got to Burrow on the final drive. Burrow was terrific on Sunday before that fumble, completing 28/37 passes for 282 yards and three touchdowns. He also had two carries for 13 yards. Perhaps if the Bengals had been buttoned up in all three phases of the game and better prepared for the two-minute drill, Burrow would have led them on that game-winning drive. Again, it’s not all on Burrow. 2021 proved what he can do in clutch situations. The Bengals were gifted chances to get the ball back with the lead and potentially put the Steelers behind by two scores. Both times, they had a roughing-the-kicker penalty and muffed a punt. The Steelers scored 10 points off of those mistakes. So, while there may be conversation about Joe Burrow not being clutch, it’s worth considering that the Bengals should never have been in that position in the first place if they’d done their job on special teams. We’ve seen Burrow excel in clutch situations before. When all three phases of the game are in sync for the Bengals, that’s when Burrow is at his best. For what it’s worth, Burrow looked like he was trying to make a play on the sack-fumble. Tee defended him, and I will too. Mr. 95.4 Total QBR https://t.co/qSxKrSK3nW pic.twitter.com/qvT9subXw3 — Ryan Michael (@ryanmichael) September 27, 2026 Download the SB Nation app on Apple and Android devices so you can come chat with us!

title: Special teams blunders swung the game in Bengals vs. Steelers
summary: Losing always stings, but giving a game away to the Pittsburgh Steelers stings a little bit more. The excitement around the Cincinnati Bengals grew quickly after starting 2-0, but the team put out a product that deserved to lose this afternoon. The defense was torn apart by one of the worst offenses in the NFL […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 27: Pittsburgh Steelers and Cincinnati Bengals scuffle during the secibd quarter of an NFL football game at Acrisure Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Jeff Dean/Getty Images) | Getty Images Losing always stings, but giving a game away to the Pittsburgh Steelers stings a little bit more. The excitement around the Cincinnati Bengals grew quickly after starting 2-0, but the team put out a product that deserved to lose this afternoon. The defense was torn apart by one of the worst offenses in the NFL heading into week 3 and allowed nearly a perfect game aside from a tipped interception. But the Bengals’ special teams were even worse and killed momentum for Cincinnati on two separate occasions, including a roughing-the-punter penalty and a muffed punt that gave Pittsburgh the ball inside the red zone. The Bengals had an opportunity to break the game open in the third quarter after forcing a punt, but Cedric Johnson ended up colliding with the Steelers punter, giving Pittsburgh a fresh set of downs. The Steelers then went down the field and took the lead, which shifted the entire game. But that was not all. The Bengals defense forced another punt early in the fourth quarter, but Ke’Shawn Williams muffed it, setting the Pittsburgh offense up inside the 15-yard line. Unbelievable…. The Bengals have forced two punts today. They roughed the punter on the first, and now muff the second. pic.twitter.com/YKMlr3umzP — Chatterbox Sports (@CBoxSports) September 27, 2026 To summarize, the Bengals defense forced two punts this afternoon, but the special teams unit collided with the punter on one and muffed the second. Brutal. “We went down and kicked a field goal, got a stop, so we’re going to get the ball back…rough the kicker, they go score seven,” Zac Taylor said after the game. “And obviously the muffed punt led to three. So that’s 10 points. That’s tough.” All in all, the Bengals made too many mistakes and did not deserve the win on the road in Pittsburgh.

title: Zac Taylor has an insanely bad record when trailing after 3 quarters
summary: After starting the 2026 season 2-0, the Cincinnati Bengals fell to the Pittsburgh Steelers in frustrating fashion this afternoon. The Bengals had multiple chances to not only break the game open but to also win it late in the 4th quarter. Special teams was disastrous, shifting momentum not once but twice, and Joe Burrow fumbled […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - AUGUST 13: Head coach Zac Taylor of the Cincinnati Bengals walks off the field at halftime during the preseason game against the Detroit Lions at Paycor Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images After starting the 2026 season 2-0, the Cincinnati Bengals fell to the Pittsburgh Steelers in frustrating fashion this afternoon. The Bengals had multiple chances to not only break the game open but to also win it late in the 4th quarter. Special teams was disastrous, shifting momentum not once but twice, and Joe Burrow fumbled the ball away during their potential game-winning drive. Despite the ugly loss, one stat was brought to all Bengals fans that is even uglier, and that is Zac Taylor is now 6-51 when trailing after three quarters during his tenure in Cincinnati. It is not easy to close out games in the NFL with how thin the margin of error truly is, but to only have 6 wins out of 57 total games trailing going into the 4th quarter is stunning. The Bengals had multiple chances this afternoon alone to break the game open and take over in Pittsburgh, but there were multiple coaching errors that prevented that from happening. After his 51st loss when trailing after three quarters of play, Taylor said, “They earned the win, we did not….We’ll go home and see what we’re made of next week.” The Bengals will return to Paycor Stadium for the first time since the season opener and look to get back in the win column, hosting the Jacksonville Jaguars. It’s not easy to come from behind in the NFL, but this seems alarming. The Bengals are 6-51 when trailing after three quarters in the Zac Taylor era. h/t @ByJayMorrison pic.twitter.com/5M3D3Ly7Sx — Chatterbox Sports (@CBoxSports) September 27, 2026
