title: Lions vs. Jets reactions: Did Detroit show enough improvement on defense?
summary: Both of the Detroit Lions’ wins can certainly be categorized as “ugly wins.” Against both the New Orleans Saints and New York Jets, Detroit blew two-score leads. Both opponents—despite very little early-game success—were able to tie the game up late, and it required Detroit’s offense to take control of the game and the Lions’ defense […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard cheer on at warmup ahead of the game between Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, N.Y., on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Both of the Detroit Lions’ wins can certainly be categorized as “ugly wins.” Against both the New Orleans Saints and New York Jets, Detroit blew two-score leads. Both opponents—despite very little early-game success—were able to tie the game up late, and it required Detroit’s offense to take control of the game and the Lions’ defense to just make one game-defining play. It worked out in both cases, but it’s clear neither win instilled much confidence in Detroit’s Super Bowl chances—particularly on defense. But at the same time, the Lions defense certainly shook things up against the Jets this week. There were interesting personnel decisions. Rock Ya-Sin was sent to the bench in favor of Roger McCreary, and it looks like even Ennis Rakestraw has jumped Ya-Sin. Detroit sent veteran linebacker Devin White to the inactive list, and, instead, leaned on both Malcolm Rodriguez and Trevor Nowaske. And Christian Izien, in his first career Lions start, was all over the field making plays. Detroit also made a some significant schematic changes. Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard cooled off the aggressive blitz packages (22.7% blitz rate compared to season average of 33.6%), hoping that seven players dropped into coverage would take some stress off the secondary. The results were…. eh… mixed. Detroit’s run defense was outstanding, and they did tally five sacks—including the game winning strip sack from Chuck Clark. But Detroit’s outside cornerbacks still could not stop Geno Smith from lighting up Ford Field yet again. And while there were fewer miscommunications and missed assignments in the secondary, there were still too many . Put it all together, and I think it’s fair to say Detroit improved defensively, but not by a lot. The question is: will they eventually get to a point where they are actually playing well. As Dan Campbell pointed out during the week, they aren’t going to fix everything overnight. This is a gradual improvement that will hopefully continue to get better as these players gain chemistry with each other and just get the reps to shake off some rust. On this week’s PODcast, we discuss everything about the Lions’ 31-24 win over the Jets. It’s not just about the defense, but the strides we’re continuing to see on the offensive side of the ball. Jared Goff is off to a red-hot start, Jahmyr Gibbs is still very much on pace to be in the Offensive Player of the Year discussion, and the offensive line (when at full health) is looking much more like the standard that has been set in Detroit. Plus, a few other weapons stood out on Sunday. At the end of the PODcast, we also discuss the pros and cons of trading for Joey Porter Jr. You can catch the PODcast on any podcasting platform by simply searching “Pride of Detroit.” Or you can just listen using the Spotify embed below. As always, if you want bonus content—plus the ability to look at our beautiful faces—be sure to check out the PODcast in its video form over on our YouTube Page and Twitch channel .

title: Detroit Lions grades: Week 3 report card vs. Jets
summary: The Detroit Lions showed incremental improvement in their Sunday afternoon win over the New York Jets. Do they look like some obvious Super Bowl contender through three games? No, there’s far too much work to do on defense. But if they can continue trending in the right direction over the next couple of months, who […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 27: Head Coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions high fives Jared Goff #16 during the first quarter against the New York Jets at Ford Field on September 27, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions showed incremental improvement in their Sunday afternoon win over the New York Jets. Do they look like some obvious Super Bowl contender through three games? No, there’s far too much work to do on defense. But if they can continue trending in the right direction over the next couple of months, who knows? Here are my positional grades for the Lions in their 31-24 win over the Jets: Quarterback: A- Early in the game, Jared Goff looked a little rattled from the pressure, particularly up the A-gap. It hurried some of his early throws and essentially ran him into a sack. But second-half Goff was nearly perfect. I mean that quite literally. In the final two quarters, Goff was 19-of-22 for 214 yards, two touchdowns, and a 137.5 passer rating. For the second straight week, his accuracy was on display, posting a +7.6% completion percentage over expected, the fifth-best mark of Week 3 thus far (MNF not included). Running backs: A Aside from an early missed pass protection by Jahmyr Gibbs, the Lions’ running backs had an outstanding day. Gibbs continues to be one of the most unstoppable weapons in football, be it on the ground (99 yards, 5.2 YPC, 2 TDs) or through the air (seven catches, 58 yards, TD). But this was also a revelation game for Sione Vaki. His pass protection was a weapon for Detroit’s offense, because the Jets defense was relentless in their A-gap pressure. But Vaki was versatile enough not to give away the play call when he was in there. He toted the rock six times in the run game—producing a successful run on four of them. And he did a nice job maximizing his yardage on an 11-yard catch. I can’t help but think about how much of a bonus Vaki’s pass protection will be against a team like the Vikings, who were able to essentially take Gibbs out of the game by exploiting his weakness as a pass protector. Tight ends: C+ Sam LaPorta and Brock Wright combined for five catches and 51 yards, but upon initial viewing, their blocking wasn’t necessarily the best. LaPorta was one of a few players who blew their block on Detroit’s critical fourth-down failed run, and it wasn’t the only time LaPorta’s man made a big play in the run game. I reserve the right to change my opinion upon replay of the game, but I was underwhelmed by the perimeter blocking by the tight ends—unless you’re talking about secret tight end Skyler Gill-Howard. I am also intrigued by the new usage of Jackson Meeks. He played just 10 snaps, but it seems like there’s potential for another versatile piece in the offense. Wide receivers: B Amon-Ra St. Brown didn’t have his best game, catching just four passes for 19 yards and having at least one drop. But the beauty of this offense is its depth of weapons. It’s not surprising Aaron Glenn tried to take away St. Brown, but that just meant feeding Jameson Williams (4 for 49) and Isaac TeSlaa (3 for 66). That duo caught all seven of their targets, and TeSlaa, in particular, came up huge. He converted a first half fourth down that led to a touchdown, and his 49-yard grab late in the fourth quarter led to Detroit’s game-winning score. Offensive line: A- The only reason this isn’t an A is because of a Penei Sewell holding call and a Blake Miller false start. Otherwise, I thought the offensive line was fantastic in all aspects of the game. In pass protection, I would argue neither of the sacks were on the offensive line, and Goff was otherwise hit just three times on 35 dropbacks. That pass protection gave Goff enough time to find receivers on long-developing plays, as well as go through all of his progressions. In the running game, they were constantly moving the Jets backward. The Lions produced 2.82 yards before contact in the running game, the fifth-highest mark of Week 3, and a 56.7% success rate (fourth). Defensive line: C+ The stat line looks better than the eye test. Detroit’s defensive line produced four of the team’s five sacks, but the pressure came late to Geno Smith. The Lions opted to scale back the aggressiveness, blitzing on just 22.7% of dropbacks (season average is 33.6%). That left the front four to generate pressure on their own, and it was mixed results most of the game. Still, the defensive front deserves a ton of credit in the run game. The Jets were stuffed on 26.3% of their rushes, the third-highest mark of the week. Linebackers: D Upon initial viewing, I thought it was a sloppy day from the Lions’ linebackers. Coverage appeared to be an issue, yet again. While this isn’t 100% on the linebacking unit, the Jets tight ends produced 13 catches for 164 yards and two touchdowns. Tackling wasn’t at its best against the elusive Breece Hall, either. Still, Barnes continues to look improved from his 2025 play (8 tackles, 1 TFL in this game), and this group deserves at least some of the accolades for a strong run defense game. Secondary: D Let’s start with the good: Christian Izien was out there doing Brian Branch-like things. He blew up at least four plays on his own by the line of scrimmage, including three tackles for loss. In Lions history, going back to at least 1950, a Lions defensive back has produced three tackles for loss only five times in history. Branch has done it twice; Izien has done it once in his first career Lions start; DeShon Elliott and Tavon Wilson are the other two. Additionally, Ennis Rakestraw finally looked the part in a situational role as the outside cornerback 2 in nickel sets. Finally, Chuck Clark made the most important play of the game, sacking Geno Smith and forcing the game-clinching fumble. But the outside cornerback position continues to be a big mess. D.J. Reed isn’t winning many of his one-on-ones, and while Roger McCreary wasn’t terrible in terms of positioning, he, too, struggled to make plays on the ball. If the Lions weren’t allowing completions, they were committing penalties. And there were at least a handful of miscommunications (still) that resulted in wide-open receivers. It’s progress, and some credit goes to the Jets’ receivers for making incredible plays on the ball. After all, Geno Smith produced a whopping 21.1% completion percentage over expected—suggesting that Detroit was in the right position to make more plays on defense, but the Jets made a perfect pass or an unbelievable catch. But it also means the Lions were in position to make a play and didn’t. Special teams: A- Jacob Saylors finally provided the spark that Detroit’s kick return had been missing this year. Jacob Saylors had returns that set the Lions up at the 38-yard line and the 47-yard line. Tom Kennedy had an 11-yard punt return to Detroit’s 39-yard line. Meanwhile, the coverage units were solid, as well. The furthest the Jets returned a kickoff was the 32-yard line, and they had no returns in the punt game. Special teams only got dinged for one penalty that erased a decent return from Kennedy and a Jake Bates kick that went for a touchback—although he deserves credit for placing most of his kicks almost exactly at the goal line. Coaching: B No real issues with how Dan Campbell managed the game. Clock management was fine, and I was very much okay with Detroit’s two decisions to go for it on fourth down. On offense, Drew Petzing continues to look very promising in the way he calls games. There’s enough variation and sequencing to put the Jets in a bind, and I really like how they adjusted to the Jets’ initial success at a-gap blitzing. The fourth-down run stuff probably could have used a little more creativity in it, but it was also just blocked up horribly. Defensively, at least a little credit goes to Kelvin Sheppard for making adjustments from the first two weeks. The Lions toned down the blitzing to help their back end a little more,…
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Film breakdown: How Detroit Lions’ defense set up game-winning play vs. Jets
summary: The Detroit Lions defense answered the call against the New York Jets when it mattered most. In a hard-fought battle against Aaron Glenn’s ascending program, Kelvin Sheppard’s defense showed signs of improvement after a rough subsequent six quarters of football. Was the performance perfect? No. But what the defense showed was closer to the commitments […]
full_text: Detroit Lions safety Chuck Clark (36) celebrates an interception against New Orleans Saints during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions defense answered the call against the New York Jets when it mattered most. In a hard-fought battle against Aaron Glenn’s ascending program, Kelvin Sheppard’s defense showed signs of improvement after a rough subsequent six quarters of football. Was the performance perfect? No. But what the defense showed was closer to the commitments that Sheppard emphasized this offseason . When asked about his confidence in the secondary prior to the start of the regular season, Sheppard raved about the veteran experience . “It’s at an all-time high,” Sheppard said. “So, the time on task that these guys have had, I think, in turn, when you look at this reverse, they’re going to allow me to do a lot of things that, quite frankly, that I couldn’t do before with younger players.” That vision of utilizing veteran experience came to fruition against the Jets when safety Chuck Clark masterfully crafted a two-play sequence to seal the victory. Let’s take a look. First, the video clips of the two plays back-to-back. The bluff The first play of this two-play sequence is the bluff. Chuck Clark (circled in blue) typically plays as the free or deep safety in Kerby Joseph’s role. As a result, Clark rarely plays at the line of scrimmage and is not typically used in blitz packages. Clark starts the play at the first-down marker and begins to creep up into the box with linebacker depth. Again, this is something the Jets veteran quarterback Geno Smith likely would have noticed given that it is not Clark’s typical role and he did not show it often during the game. Once Geno Smith kicks his knee to signal he is ready for the snap, Clark bails and drops back deep into his zone responsibility. Ultimately, Clark breaks on the pass here, resulting in an incompletion and a second-and-10. The payoff The second play in the sequence is the payoff. Clark (again, circled in blue) starts the play at the sticks before beginning his pre-snap creep into the box. From there, he initially shows that he is bluffing just as he had on the snap prior. But after taking one step back, he begins to attack the line of scrimmage. Right before the snap, the Lions defense is now showing six defenders at the line of scrimmage, including the atypically present free safety. There are two keys to note here on this pressure design that I believe are intentional. First, unlike the first play in the sequence, Jack Campbell (circled in yellow) is showing pressure in the field-side A-gap. This immediately forces the offensive line and running back to consider Campbell in their called protection. The Jets do this by sliding the protection to the offensive right side, with the running back also stepping up to the right. Second, on the play at left guard for the Jets, backup interior offensive lineman Jordan Meredith (No. 67) stepped in after starting left guard Dylan Parham was ruled out with an injury in the second half. This is where Kelvin Sheppard called the late pressure by Clark. Clark blitzes the B-gap untouched. Was there a missed assignment between the backup left guard and/or the running back? Or were the Jets unable to recognize and account for Clark as a true pressure threat due to his pre-snap disguises? “The coaches call line up for me to go get it,” Clark said following the game. “I kinda tipped my hat a little early, but hey, you got to go make plays.” For what it’s worth, Jets center Josh Myers called it a miscommunication . Sheppard was adamant about accountability and correcting the mistakes from the first two weeks of the season. “Tell me what you’re doing. Tell me what you’re supposed to be doing. Coaches, don’t say a word. Let’s let them talk because right now guys, there’s a gap. There’s a clear gap from meetings and practice.” From meetings to practice, from practice to games. The translation finally took hold. “We repped that play all week for that same scenario,” Christian Izien said in the locker room after the game. These are the incremental signs of improvement. While the outside grew skeptical of Kelvin Sheppard during the long ten days between the game at Buffalo and Sunday’s palate cleanser, Dan Campbell stood by his guy. “It was an outstanding call by him,” coach Campbell said of Sheppard. “I’m proud of him.”
author: Anthony Balaj

title: Lions vs. Panthers odds: Opening lines for Week 4 matchup
summary: The Detroit Lions (2-1) are back on the road this Sunday night to take on the reigning NFC South champion Carolina Panthers (1-2), and the folks over at FanDuel Sportsbook have set the opening betting line at Lions -3 points. In head coach Dave Canales’ first year with the Panthers, they went 5-12, but they […]
full_text: Detroit Lions tight end Sam LaPorta makes a catch against Carolina Panthers during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Oct. 8, 2023. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions (2-1) are back on the road this Sunday night to take on the reigning NFC South champion Carolina Panthers (1-2), and the folks over at FanDuel Sportsbook have set the opening betting line at Lions -3 points . In head coach Dave Canales’ first year with the Panthers, they went 5-12, but they improved last season, winning the South—albeit with an 8-9 record—before the Rams bounced them in the Wild Card round of the playoffs. Wanting to take advantage a developing team, the Panthers were aggressive in free agency, signing EDGE Jaelan Phillips (to replace DJ Wonnum, who signed with the Lions) and linebackers Devin Lloyd and Bobby Okereke to a budding defense, then adding OT Rasheed Walker, C Luke Fortner (to replace Cade Mays), and RB AJ Dillon to the offensive side of the ball. In the Draft, Carolina added another starting OT in Monroe Freeling, then snagged defensive tackle Lee Hunter in round two, and WR Chris Brazzell in the third (who is currently on injured reserve). In Week 1 of the 2026 season, the Panthers went toe-to-toe with the Bears offense, trading touchdowns before Chicago pulled away in the second half winning 59-37. In Week 2, the Panthers evened their record at 1-1 by jumping all over the Falcons 34-3, in a battle of NFC South rivals. This past Sunday, the Panthers squared off with the Browns, and while Cleveland jumped out to a 10-0 lead, the Panthers kicked four unanswered field goals to make it a 12-10 score early in the fourth quarter. The Browns finally responded with a field goal of their own, but the Panthers went right back to work, drove the field, and scored their first touchdown of the game, but failed to make the two-point conversion, making it 18-13 with just over four minutes left to play. Unfortunately for Carolina, their defense couldn’t hold the lead. The Browns scored a touchdown and two-point conversion to take a 21-18 lead, then intercepted Bryce Young to seal the win. The Browns laid out a decent blueprint for the Lions to utilize against the Panthers. Cleveland did well to stop the run early—though they did give up chunks of yardage late in the game—and they pestered Young with a reported 29 pressures (per PFF), which equated to pressure on 52% of their dropbacks (according to Next Gen Stats), yet Young still managed to throw for 291 yards. title: Discussion: Do you feel better or worse after the Detroit Lions’ win over the New York Jets?
summary: A week after getting drubbed by the Buffalo Bills, the Detroit Lions had a potential palate cleanser in the form of the New York Jets. However, it was never going to be a cakewalk and the Lions knew that. Head coach Dan Campbell predicted a brawl against Aaron Glenn and company, and that proved true […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 27: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions reacts to play against the New York Jets during the third quarter at Ford Field on September 27, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images A week after getting drubbed by the Buffalo Bills, the Detroit Lions had a potential palate cleanser in the form of the New York Jets. However, it was never going to be a cakewalk and the Lions knew that. Head coach Dan Campbell predicted a brawl against Aaron Glenn and company, and that proved true to the tune of a 31-24 victory. The Lions got back in the win column and now have two games upcoming before their bye, and there are positives and negatives to work on. Some units have shown progress from last week , while others continue to be points of concern. The key task for the Lions going forward is to correct those issues and lean into their strengths. Did the Lions do enough to ease your worries versus the Jets, or are they still a flawed football team? Today’s Question of the Day is: Do you feel better or worse after the Detroit Lions’ win over the New York Jets? My answer: A little better. I think this game was eerily similar to the Week 1 victory over the New Orleans Saints. In both games, Detroit took an early lead, but their opponent managed to claw their way back in the second half, with the Saints forcing overtime and the Jets 28 yards away from doing the same. In both games, the Lions had opportunities to put a nail in the coffin, but miscues (penalties in Week 1, a turnover on downs in Week 3) gave life to their opponent. The reason why I feel a bit better about this game compared to the Saints game is that the run defense looked improved. After getting gutted by the Buffalo Bills in Week 2 (203 rushing yards allowed on 36 carries), the Lions did a good job of stymieing the Jets’ ground game. Breece Hall, a dynamic running back, tallied only 32 yards on 13 carries. His backup, Braelon Allen, did little as well, finishing with just four carries for 14 yards. Yes, the Jets were trailing early, but they had ample opportunities to establish the run game—Detroit shut the door when it mattered. The secondary looked better than in previous weeks— Christian Izien in particular was a revelation —but I am still far from confident in them. Getting Brian Branch at some point would be a phenomenal boost to the defense, as he and Izien would give the Lions versatility in the slot and in the box. Regardless, the cornerbacks need work. The Lions experimented with more Roger McCreary this week, and while he was better than Rock Ya-Sin, he is still far from a permanent solution. Ennis Rakestraw looked solid in limited snaps, so perhaps he will get an extended look in the coming weeks. At the end of the day, the Lions will be carried by their offense, and that was yet again the case in Week 3. Jared Goff and Jahmyr Gibbs have been as perfect as can be through three weeks. The passing attack is diverse enough that they can weather a sub-par game from Amon-Ra St. Brown. The offensive line looked rekindled with Blake Miller back at right tackle. Jameson Williams and Isaac TeSlaa each made impactful catches. Even Sione Vaki was showing up in a positive way. My only desire for the offense is for them to score earlier in games. Against the Saints, five of their first six drives ended with a punt or turnover. Against the Bills, their first two drives combined for seven plays and -1 yard. Against the Jets, the offense opened up with two punts and a field goal. There is certainly room to improve, and the offense has the talent to do so. This win over the Jets was a step in the right direction and an opportunity to calm some nerves after a rough outing the week prior.
author: John Whiticar

title: 4 takeaways from Detroit Lions’  31-24 win against New York Jets
summary: When your favorite football team takes an extended break, the wait to see them hit the field feels like forever. It feels even longer when they lose in an embarrassing fashion. After 10 long days, the Detroit Lions returned to the field, looking to get back in the win column against the New York Jets. […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 27: Jahmyr Gibbs #0 of the Detroit Lions celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the New York Jets during the fourth quarter at Ford Field on September 27, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images When your favorite football team takes an extended break, the wait to see them hit the field feels like forever. It feels even longer when they lose in an embarrassing fashion. After 10 long days, the Detroit Lions returned to the field, looking to get back in the win column against the New York Jets. Here are my four takeaways from the Lions’ 31-24 against the Jets in Week 3. Offensive line rebounds, boosts ground attack Detroit got two offensive line starters back against the Jets, left guard Christian Mahogany and right tackle Blake Miller. When they weren’t playing last week, the Lions’ offense struggled overall, but the run game felt the impact most. This week, the ground game proved to be the biggest difference. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs led it, channeling his inner Barry Sanders on his first of three touchdowns on the day: Jahmyr Gibbs with a Barry Sanders-esque TD pic.twitter.com/QbPYgc0RMk — Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) September 27, 2026 Gibbs remains the focal point of the offense, but it felt a bit more balanced and spread out than in Week 1. He had 20 carries for 99 yards and two rushing touchdowns, while backup Sione Vaki had six carries for 26 yards. Gibbs came alive through the air when the team needed him most, tallying seven catches for 65 yards and the game-winning touchdown. Quarterback Jared Goff threw for 269 yards and two touchdowns, getting sacked twice. One of those sacks came because of Gibbs’s poor pass protection; he was bulldozed over, forcing Goff to move quickly in the pocket. The offensive line was only flagged twice, a false start and a hold, playing disciplined football. Jets EDGE David Bailey came in with a sack in each game and finished with five tackles and one tackle for loss. Tight end coverage issues continue A few years ago, the Lions struggled to cover any tight end they faced. Whether it was the best tight end in the NFL or a practice squad call-up, it was a weekly issue. That issue hasn’t been relevant too much in the past few seasons, but so far it seems to be a problem this season. Against the New Orleans Saints, tight ends Juwan Johnson and Noah Fant combined for seven catches, 87 yards, and two touchdowns. Facing the Bills, Dalton Kincaid and Dawson Knox had nine catches for 100 yards and two touchdowns. The Jets entered the game limited in the passing game, without second-year tight end Mason Taylor and wide receiver Adonai Mitchell. That meant wide receiver Garrett Wilson would be the top receiving option, but rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq would see more targets, as would third-string tight end Jeremy Ruckert. You think that’s it? Jelani Woods also got involved, and all three tight ends finished with a combined 10 catches for 137 yards and two touchdowns. This assignment for Detroit should’ve been easier, even with a secondary that has struggled so far this season. The Jets called up multiple practice squad players to help fill out their offense, and the tight end position hurt Detroit most. They must address this issue in the bye week because they won’t have time to fix it quickly, and they have tough tight end competition approaching. Lions can’t hold onto a lead In Week 1, the Lions blew a 21-point lead against the Saints, and the game headed to overtime, where Detroit won on a two-point conversion stop, 31-30. This week, Detroit went up 24-10 to start the fourth quarter, and while it felt like they had momentum, the Jets stayed in the game. They moved downfield and scored in under four minutes, thanks to a defensive pass interference call on cornerback D.J. Reed, and now it’s 24-16 after a failed two-point conversion. Detroit’s offense sputtered and failed on a fourth-down attempt near midfield, giving the Jets possession with plenty of time left. Reed was flagged again for defensive pass interference, and while it didn’t matter because Wilson still scored, it was a bad defensive call. In a situation like that, fourth-and-six with four minutes left, the defense trusted Reed with no safety help, and that was a big mistake. When a guy is dominating all game long, you need to do whatever you can to slow him down, not make it easier. After failing to stop a two-point conversion, Detroit luckily moved down and scored a touchdown to take back the lead. The defense came up big with a forced fumble when safety Chuck Clark sacked Jets quarterback Geno Smith, and linebacker Jack Campbell scooped it up for the win. Both wins for Detroit should have been less stressful. They had double-digit leads and blew them both times, relying on a defensive stop to get back in it. You take a win in the NFL however you can get it, but, eventually, Detroit won’t be able to recover, or they need to continue to execute and make sure no team can come back. Kick return game comes alive With the offense moving the ball in spurts, the kick return team did all they could to give them extra juice. Running back Jacob Saylors had two impressive returns for 81 yards combined, putting Detroit at the 38 and 47-yard line, leaving them a shorter field to work with. Wide receiver Tom Kennedy returned a kick for 23 yards and another for 37 yards, but a penalty wiped it away. With a strong offense with a lot of firepower like Detroit’s offense has, a kick return game that makes their job easier helps a lot. The offense needed anything it could get to move the ball against this Jets’ defense. They say you need to win in all three phases, and without Saylors’ solid kick returns, the margin for error on those drives for Detroit’s offense would have been that much closer.

Jahmyr Gibbs pays homage to former coach and current Jets HC Aaron Glenn 😂 @Jahmyr_Gibbs1 @Lions pic.twitter.com/7EQw9AlgQG — FOX Sports: NFL (@NFLonFOX) September 27, 2026 “When I saw it last year, it took me a little bit (to learn it),” Gibbs said. “I don’t know why it took me so long.” Gibbs is off to a fantastic start to his 2026 season. title: Packers will face rookie QB Jalen Daniels for Buccaneers in Week 4
summary: On Monday, the Tampa Bay Buccaneers confirmed what football fans expected: Baker Mayfield will miss the team’s Week 4 matchup with the Green Bay Packers due to a dislocated thumb. Bucs head coach Todd Bowles confirmed the injury to the media in his Monday press conference, and said that they expect Mayfield to be out […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - AUGUST 28: Jalon Daniels #10 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers runs the ball during the second quarter of their preseason matchup against the Jacksonville Jaguars at EverBank Stadium on August 28, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Monday, the Tampa Bay Buccaneers confirmed what football fans expected: Baker Mayfield will miss the team’s Week 4 matchup with the Green Bay Packers due to a dislocated thumb. Bucs head coach Todd Bowles confirmed the injury to the media in his Monday press conference, and said that they expect Mayfield to be out “a minimum of three weeks.” Tampa Bay had just two quarterbacks on their 53-man roster, along with one on the practice squad. Jalon Daniels, an undrafted rookie out of Kansas, had backed up Mayfield through the first three games and is expected to start in Sunday’s game against Green Bay, while Easton Stick, a veteran journeyman, is likely to get called up from the practice squad as Daniels’ backup. So what exactly is Daniels? For those who did not follow the Jayhawks the last few years and did not take a deep dive into the depths of this year’s draftable quarterbacks, here’s a quick primer. Daniels is a short, mobile quarterback, who made his name for the Jayhawks as a dual threat. At the 2026 NFL Combine, Daniels measured in at just under 6-foot-1 and 219 pounds, and he ran a 4.65-second 40-yard dash, which illustrates his scrambling ability. Daniels enrolled at Kansas for the 2020 season and he started six of their nine games as a true freshman in the COVID-shortened campaign. He only managed 718 passing yards, then split the starting job as a sophomore in 2021. He eventually took over the starting job in 2022 and despite dealing with some injuries then on (particularly in 2023, when he only played in three games), the job was his when healthy and he stayed in Lawrence for all six of his college seasons. In the 2022, 2024, and 2025 seasons, Daniels started 9, 12, and 12 games and passed for at least 2,000 yards and ran for 400-plus each year, demonstrating his mobility. Interestingly, however, the Jayhawks’ best season in that span came in 2023, the year when he was injured for much of the season, when they finished 9-4 and ranked 23rd in the final AP poll of the season. That Jayhawks team ran the offense through running back Devin Neal, while senior Jason Bean stepped in for the injured Daniels to lead the team to a win over UNLV in the Guaranteed Rate Bowl. NFL.com’s Lance Zierlein’s prospect notes indicate Daniels has “enough arm talent” to make some deep throws and highlights his athleticism and mobility as strengths. However, accuracy and reading coverages appear to be issues, and Zierlein notes that Daniels’ footwork “unravels on occasion, even without heavy pressure.” With a player like this under center for the opposition, expect Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon to get creative with his pressure schemes. Mayfield took a whopping 13 sacks over the first three games of the season, and although he tends to have a moderately high sack rate for his career, a 12% rate is absurd and indicative of a line that is allowing significant pressure. Meanwhile, Daniels entered Sunday’s game against Minnesota late, going 0-for-3 passing with an interception. A quarterback matchup like this could be just what the doctor ordered for the Packers’ defense to bounce back after an abysmal showing last Thursday night against the Atlanta Falcons.
author: Evan "Tex" Western

title: A history of Mekhi Becton, the Packers’ latest offensive line addition
summary: The Packers are making a big move in signing Mekhi Becton, but then again, every move involving Becton is big. He’s a massive human being even in a game dominated by other massive human beings. That’s the book on Becton: he’s monstrously big, but the eternally open question is whether or not he can parlay […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JANUARY 12: Mekhi Becton #77 of the Philadelphia Eagles lines up before the snap during an NFL football wild card playoff game against the Green Bay Packers at Lincoln Financial Field on January 12, 2025 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Packers are making a big move in signing Mekhi Becton , but then again, every move involving Becton is big. He’s a massive human being even in a game dominated by other massive human beings. That’s the book on Becton: he’s monstrously big, but the eternally open question is whether or not he can parlay that size into effective work on the offensive line. It worked out at times with the New York Jets. It worked wonderfully well for the Philadelphia Eagles. It failed in spectacular fashion with the Los Angeles Chargers. What will the Packers’ phase of Becton’s career hold? Becton was a three-year starter for the Louisville Cardinals, ending his career having appeared in 35 games over three seasons. Though he got the ultimate offensive line honor in 2018 ( a specially called big man touchdown play ), his 2019 effort earned him the biggest accolade of his career: a first-team All-ACC nod for his work in the Cardinals’ 8-5 season. Declaring early for the 2020 NFL Draft, Becton was a much-debated prospect. Though his athleticism and physical upside was never in doubt ( he posted a 9.85 Relative Athletic Score ), scouts were split on his technical abilities. Bleacher Report called him “ the biggest boom-or-bust prospect in the 2020 draft class ” for that reason, while Pro Football Network questioned whether or not he had the foot speed to make it as a left tackle in the NFL . But he had his backers, too, preeminent draft scout Dane Brugler of The Athletic among them. He correctly predicted Becton would land with the New York Jets , who took him with the 11th overall selection, banking on his athletic ability to overcome whatever sloppy tendencies might exist in his game. Early on, Brugler looked prescient. Becton appeared in 14 games as a rookie, starting 13 — all at left tackle — and he graded out fairly well, too. Pro Football Focus ranked him as the 30th best tackle (out of 60) to play at least 500 snaps in 2020. That’s not a world-beating ranking, but it’s solid enough for a rookie going against NFL athletes for the first time. Unfortunately, that would be the high point for Becton’s Jets career. An early season injury in practice limited him to a single game in 2021, and an avulsion fracture in 2022 ended his season in training camp. Then, in 2023, Becton had a front row seat to Aaron Rodgers’ torn Achilles tendon. (He wasn’t to blame, having switched to right tackle by that point, but was one of the two players closest to Rodgers when it happened.) Predictably, Rodgers’ injury tanked the Jets’ season, and Becton left town the next offseason, a free agent for the first time in his NFL career. He’d land in about the best possible situation, signing with the Philadelphia Eagles and beginning the comeback arc of his career. Originally signed as a swing tackle option, an injury to guard Tyler Steen opened the door at right guard, and Becton stepped through. The move might not have happened had the Eagles’ offensive line coach not been Jeff Stoutland, w ho’d tended toward playing bigger-than-average players at guard . Though initially skeptical, having never played guard before, Becton embraced the move and thrived. “I’m having fun learning as much as I can about what Stout [Jeff Stoutland] wants from us. He pushes us to be the best, to bring out the best in us. That’s what I want,” Becton said . His size, atypical at guard, was an asset. Center Cam Jurgens, facing the tall task of replacing Jason Kelce, loved having Becton next to him at guard. “Mekhi’s got long arms, insanely long arms and he’s able to use them really well,” Jurgens said . “It’s super helpful, especially when you’re going into the run game and he’s able to put those long arms on people and keep people at a distance.” Counting playoffs, he’d play 1,158 snaps at guard for the Eagles across 19 games, starting every single one. That included two wins over the Packers and, even more importantly, a Super Bowl championship. And his mass paid dividends in the ground game; he posted a run blocking grade of 70.3 in 2024, per PFF — higher than any of the guards the Packers played that year, and higher than that of Aaron Banks, for that matter, then a member of the San Francisco 49ers. Becton parlayed his solid season and Super Bowl title into a two-year, $20 million contract with the Los Angeles Chargers, where things promptly fell apart again. Becton played 794 snaps in 15 games (with 14 starts), but posted career-worst grades overall, as a pass blocker, and as a run blocker. The Chargers cut him this spring, saving $9.7 million against the cap in the process. However, there’s more to the story of his 2025 season. The Athletic’s Matt Schneidman reports Becton was dealing with an undiagnosed torn labrum in Los Angeles , which required surgery this past March, which may explain both why he played so poorly last year and why nobody showed any interest in him in the first waves of free agency. It’s worth noting, though, that Belton never appeared on the injury report with a designation tied to his shoulder; it was only knee issues and a concussion that popped up during the course of the season. I’m not saying Becton wasn’t hurt, for the record, but rather that we should have a healthy grain of salt when looking to the injury as a potential factor in his poor play. Becton is also reportedly down to 345 pounds, which would be the lightest listed weight of his career, but still heavier than any other player on the Packers’ offensive line. The Packers have consciously tried to get bigger up front over the past couple of seasons, and if that’s still the goal, you can’t do much better than Becton, even at a lighter weight. Our Justis Mosqueda identified Becton as a potential cap casualty to watch back in March, and his prognostication has ultimately come to pass. Whether or not the former first round pick can resurrect the offensive line remains to be seen, but as with the Laken Tomlinson signing, the Packers aren’t exactly in a position to turn down any help.
author: Jon Meerdink

title: Packers keep adding veteran offensive linemen by signing Mekhi Becton
summary: At least this can be said for the Green Bay Packers’ front office: they are trying to do something to address the team’s issues on the offensive line. A few days after signing former Pro Bowl guard Laken Tomlinson off the Dallas Cowboys’ practice squad over the weekend, the Packers are adding another former first-round […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JANUARY 12: Mekhi Becton #77 of the Philadelphia Eagles lines up before the snap during an NFL football wild card playoff game against the Green Bay Packers at Lincoln Financial Field on January 12, 2025 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images At least this can be said for the Green Bay Packers’ front office: they are trying to do something to address the team’s issues on the offensive line. A few days after signing former Pro Bowl guard Laken Tomlinson off the Dallas Cowboys’ practice squad over the weekend, the Packers are adding another former first-round draft pick to the roster. Joining Tomlinson in Green Bay will be Mekhi Becton, a six-year NFL veteran and the 11th overall pick in the 2020 NFL Draft out of the University of Louisville. Jeremy Fowler of ESPN reported that Becton worked out for the Packers on Monday morning and then signed with the team almost immediately. Becton has been a primary starter for three different teams over the last three years, spending 2025 with the Los Angeles Chargers after starting at right guard for the Super Bowl-winning Philadelphia Eagles during the 2024 season. He started his career with the New York Jets, but he missed almost all of the 2021 season with a torn ACL. He then injured the same knee in training camp the following season and missed the entirety of the 2022 campaign before returning to play 16 games in 2023. With the Chargers, Becton struggled a bit, but he played 16 of the team’s possible 18 games with 15 starts, all at right guard. Becton also played against the Packers twice as an Eagle in 2024, playing every snap at right guard in the Eagles’ Week 1 and Wild Card victories. The 6-foot-7, 360-pounder becomes a real candidate to step in and get immediate playing time, possibly competing with Tomlinson for snaps at guard. Interestingly, Becton and Tomlinson overlapped as teammates with the Jets for two seasons, during the 2022 and 2023 seasons. As noted earlier, Becton missed the entire 2022 campaign, but the two started at left tackle and left guard, respectively, during the 2023 season. Also involved in the Jets’ organization that year were a slew of former Packers: former Green Bay offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett held the OC and playcalling duties in New York, while wide receivers Allen Lazard, Randall Cobb, and Malik Taylor and quarterback Tim Boyle were on that team as well. There was one other notable former Packer on the Jets’ roster that year: 2023 was the year that the Packers traded Aaron Rodgers to the Jets as well, though his season ended just a few plays into Week 1 when he tore his Achilles tendon. The signings of both players will likely appear on the NFL’s transaction wire on Monday afternoon. Expect the Packers to make room for these two players on the 53-man roster by placing Zach Bako-Bewele and Jayden Reed on injured reserve.

summary: Before the Tampa Bay Buccaneers played the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday in Week 3, the Green Bay Packers looked like they might be headed out on the road in week 4 as underdogs. The Bucs had not been a good team through their first two games, starting out 0-2, but then again neither had the […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - SEPTEMBER 27: Baker Mayfield #6 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers is sacked by the Minnesota Vikings during the second half of the game at Raymond James Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Before the Tampa Bay Buccaneers played the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday in Week 3, the Green Bay Packers looked like they might be headed out on the road in week 4 as underdogs. The Bucs had not been a good team through their first two games, starting out 0-2, but then again neither had the Packers, who fell to 1-2 with an abysmal loss in their home opener on Thursday Night Football in Week 3. But then, the Bucs went and lost to the Minnesota Vikings at home on Sunday afternoon, losing starting quarterback Baker Mayfield to a dislocated thumb late in that game. Even with Mayfield playing for most of the game, however, the Buccaneers’ offense gained just 243 net yards and went 2-for-17 on third down. With undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels expected to make his first NFL start, the Vegas line now swings in favor of the Packers against a struggling 0-3 Buccaneers team. As of Monday morning, FanDuel Sportsbook has the Packers favored by 3.5 points in Week 4. For a Packers team that has mightily struggled on offense, this might seem to be a shock. But the Bucs’ quarterback situation and their anemic offense in general is the reason for this projection, more so than even the Packers’ own struggles. Still, the books expect a less-than-exciting, low-scoring affair on Sunday, with the total points line set at just 39.5. Mayfield isn’t the only key player dealing with injury for the Bucs. Rookie first-round pick Rueben Bain, Jr. missed Sunday’s game with a groin injury, while linebacker Josiah Trotter also was ruled out with a shoulder issue. Keep an eye on Mayfield’s injury throughout this week, however, as he will likely be the biggest single factor for the spread. If he is able to play in Week 4, that would surely shift the line significantly back towards a more even matchup. History isn’t overly kind to the Packers in recent meetings with the Bucs, however. The Packers are 2-3 in their last five road games against the Buccaneers, dating back to 2008, and they are 1-3 in their last four overall, including a playoff loss in the 2020 NFC Championship Game. However, Green Bay did win 14-12 in the most recent meeting at Raymond James Stadium back in 2022. Go Pack Go—wherever you go! title: Green Bay Packers News: Do the Packers actually have some get-right games coming?
summary: The Green Bay Packers have been hammered by injuries to start this season, particularly on the offensive line. That has led to a 1-2 start with Jordan Love taking 8 sacks through three games — a number that could well be more with how much pressure his line has allowed in front of him. However, […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - SEPTEMBER 27: Jalon Daniels #10 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers makes his NFL debut with a pass attempt against the Minnesota Vikings during the second half of the game at Raymond James Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers have been hammered by injuries to start this season, particularly on the offensive line. That has led to a 1-2 start with Jordan Love taking 8 sacks through three games — a number that could well be more with how much pressure his line has allowed in front of him. However, a pair of factors over the next two weeks could actually make the Packers’ matchups with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Chicago Bears an opportunity to get their season back on track. First, both opponents’ quarterbacks are dealing with injuries. Baker Mayfield and Caleb Williams look like both could miss the upcoming games against the Packers, leaving Green Bay’s defense to face some inexperienced quarterbacks. Jonathan Gannon will surely dial up some creative pressures in these next two games in that case to try to force mistakes. Meanwhile, those two teams have some of the worst pass rush groups in the NFL. An easier pair of matchups is something the Packers’ offensive line desperately needs after giving up those 8 sacks, 20 QB hits, and a whopping 37 pressures through the first three games, according to Pro Football Reference. Green Bay needs to win these next two games if they have any hope of turning this season around. Thankfully, the situation looks a lot more favorable for them, if they can get their own issues a bit better sorted out. Injuries Sidetracked Packers; Injuries Might Get Them Back on Track | SI.com Baker Mayfield’s dislocated thumb and Caleb Williams’ hamstring strain likely mean that the Packers will get to face backup QBs in each of the next two games to try to get their NFL Network: Case Keenum expected to start for Bears vs. Eagles | NFL.com Those Bears will start Keenum tonight despite Tyson Bagent being cleared from the concussion protocol over the weekend, presumably because Keenum got all the reps in practice this week. title: Baker Mayfield dislocated his thumb on his throwing hand on Sunday
summary: The Green Bay Packers’ next opponent, the 0-3 Tampa Bay Buccaneers, faced some tough news in the fourth quarter of their loss to the 3-0 Minnesota Vikings: Their starting quarterback, Baker Mayfield, dropped out of action with a dislocated thumb on his throwing hand, according to Buccaneers head coach Todd Bowles. Mayfield went 17 of […]
full_text: (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers’ next opponent, the 0-3 Tampa Bay Buccaneers, faced some tough news in the fourth quarter of their loss to the 3-0 Minnesota Vikings: Their starting quarterback, Baker Mayfield, dropped out of action with a dislocated thumb on his throwing hand, according to Buccaneers head coach Todd Bowles. Mayfield went 17 of 34 for 217 yards and 1 touchdown and 1 interception (along with six sack) against Minnesota, while QB2 Jalon Daniels was 0 of 3 for an interception on a Hail Mary attempt. Daniels is an undrafted rookie, and this was his first NFL regular-season action of his career. For what it’s worth, the Buccaneers’ practice squad quarterback is Easton Stick, a 31-year-old former fifth-round pick who was with the Indianapolis Colts during training camp until the roster cutdown deadline. Stick has only been with Tampa Bay since August 31st. The Buccaneers haven’t rule out Mayfield against the Packers in Week 4, yet, but keep an eye on the situation this week. If Mayfield can’t go, Tampa an undrafted rookie is likely to get the start against Green Bay.

title: Rapoport: Josh Jacobs’ return is not imminent
summary: NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport gave us an update on where the league stands on Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs on Sunday. According to Rapoport, the league has officially filed a Freedom of Information Act request with the Hobart-Lawrence Police Department for previously sealed evidence in Jacobs’ case, where he plead no contest to […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport gave us an update on where the league stands on Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs on Sunday. According to Rapoport, the league has officially filed a Freedom of Information Act request with the Hobart-Lawrence Police Department for previously sealed evidence in Jacobs’ case, where he plead no contest to battery and criminal damage to property in an incident involving his girlfriend. According to the police report, which Jacobs stated was accurate during his court date, Jacobs grabbed and threw the anonymous woman to the ground, resulting in injury. The police report claims that there’s video that was recovered from Jacobs’ garage, where his girlfriend attempted to exit his property, that at minimum shows her on the ground for roughly 40 seconds before Jacobs returns to the scene and damages her cellphone — but the report stops short of saying that it captures Jacobs throwing the victim, as the report is worded fairly vaugely. Jacobs’ camp requested a temporary seal of evidence in the case, which was approved, while the victim requested a permanent seal of evidence in the case, which was denied by Judge Marc Hammer — essentially on the basis that the decision should be made by Hobart-Lawrence Police Department, not the district attorney’s office. Hobart-Lawrence has 10 days to fulfill public records requests for evidence, with the clock having started on Friday September 25th. Rapoport stated: “I do not expect an imminent return for Josh Jacobs. It is not expected to be something where they’re gonna snap their fingers and gonna be back on the field next week.” According to Rapoport, Jacobs’ “potential return” to the field could come after five to eight games of “time served” while on the commissioner exempt list. From @NFLGameDay Morning: The NFL has officially requested to view the video of the Josh Jacobs incident, while the #Packers RB remains on the exempt list. pic.twitter.com/X9MFHPfXI8 — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) September 27, 2026

title: Value of Things: In the rearview mirror
summary: Another game. Another close loss. There isn’t much to say at this point in this particular piece, but I will have a lot to say later in the week. In this edition we always look at numbers inside the game to determine which ones correlate best with winning and losing. We can guess the usual […]
full_text: Another game. Another close loss. There isn’t much to say at this point in this particular piece, but I will have a lot to say later in the week. In this edition we always look at numbers inside the game to determine which ones correlate best with winning and losing. We can guess the usual suspects like turnovers, but this one might be a game where that is not the case. More on that later. As per usual over the last four seeasons, when the Texans come up short it is almost always on the offensive side of the football. Sure, there were mistakes made on the other end and we can look at those individually, but again you had a football team being held to 20 points or less and yet again your offense wasn’t enough to get it done. However, let’s take a look at the numbers. The Key Statistics Total Yards: Texans 51/223, Colts 71/300 Rushing Yards: Texans 21/70, Colts 30/89 Passing Yards: Texans 30/153, Colts 41/211 Sacks: Texans 4, Colts 3 First Downs: Texans 17, Colts 19 Third down conversion: Texans 4/11, Colts 7/15 Fourth down conversion: Texans 0/1, Colts 2/2 Turnovers: Texans 0, Colts 3 Time of Possession: Texand 24:47, Colts 35:13 It takes a special kind of effort to win the turnover battle by three and lose the football game. The DeMeco Ryans Texans have done that on a few occasions and this is something that just doesn’t happen often. The last notable time was on a Monday night tilt with the Detroit Lions. So, while the defense gave up some big chunk plays, I’m not going to crack on them that hard. The Good Will Anderson is good at football. It really is that simple. He tallied 2.5 sacks, two forced fumbles, and had one fumble recovery. That should be enough to lead the team to victory. He has done that the last two weeks. He has shown up to play in each of the last two weeks and made plays. That is all you can ask from a guy when you are paying him top of the market money. You have to make plays and he is making plays. In point of fact, the defense has played better in each of their three games. They allowed fewer explosives than in the last two and held Jonathan Taylor to under 100 yards rushing. These are usually things that lead to victory. It didn’t this time around and that is why we have the bad and ugly categories. The Bad This is one of those moments where I have to decide between bad coaching and bad players. I will go with the coaching this time around. This is simply not good enough. Gaining 220+ yards is just not good enough against the worst defense in the NFL. Yes, you have no Nico Collins. Yes, you have no Ed Ingram. Yes, the other side is paid to play football too and they will make the occasional plays. You cannot continue to simply not turn over the football and expect that to be enough to win. You have to move the football. You have to put points on the board. Great offensive coordinators make chicken salad out of chicken crap. Good offensive coordinators can coax enough plays out of their team when the opposing team punches you in the mouth. This team doesn’t do that. That is on Nick Caley. The Ugly When you say you are a tough running football team you have to get the players needed to be a tough running football team. If you can’t be a tough running team then you get the players necessary to move the ball through the air. It really is that simple. This team does neither. That is on Nick Caserio and DeMeco Ryans. A coaches job is to put his players in the best position to win football games. The general manager’s job is to give them the players needed to do it. You have done fruit basket turnover on the offensive line for three years now. You are literally no closer to getting it right than when you started. Like I said at the beginning, I will have more to say on this problem this week. Focus on Stroud The official line will say he went 16 for 27 with 167 yards and one touchdown. He did not throw any picks and he did not fumble the ball. So, it’s not like it was a crummy performance. He would probably give himself either a B- or a C+ and that would be perfectly reasonable. I honestly couldn’t say if either of the last two weeks really helped or hurt his chances. It’s probably an incomplete because of the ineptitude of this offense. This is where it all depends on who you want to blame. If youa are blaming bad personnel then it is hard to justify giving him the bag because the bag will prevent you from paying others. However, if it is crummy coaching then that criticism doesn’t apply. We will chew on this question later on in the week.

title: Texans Lose Heartbreaker to Colts, 19-17
summary: After all of the additions the Texans made this offseason both through free agency and the draft, all of the offensive lineman that were supposed to establish Houston’s ground game in earnest after years of sloppiness, after trading for RB David Montgomery and WR Kayshon Boutte – the Texans still find themselves in the same […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 27: C.J. Stroud #7 of the Houston Texans warms up before the game against the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images After all of the additions the Texans made this offseason both through free agency and the draft, all of the offensive lineman that were supposed to establish Houston’s ground game in earnest after years of sloppiness, after trading for RB David Montgomery and WR Kayshon Boutte – the Texans still find themselves in the same hole they began the 2025 season with, a record of 0-3. Although, instead of a purely putrid offense that plagued Houston last year, it’s been a menagerie of issues that has stricken the team in 2026. The first loss against the Buffalo Bills was highlighted by great offense and lowlighted by shockingly poor pass-defense; the second game was a return to form for Houston’s defense, but showcased extreme regression for Houston’s offensive line. Now, in Houston’s heartbreaking 19-17 loss to the Indianapolis Colts, the Texans failed to overcome the mistakes they made in the first half and in the fourth quarter. Houston’s offense was as ugly as ugly could be for much of those first two quarters, getting a total of 15 yards on three of their four drives, turning the ball over on 4th & 1 after DE Will Anderson Jr. forced a fumble from Colts QB Daniel Jones, and giving up three sacks. Colts DTs Grover Stewart and DeForest Buckner ripped Texans linemen Wyatt Teller and Evan Brown apart, and offensive coordinator Nick Caley’s aggressive plan on offense led to multiple punts. On defense, Houston’s coverage looked to be back to their old Week 1 ways, with Daniel Jones consistently finding WR Josh Downs for big gains. He picked on Ss Calen Bullock, Reed Blankenship, and rookie LB Wade Woodazz to start the game, which led to Indy’s first touchdown at the beginning of the second quarter. SLAYER‼️ 📺: #HOUvsIND on CBS pic.twitter.com/46vrMHN9PK — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) September 27, 2026 But, on the Texans following drive, they finally got into a consistent blocking rhythm, allowing David Montgomery to get downfield, forcing a few penalties out of the Colts’ defense – including a pass interference call as he targeted WR Jared Wayne in the end zone on a trick play – which resulted in a CJ Stroud touchdown pass to TE Foster Moreau. That score would make it a 10-7 ballgame, and even thought the Texans defense would give up a field goal drive to make it 13-7 at the half, the Texans had finally shown some life on offense and established hope that they might be emerging from their offensive rut that reminded fans all too much of their early 2025 woes. 0-3 looked inevitable in the first quarter, but by halftime, the Texans looked like they might have life….against the NFL’s worst defense… In the second half, the Texans offense returned to the doldrums they began the game with, but now the defense was starting to improve. Calen Bullock’s reaction time and coverage seemed to improve, and Reed Blankenship would cut off a promising third-quarter Colts drive with an interception at the Houston one-yard line! Reed READ that 😏 📺: @nfloncbs / @paramountplus pic.twitter.com/OBYpOL1vQt — Houston Texans (@HoustonTexans) September 27, 2026 It would unfortunately result in a three-and-out by the Texans’ offense (go figure), but the Texans defense would once again come up big time, sacking Daniel Jones on the subsequent drive and giving the ball back to their offense. The Texans would…go three-and-out again, and then in the fourth quarter, the Colts would score a field goal to take a 16-7 lead with 12:43 left in the game. Now, the Texans offense HAD to build off of that promising second quarter drive. This is where a familiar refrain to the 2026 season began to be heard, again: CJ Stroud made some incredible plays to backup receivers Xavier Hutchinson and Jared Wayne, but the Texans offense failed to punch it in the end-zone. They would finish this fourth-quarter drive in a field goal, making it a 16-10 ballgame. However, the defensive-line was now banging on all cylinders and back in their 2025 form, and on the following Colts drive, Will Anderson Jr. would force Daniel Jones to fumble AGAIN, resulting in a Texans recovery thanks to DT Tommy Togiai. Anderson would finish the game with 7 tackles, 2.5 sacks, and 2 forced fumbles, both coming at crucial times for the team. Now, the Texans would have to show they had improved from the first quarter, and actually score off of this turnover. TEXANS BALL!!!!!!! 📺: @nfloncbs / @paramountplus pic.twitter.com/TWdLNgI53A — Houston Texans (@HoustonTexans) September 27, 2026 And they did!!! They did it! CJ Stroud would throw two of his best passes of the day: one 15-yard completion to Hutchinson to the Indy 44-yard line, then a 15-yard completion to Kayshon Boutte to the Indy 27. Stroud and the offensive line were in their bag on this drive, and they would finish it with a Woody Marks one-yard touchdown run to make it 17-16 Texans with 1:48 left in the game: 4️⃣ with the TD!! 📺: @nfloncbs / @paramountplus pic.twitter.com/ONic5M9oPO — Houston Texans (@HoustonTexans) September 27, 2026 Finally, the Texans had started to take the appearance of their November/December 2025 squad rather than the lowly September/October version. An actual complimentary team in Houston? In this economy? Well, unfortunately for the Texans, 1:48 would be too much time on the clock, and when Daniel Jones would throw in the direction of Calen Bullock one last time, it would result in a backbreaking 20-yard completion to WR Laquon Treadwell. Houston still had two timeouts to use, but elected not to use them after a 5-yard run from Jonathan Taylor with a little over a minute left. A quick pass to WR Keenan Allen, and the Colts would score the game-winning 53-yard field goal with 16 seconds left. That would be enough time for Stroud to get his offense in position for a Hail Mary, but not enough time to steal the win away from Indianapolis. And, it certainly wasn’t enough to take attention away from head coach DeMeco Ryans questionable decision-making at the end of the game: Objectively speaking: On 1st and 10 from Houston's 45, the Colts ran the ball for 5 yards and the clock read 1:05. Texans coach DeMeco Ryans didn't call a timeout until 29 seconds left on the clock. That's inexcusable. — DJ Bien-Aime | NASM CPT (@Djbienaime) September 27, 2026 If there’s any positive takeaways from this game, it’s that Stroud seems to be back to his old self for the most part, despite all of the dysfunction surrounding him. Ultimately, however, scoring only 17 points against the league’s worst defense is a profound disappointment, even if Stroud wasn’t terrible. Offensive coordinator Nick Caley will have a lot of questions to answer following this games ugly result, and general manager Nick Caserio will have to do some serious soul-searching as he continues to hit a brick wall with this offensive line problem. The Texans are starting to get their groove back on defense, and the offense appears to be making strides from last week, but, just like the result of this game, it could end up being too little too late for the Texans as a whole. 0-3 is a near-impossible hole to climb out of, with only one of 24 teams to start 0-3 since 2020 finishing their season in the playoffs. Fortunately for Houston, that one team happened to be the 2025 Texans! So, if there’s a team that can repeat history, it’s this one! What do you think of this game? Were the Texans as bad as they’ve ever been, or do you think they’re starting to turn a corner? Is this 0-3 start just as bad as last year’s, or is it even worse? Do you have any confidence that this team will be able to right the ship like they did last year? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below!

title: Horsepower or Horseplay? Individual highlights from Week 3’s big victory vs. Texans
summary: The Indianapolis Colts (1-2) picked up their first win of the 2026 regular season and against their AFC South divisional rival, the also still winless Houston Texans (0-3), no less. The Colts led nearly the entire way until with 4:45 left in regulation, Texans edge Will Anderson Jr. strip-sacked Colts starting quarterback Daniel Jones again, […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - SEPTEMBER 27: Indianapolis Colts cornerback Justin Walley (27) looks on during the NFL game between the Houston Texans and the Indianapolis Colts on September 27, 2026, at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Allio/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts (1-2) picked up their first win of the 2026 regular season and against their AFC South divisional rival, the also still winless Houston Texans (0-3), no less. The Colts led nearly the entire way until with 4:45 left in regulation, Texans edge Will Anderson Jr. strip-sacked Colts starting quarterback Daniel Jones again, which led to the Texans taking the lead, 17-16, on an ensuing scoring drive that was capped off by Houston running back Woody Marks’ 1-yard touchdown run. To their credit, the Colts didn’t quit though. Jones made a big 20-yard completion to veteran wideout Laquon Treadwell, and after consecutive Jonathan Taylor runs, found Keenan Allen for a 6-yard reception that set up kicker Spencer Shrader for the game-winning 53-yard field goal with a little over 15 seconds left to spare. Without further ado, here are our individual performances to highlight, both good and bad: HORSEPLAY Colts Offensive Line: Make no mistake about it, the Texans are a formidable defense foe. The Colts offensive line had their hands full with their front seven featuring the star pass rushing edge pairing of Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter. Jones was pressured on 46.3% of his dropbacks, which was the 3rd most in the NFL during Week 3 t0-date. In particular, starting right tackle Jalen Travis, despite an initial solid start to the 2026 campaign, clearly struggled containing Anderson Jr. in pass blocking. Specifically, Travis surrendered 3.0 sacks, 11 QB pressures, 7 hurries, and 1 QB hit in pass protection for what was clearly a long afternoon for the Colts’ first-year full-time starter at right tackle. Rather than single out Travis individually here though, I was a bit disappointed that the Colts also couldn’t get the run game going either. Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor, was largely bottled up all afternoon, averaging just 3.0 yards per carry on 23 carries, with his lone big run being called back because of a Laquon Treadwell hold. The Texans are really good up front, but even with the mismatch in pass blocking, and conceding that the Texans are elite in getting after the quarterback off the edges, I expected the Colts to be a bit better in the offensive trenches, particularly in run blocking collectively as a unit. QB Daniel Jones: I’ll hedge a bit here, as see below. However, Jones threw a duck under duress that that Texans safety Reed Blankenship easily intercepted early in the 3rd quarter , and had 3 fumbles on the afternoon, two of which were caused by Anderson Jr. strip-sacks (see above) and lost to Houston. It’s hard to simulate being physically hit in the moment, but ball security has been a consistent issue for Jones, even dating back to his days as a franchise quarterback hopeful with the New York Giants. He has to anticipate or better feel that incoming pocket pressure and either throw the ball away or go down safely and protect the football (like Peyton Maning infamously used to do). He can’t put the ball on the deck that many times, let alone commit three turnovers entirely. It’s typically hard to win that way. HORSEPOWER QB Daniel Jones (Contd.): To his credit, when under constant pressure (which was 46.3% of his dropbacks), Jones completed 9 of 15 pass attempts for 115 total passing yards, a passing touchdown, and an interception , meaning he largely performed well when actually pressured (aside from the lone ill-advised thrown duck). Opposing defenses have been bringing the heat against him since really around midseason of last season and forced the Colts to adjust. It was really a mixed bag for Jones on the afternoon collectively, but after another critical strip-sack from Anderson, he did successfully navigate the Colts into scoring position for Shrader’s game-winning field goal with seconds left after two big completions to his wideouts. Colts Wide Receivers: With Alec Pierce out, Downs had a big afternoon for the Colts, catching 5 receptions for 77 total receiving yards with a career high 172 air yards . His teammate, veteran wideout Keenan Allen also stepped up, and showed that he wasn’t two more games from retirement—as it was starting to look the Colts debuting 34-yard wideout had lost another step through his first two starts in Indianapolis. Rather, Allen had 6 receptions for 63 total receiving yards and Indy’s lone TD reception . Colts Defensive Tackles : Colts Pro Bowl veteran defensive tackle DeForest Buckner was a menace in this one, with 7 tackles, 1.5 sacks , a tackle for loss, and 2 QB hits. His defensive tackle counterpart, Ade Adebawore, gave the Texans fits as a sub-package speed pass rushing defensive tackle, finishing with 1.5 sacks , a QB hit, and a QB hurry. That DT duo appears to pretty fearsome pass rushing so far this season. CB Justin Walley: Having clearly endured a lot of growing pains to begin his pro career, and picked on in coverage, Walley had his best game to-date with a number of key pass breakups. He was targeted 6 times against the Texans on Sunday, allowing 4 receptions for just 30 total receiving yards and 2 pass breakups— including a big one in the end zone near midway through the 4th quarter. PK Spencer Shrader : Despite battling a groin injury suffered in pregame warmups, the Colts placekicker was “money” on Sunday afternoon, going a pristine 4 for 4 with makes from 39 yards, 58 yards, 37 yards, and the game-winning 53 yard field goal kick with 16 seconds left in regulation. Shrader not only won the game for the Colts, gutting it out through injury, but arguably saved their season, by avoiding an incredibly challenging 0-3 start that would’ve been difficult to overcome to keep Indy’s AFC playoff hopes very much alive.
