title: How the Colts schemed Laquon Treadwell open for a huge play vs the Texans
summary: The Colts were staring at another close loss. Trailing Houston by one with just over 90 seconds remaining, Indianapolis had the ball on its own side of the field and needed one more big play to give Spencer Shrader a legitimate chance to win it. After what happened in Kansas City a week earlier, the […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 27: Keenan Allen #10, Tyler Warren #84 and Laquon Treadwell #13 of the Indianapolis Colts celebrate after a touchdown during the first half of the game against the Houston Texans at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Colts were staring at another close loss. Trailing Houston by one with just over 90 seconds remaining, Indianapolis had the ball on its own side of the field and needed one more big play to give Spencer Shrader a legitimate chance to win it. After what happened in Kansas City a week earlier, the last thing the Colts wanted was to let another late opportunity slip away and find themselves staring at third-and-long with the season already starting to get away from them. That is when Laquon Treadwell delivered the biggest play of the game, and arguably the biggest play of the Colts’ season so far. On his first target of the afternoon, Treadwell broke open over the middle and Daniel Jones stepped up in the pocket, stayed composed and fired a strike that moved Indianapolis safely into Texans territory. Treadwell wisely stayed down after the catch, something he joked afterward that he had learned from the near-fumble in Kansas City the week before. The catch put the Colts in position for Shrader’s eventual game-winning field goal and helped snap a nine-game losing streak. The throw itself was excellent, but the design deserves just as much attention. Indianapolis used a concept that attacked exactly how Houston was defending the play, and once Jones stepped up through the pressure, the window opened for Treadwell right where the Colts needed it. Dagger Concept Dagger Concept on the big Treadwell catch that led to the game winning field goal. #Colts pic.twitter.com/xvzoz5kIz5 — Andrew Aziz (@AndrewAzizSB) September 28, 2026 A Dagger concept is essentially a go route from the slot paired with a deep dig from the outside receiver. Josh Downs is the slot receiver on the play and pushes vertically, while Treadwell runs the dig at around 15 yards. Against this Cover 3 look, Downs is basically the clear-out route. He does not need to win the rep or even run it with the same urgency he would if he expected the ball. His job is to occupy the deep safety and make sure that defender cannot drive downhill on Treadwell. The safety still has to respect Downs running through his area, and that is enough to create the space underneath. Houston shows a one-high safety look before the snap and drops into what looks like a match Cover 3. The free safety is sitting extremely deep in the middle of the field, while Lassiter and Stingley (their top two cornerbacks) handle the other two deep thirds. Underneath, the safety Blankenship to Allen’s side drops toward the middle of the field, the nickel who starts over Downs works toward the flats, and the two linebackers who initially show pressure bail into the hook-curl areas. By the time Treadwell reaches the top of the dig, there is a pocket sitting between essentially every layer of the coverage. The deep defending safety is over the top, the linebackers have dropped underneath, and the flat defender has widened and the dropping safety can’t get deep enough in time. Treadwell gets to roughly 15 yards, breaks inside and settles right in the middle of all of it. He does not need to separate by five yards from one defender because the structure of the coverage has already created the space for him. He just has to get to the landmark at the right time. The backside of the play gives Jones a few other answers if Houston plays it differently. Tyler Warren chips before releasing underneath, likely serving as the safety-valve option if nothing develops downfield. Keenan Allen runs a shallow cross or drag from the other side, which is especially useful if Houston ends up playing man coverage. Allen probably is not outrunning many defenders at this point in his career, but the route still gives Jones a quick underneath option moving across the formation. The running back is responsible for checking the blitz and any immediate pressure first before releasing late if the pocket stays clean. The other interesting part of the play is Jones’ footwork. It is not a textbook three-step drop where he hits the back foot and immediately lets the ball go. He takes more of a modified drop, with a typical drive step followed by three steps, but then adds a small shuffle to buy more time before hitching up twice in the pocket. The footwork is not especially clean, but it works for what the Colts are trying to accomplish. Treadwell is not a fast receiver, and a 15-yard dig takes time to develop with him running it. If Alec Pierce were running this route, the timing would probably look different. With a faster receiver, a normal three-step drop with one hitch might line up perfectly with the break. Jones seems to adjust to Treadwell’s pace here, gives the route enough time to develop and stays patient rather than forcing the ball before the window opens. Once Treadwell gets into the hole between the linebackers and the deep coverage, Jones steps up and delivers the ball on time. The design creates the window, Treadwell gets exactly where he needs to be and Jones gives the route enough time to fully develop. It is a simple concept executed very well at the biggest point of the game. The Colts did not do much after the Treadwell catch, which only makes the play more important. Indianapolis gained just 10 more yards over the final minute or so before Spencer Shrader came out to attempt the winning field goal. Without Treadwell getting 20 yards on that dig, the Colts are probably asking Shrader to attempt something well outside normal field-goal range, if they even get into position to try one at all. Instead, Jones stepped up in the pocket, found Treadwell in the middle of Houston’s coverage and completely changed the final possession. The Colts only needed a handful of yards after that to give Shrader a realistic attempt, and he finished the job. The difference between winning and losing this game was much bigger than one result in September. Historically, only around 2.5% of teams that start 0-3 go on to make the playoffs. At 1-2, that number rises to roughly 25%. That is a 22.5 percentage-point difference between the two starts. Obviously, one catch does not literally increase a team’s playoff chances by exactly 22.5%. There are too many variables over the remaining 14 games for that. Still, it shows how much was riding on that final drive. The Colts were staring at 0-3 and another close loss after what happened in Kansas City. Instead, Treadwell made the biggest catch of the game, Jones made one of his best throws of the afternoon and Shrader finished it with the kick. When the Colts look back on this season, that play may end up being much bigger than a 20-yard completion in the box score.

title: The Colts showed they have a defense after all
summary: It has been a rough start to the season for the Indianapolis Colts. The offense hasn’t always been the best, but so much of the blame for an 0-2 start falls on the defense. They were atrocious. Like, last in the league in almost every category atrocious. If you watched the game against the Texans, […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - SEPTEMBER 27: Indianapolis Colts defensive tackle DeForest Buckner (99) reacts after the NFL game between the Houston Texans and the Indianapolis Colts on September 27, 2026, at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Allio/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images It has been a rough start to the season for the Indianapolis Colts. The offense hasn’t always been the best, but so much of the blame for an 0-2 start falls on the defense. They were atrocious. Like, last in the league in almost every category atrocious. If you watched the game against the Texans, however, you would have had no clue how bad it’s been. The Colts were so bad on defense they had to change green dot duties after the first game. A little embarrassing to say the least… Games of 503 and 523 yards against the Ravens and Chiefs, respectively, were tough to watch at times. Allowing 41 and 33 points is too much for an offense to keep up with. Yes, it’s too much, but to be fair, the Chiefs game did go to overtime, so those stats are slightly misleading. That performance was at least a step in the right direction after the train wreck that was Week 1. The Colts swallowed up the Texans on Sunday and look like they turned over a new leaf. Yes, this is the same Texans team that only scored 6 points against the Bengals, but they did put up 378 yards in that one along with 381 yards and 31 points against the Bills to open the season. The Colts held them to 223. They may not be the Ravens or Chiefs, but they are no slouch either. DeForest Buckner was in beast-mode, and the rest of the defense followed suit. They were still shaky down the stretch and did allow a late touchdown to lose the lead, but comparatively, they were light-years better than before. So, what’s the real story? Are the Colts closer to Week 1 or Week 3? They are probably somewhere in the middle but closer to what we saw against Houston. In regulation, they gave up 27 points to the Chiefs and were closer to 400 yards. That isn’t great, but against the Chiefs, it might not be that bad. Ideally, the defense on Sunday is what we see the rest of the year. For the Colts to have success, they’re going to need it.

title: Spencer Shrader’s heroics lifts Colts past Texans, snapping NFL’s worst losing skid
summary: The Indianapolis Colts defeated the Houston Texans 19-17 inside Lucas Oil Stadium, snapping a nine-game winless drought dating back to last October and a five-game drought to their divisional rivals. Kicker Spencer Shrader delivered a career performance with four made field goals, including a much needed career-long 58-yarder before halftime, plus a 53-yarder to win the […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 27: Keenan Allen #10 and Laquon Treadwell #13 of the Indianapolis Colts celebrate a touchdown during the first half against the Houston Texans at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Hickey/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts defeated the Houston Texans 19-17 inside Lucas Oil Stadium, snapping a nine-game winless drought dating back to last October and a five-game drought to their divisional rivals. Kicker Spencer Shrader delivered a career performance with four made field goals, including a much needed career-long 58-yarder before halftime, plus a 53-yarder to win the game in the final seconds. For nearly 60 minutes, the Colts made the Texans play their game. Then, just when the game started to slip away, they found one more way to win it as Shrader drilled a 53-yard field goal with 16 seconds remaining to end the NFL’s worst losing streak dating to last season. Spencer Shrader nails the 53-yard field goal to give the Colts the late lead! pic.twitter.com/5DFKtnodPM — NFL on CBS 🏈 (@NFLonCBS) September 27, 2026 It was the kind of gritty win the Colts needed to salvage their slow start and avoid the dreaded 0-3 record out of the gate. Houston rallied from a nine-point deficit to momentarily grab its only lead when running back Woody Marks powered into the end zone, taking a 17-16 advantage with just 1:48 left to play. Colts quarterback Daniel Jones ignited the final drive by finding Laquon Treadwell for 20 yards to march right striking distance. The duo worked together in sync during the two-minute drill sessions throughout training camp, so it’s no surprise that the veteran receiver was ready to step up while Alec Pierce is placed on injured reserve. After a replay overturned a first down ruling on Keenan Allen’s six-yard catch, the Colts faced fourth-and-1 at the Houston 36. Shrader’s winning kick sailed through the uprights, sending the home crowd into a roar that it hadn’t felt in 11 months. He was automatic, making all four of his field goals from distances of 39, 58, 37 and 53 yards, while accounting for 13 of the Colts’ 19 points in the divisional win. 𝓦 pic.twitter.com/eQWu3hUWZd — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) September 27, 2026 The stampede in anthracite refused to let Houston walk them down and repeatedly rushed into the backfield to corral the opposing QB. DeForest Buckner terminated the Texans’ opening drive by sacking C.J. Stroud, then Adetomiwa Adebawore added a sack to end another Texans drive. The Colts held Stroud to just 40 passing yards in the first half and forced Houston into five three-and-outs throughout the game. Perhaps it was the new Anvil Strike Rivalries uniforms that gave new life to this defensive unit, who held the Texans to just 4-for-11 on third down and 223 total yards of offense. Indianapolis converted both of its tries on fourth down, including a first-quarter keeper by Jones that extended a key scoring drive. Jones kept it and ran around the edge, then took on the contact and powered through cornerback Derek Stingley Jr. to move the chains before Shrader broke the ice with a 39-yard FG. The Colts marched into the end zone once, when Jones connected with his reliable target Keenan Allen for a 6-yard touchdown early in the second quarter. One of the biggest flaws coming into the season was sustaining drives and Allen was added to become the chain mover to keep possessions alive. Allen finished with six catches for 63 yards and a touchdown, passing Andre Johnson for 12th on the all-time receptions list. SLAYER‼️ 📺: #HOUvsIND on CBS pic.twitter.com/46vrMHN9PK — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) September 27, 2026 Jones finished 24-of-36 for 235 passing yards and one touchdown, but his afternoon would not be considered clean by any standard. He took more hits than necessary as he was sacked four times, lost two fumbles and threw an interception caught by Reid Blankenship near the goal line. Indianapolis won despite losing the turnover margin (-3) to become the first Colts team this century to emerge victorious under those circumstances. It took extra effort on defens and more toughness from Jones, but in the end, the decision was left to the leg of Shrader, who found a way to deliver the game-winner from distance. The Colts will travel to London next week to face the Washington Commanders at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, with the early kickoff scheduled for 9:30 a.m on NFL Network.
author: Thomas Butler-Guerrero

title: Colts PK Spencer Shrader’s late game heroics hold off Houston for 1st win of 2026 season
summary: Gritty, not pretty, right? The Indianapolis Colts led the entire game leading up to that point, and ahead 16-10, near the Houston 40-yard line with 4:45 left in regulation, the thought was that it was time to finally put the Texans to bed. This was the moment that Colts fans have been clamoring for, that […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 27: Spencer Shrader #3 of the Indianapolis Colts kicks the ball for a field goal during the first quarter of the game against the Houston Texans at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Gritty, not pretty, right? The Indianapolis Colts led the entire game leading up to that point, and ahead 16-10, near the Houston 40-yard line with 4:45 left in regulation, the thought was that it was time to finally put the Texans to bed. This was the moment that Colts fans have been clamoring for, that Indianapolis finally show that “killer instinct” late in games and successfully close this one out in front of the home faithful for what looked like a “must-win” game to avoid an 0-3 start. Instead, Texans star edge Will Anderson Jr. strip-sacked Colts starting quarterback Daniel Jones on 2nd & 10, and the Texans defense recovered (which was Jones’ second strip-sack of the game at the hands of Anderson Jr., both lost). Houston would then march all the way down the short field on the ensuing drive and take the go-ahead lead on a 1-yard touchdown run by running back Woody Marks, going ahead 17-16 with 1:48 left in the 4th quarter. Despite an underwhelming performance individually, with three turnovers on the afternoon (and another fumble recovered), Jones helped the offense surprisingly answer with a big 20 yard completion to veteran wideout Laquon Treadwell, and following a pair of Jonathan Taylor runs, another 6-yard completion to fellow veteran wide receiver Keenan Allen to set up placekicker Spencer Shrader, who was banged up in this one, but gutted it out to nail a 53-yard field goal kick with just 16 seconds left in regulation. The Colts defense held the Texans in desperation, and that was ball game! The Colts got their 1st win of the 2026 campaign against an also winless AFC South rival, even though it unfortunately, looked like the “same ‘ole Colts there” for a bit late again. Hats goes off to the Colts defense, which rebounded in a major way from their first two showings of the 2026 season, holding starting quarterback CJ Stroud and the Texans passing offense to just 167 total passing yards, and their rushing game to a mere 70 yards (averaging 3.3 yards per carry). While I’m not a big time of possession guy, the Colts dominated the Texans in this one, 35:13 to 24:47. As mentioned, a game ball definitely has to go out to Shrader, who was a perfect 4 for 4 from field goal range, as in addition to his game-winning field goal of 53 yards, also had makes of 39 yards, 58 yards, and 37 yards.

title: Indianapolis Colts discussion: Week 3 live chat during the Texans game
summary: The Indianapolis Colts are at home to take on the Houston Texans in week 3 of the 2026 season, kickoff is at 1:00 p.m. EST. The season has not started how the Colts would have liked. It did start fairly predictably, however. Finishing last season on a seven game losing streak and starting the season against two, […]
full_text: Indianapolis Colts mascot Blue celebrates with Indianapolis Colts safety Cam Bynum (0) after making an interception Sunday, Sept. 14, 2025, during a game against the Denver Broncos at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Indianapolis Colts are at home to take on the Houston Texans in week 3 of the 2026 season, kickoff is at 1:00 p.m. EST. The season has not started how the Colts would have liked. It did start fairly predictably, however. Finishing last season on a seven game losing streak and starting the season against two, multi-time MVP award winning quarterbacks, an 0-2 start, while very disappointing, was highly predictable. Less predictable was the Houston Texans 0-2 start. The Texans also started the season against top flight quarterbacks, Josh Allen and Joe Burrow. However, the Texans were coming off of a 12-5 season with the NFL’s top ranked defensive unit. There was plenty of reason to believe, even if the defense took a step back, they wouldn’t give up 338 yards and 28 points per game. A season ago they gave up just over 277 yards and 17 points per game. Further while their offense has had little issue moving the ball down the field, they’ve managed to score just 18.5 points per game through their first two games. A large departure from the nearly 24 points they scored per game in 2025. Join Stampede Blue on game day! Stay on top of every Colts update and debate every snap with other diehard fans. Game-day discussion is smoother in the SB Nation app. Fewer ads Jump easily between conversations Faster commenting and posting Download on iOS or Android . I’m not going to tell you that as a Colts fan you shouldn’t be disappointed. Even though the losses were easy to predict, the Colts brass has set expectations high in a make or break season for nearly everyone who has an office in the West 56th street facility. But Texans fans expected their team to be legitimate AFC contenders and through two weeks they haven’t been able to keep up with two actual AFC contenders. This week is a very rough matchup for our reeling Colts. Indy’s offense will be without Alec Pierce, the only explosive element the offense could rely on in the team’s recent past. Per NFL’s Next Gen Stats Houston’s defense has the number one ranked defensive success rate at just 34.2%. Conversely they have an explosive pass rate allowed of 26.5%, which ranks dead last in the NFL. Which means the Bills and Bengals didn’t have much success throwing the ball on a down to down basis but instead lived on deep, explosive passes. And with Alec Pierce out, I have serious concerns about who Indy will use to stretch the field, to create those downfield plays and continue to stress a Texans secondary struggling to stop the deep ball. Further Daniel Jones has only attempted 14 passes of 10+ air yards through two weeks. Indy’s passing game will not produce if they can’t find an answer downfield. On defense things won’t get much easier for Indy. CJ Stroud is averaging almost 314 passing yards per game but the Texans offense is ranked 24th scoring touchdowns inside the redzone just 44% of the time. Meanwhile the Colts defense is ranked 18th in redzone touchdowns allowed, giving up six points on nearly 67% of their attempts. Something has to give in this game. The only upside for Indy is that dating back to 2025 without Nico Collins (who will miss today’s game) the Texans redzone touchdown rate drops from the mid-40’s, down to just 15%. Conversely if Houston figures out a way to turn their redzone trips into points this week it will be all the more disappointing. Ultimately, both the Colts and Texans offenses will be without their best pass catching weapons this week and both offenses have had successes and struggles through the first two weeks of the season. Houston’s defense is lightyears ahead of Indy’s but neither unit is without it’s warts. I hope I’m wrong about how this one is going to go, but this is a rough matchup for our Colts. Prediction: Texans: 24 Colts: 20 As always, go Colts. title: Jaguars Winners & Losers From Week 3: Jags Deliver Knockout Against New England
summary: How about that for an ass-kicking? After a ho-hum showing against Denver last weekend, the Jacksonville Jaguars and its fans had to spend the entire week debating whether or not this team was cooked just two games into the season. Admittedly, I fell victim to some of that chatter based on how lifeless the team […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - SEPTEMBER 27: Runningback Bhayshul Tuten #33 of the Jacksonville Jaguars is defended by Cornerback Charles Woods #22 of the New England Patriots on a running play during the first half of the game at EverBank Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Don Juan Moore/Getty Images) | Getty Images How about that for an ass-kicking? After a ho-hum showing against Denver last weekend, the Jacksonville Jaguars and its fans had to spend the entire week debating whether or not this team was cooked just two games into the season. Admittedly, I fell victim to some of that chatter based on how lifeless the team looked in Mile High. All the Jags did in response was beat the brakes off of visiting New England , 35-6, getting defending Super Bowl runner-up quarterback Drake Maye benched in the process. Everything that went right against the Cleveland Browns went right Sunday. Basically everything that went wrong against the Broncos corrected itself. The Jags that played Sunday demoralized a team that had aspirations of making it back to the biggest game in sports, doing so from the very moment the two teams both took the field. There’s much to celebrate after that victory. Especially considering it came against THAT franchise. Outside of a dropped pass and a missed field goal, it really couldn’t have gotten much better for the Jags against the Patriots over the weekend. Victory Monday is going to feel a little sweeter this time around. WINNERS Trevor Lawrence There must be something about the river breeze that Trevor Lawrence likes, because he has been nothing short of animalistic when playing in Jacksonville recently. Lawrence balled out against the solid Patriots defense, going 19-29 for 182 and three touchdowns. Despite passing for more yards a week ago (189 versus 182), Lawrence was in complete control for basically the entire game. He was throwing the ball around the yard in ways that he did against Cleveland that not many quarterbacks can. He also essentially opted out of a rushing score which could’ve further bolstered his stat line. In Jacksonville through two games, Lawrence has seven passing touchdowns to just one interception. Maybe it’s the Prowler uniforms. Maybe it’s just the home crowd. But Lawrence is playing some really solid football at home this year. Now he just has to take it on the road next weekend. Most games with 3+ touchdown passes (including playoffs) in Jaguars history: 13 – Trevor Lawrence 12 – Mark Brunell 9 – Blake Bortles 8 – David Garrard pic.twitter.com/b7ZFdnxeKj — Gus Logue (@gus_logue) September 27, 2026 Bhayshul Tuten The beneficiary of Lawrence’s infamous kneel down was Bhayshul Tuten, who has been a sort of quiet portion of this Jags offense thus far. Tuten has put together some bruising, long runs prior to Sunday but hasn’t had a real signature moment. That moment came when he punched in a one-yard score for his second rushing touchdown of the year which put the nail in the coffin of one of the worst losses suffered by the Pats in recent history. The second-year man Tuten led the Jags running backs with a season-high 73 yards on 15 touches. By himself, Tuten came just 10 yards shy of the entire rushing output from New England. He was helped by solid play along the offensive line and a dominant passing game, but he nonetheless played well in his own right. Tuten is coming into his own as a full time starting running back. Early returns are positive for him, even if he isn’t going for over 100 yards every weekend. More touches and more responsibility on offense will probably only serve to help the young starter. At the very least, it’s still very fun to say “toot toooot” anytime he touches the ball. Bhayshul Tuten Week 3 – 48% snaps – 15 carries, 73 yds, TD (4.9 YPC) – 8 routes – 2 targets, 2 catches, 17 yards Continues to be highly productive. Just needs more work to hit on that lofty upside — Michael F. Florio (@MichaelFFlorio) September 27, 2026 Parker Washington If you look at Parker Washington’s stat line and just see the numbers — three catches, 40 yards and one touchdown — you might miss just how good that line was. Washington made back-to-back circus catch plays that resulted in his second touchdown of the season. After making a You Got Moss’d level catch in the back of the end zone that was called back due to a penalty, Washington plucked a bomb of a ball from Lawrence off the ground and caught it across the goal line for six points. This guy is WR1 material. Week after week he continues to make mind-blowing plays all over the field. Chop wood, carry water, catch touchdowns. Which TD catch is better by Parker Washington? pic.twitter.com/FoR45hgvLK — Fitz (@LaurieFitzptrck) September 27, 2026 The Offensive Line It would be hard to give credit to this offense without giving it to the offensive line. The front five for Jacksonville did its job well on Sunday, keeping Lawrence upright and giving the offense enough time to work. Last week, that was seemingly an impossible task. This week against another good front, the Jags excelled. The Jags rushed for over 100 yards and beat a team by 29 points. You don’t do those things without solid line play. For fun, watch Anton Harrison chuck Christian Gonzalez downfield on that Lawrence kneeldown run. Trevor Lawrence really kneeled it at the goal line with over 8 mins left in this game 😂 👀 Anton Harrison just tossed Gonzalez pic.twitter.com/9B6rbcdYEB — Fitz (@LaurieFitzptrck) September 27, 2026 The Defensive Tackles I didn’t think this would be a position group myself or anyone would be talking about anytime soon. But after Sunday’s game it’s hard not to mention both DaVon Hamilton and Ruke Orhorhoro. During the week I wondered aloud if Sunday could be a get-right game for the Jags along the defensive line following a nonexistent showing at Denver. Somewhat randomly, it was the team’s two defensive tackles who accounted for 1.5 sacks and not Travon Walker on Josh Hines-Allen, who I was hoping for big games out of. Orhorhoro was second on the team in tackles with six to go along with a sack. Hamilton was third on the team in tackles with five to go along with half a sack and a fumble recovery. These two dudes were in the middle of everything New England was doing and were a large part of the troubles the Patriots offense was experiencing. The Pats have solid running backs, but ended the days with 83 yards on the ground and no run longer than nine yards. Cleveland and Denver both rushed for more yardage than New England was able to muster Sunday. A big reason why things changed was the big nasties in the middle. The whole defense played great. But a special shoutout has to go to the guys in the middle for getting the work done. Ruke Orhorhoro said he knew this one could be different from the first practice of the week. 💪🏈 #jaguars #duuuva pic.twitter.com/Gt0ZDyanU5 — Action Sports Jax (@ActionSportsJax) September 27, 2026 Liam Coen Though Coen will probably never say it aloud, it has to feel good to beat the piss out of the guy that stole Coach of the Year honors away from you last season. In all facets, Coen’s team dogwalked Vrabel’s. The Jags were leaps and bounds more put together than New England. Neither team played a truly clean game, but Jacksonville did commit less penalties and turned the ball over fewer times. The coach whose team does that typically wins. Coen is the fastest coach in franchise history to reach 15 wins, doing so in just 20 games. That is absolutely bananas to think about considering how many coaches the Jags have had through the years. This team found the right guy. In turn, he is putting the right product on the field. Let him tell you just how well his team played in this clip: That one feels good, Coach 🔥 pic.twitter.com/vNiuMCz7XT — Jacksonville Jaguars (@Jaguars) September 27, 2026 Josh Cameron I’m not sure that when you look at the Jags’ roster, you see a glaring need for wide receiver. Take into account…

title: 3 Reasons Why the Jacksonville Jaguars Beat the New England Patriots
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars needed a response. A week after letting a game slip away in Denver, Liam Coen’s team returned home to face the defending AFC champions with a fairly simple challenge: prove that the 20-13 loss to the Broncos was a stumble rather than a sign of things to come. They did considerably more […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - SEPTEMBER 27: Trevor Lawrence #16 of the Jacksonville Jaguars throws a pass against the New England Patriots during the first quarter at EverBank Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Rich Storry/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jacksonville Jaguars needed a response. A week after letting a game slip away in Denver, Liam Coen’s team returned home to face the defending AFC champions with a fairly simple challenge: prove that the 20-13 loss to the Broncos was a stumble rather than a sign of things to come. They did considerably more than that. The Jaguars dismantled the New England Patriots 35-6 on Sunday, turning what initially looked like a competitive game into a procession after halftime. The Patriots were held without a touchdown, Drake Maye was responsible for three turnovers, and Jacksonville scored 28 unanswered points after New England’s second field goal. The Jaguars are now 2-1, have won 10 of their last 11 regular-season games and have won six straight at EverBank Stadium. There were plenty of individual performances worthy of praise, but three things in particular explain why this became such a one-sided afternoon. Trevor Lawrence and Liam Coen are in lockstep "We just trusted our plan…when you have confidence in what you're doing and the guys around you, you can make some pretty cool plays." Trevor Lawrence after the Jaguars beat the Patriots 35-6 🎤: @AKinkhabwala pic.twitter.com/Ob0yM2u71f — NFL on CBS 🏈 (@NFLonCBS) September 27, 2026 There is a difference between a quarterback playing well and a quarterback looking completely synchronized with his offensive system. Trevor Lawrence looked like the latter on Sunday. The numbers themselves are solid rather than spectacular: 19-of-29 for 182 yards and three touchdowns. The significance was in the timing. Jacksonville’s first touchdown came after DaVon Hamilton recovered Drake Maye’s fumble, with Lawrence immediately hitting rookie Josh Cameron for 12 yards. The drive was kept alive by an 18-yard completion to Parker Washington on third-and-5, and Lawrence was consistently making the throws Coen’s offense needed him to make. The most telling sequence came after New England finally got a break. Marcus Jones intercepted Lawrence’s pass after it deflected off Brenton Strange’s hands, giving the Patriots possession at the Jacksonville 21-yard line. New England converted that mistake into a field goal and suddenly had the deficit down to 7-3. Lawrence’s response was exactly what you want from a franchise quarterback. Jacksonville went 65 yards in nine plays, and Lawrence finished the drive by finding Jakobi Meyers for a 10-yard touchdown. No panic, no attempt to manufacture something spectacular, just an immediate answer. That touchdown also moved Lawrence past Blake Bortles into second place on the Jaguars’ all-time touchdown passing list, with 104. Then came the dagger. A 15-play, 72-yard drive consumed 8:42 of the third quarter, and Lawrence eventually found Washington for a remarkable 17-yard touchdown catch from the 17-yard line. It was the sort of drive that demonstrates the relationship between quarterback and play-caller: Coen kept asking the Patriots defense questions, and Lawrence kept giving him the right answers. This isn’t about Lawrence “silencing doubters.” That storyline has become increasingly tired. It’s about a quarterback and a coach who appear to be seeing the same game. On Sunday, they were in lockstep. The Jaguars’ defense made every Patriots mistake hurt TRAVIS HUNTER INT ALERT 🚨 @NEvsJAX on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/wILwED2EBi — NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026 Jacksonville’s defense did not need to produce a 2017 AFC Championship-style spectacle. There was no need for a repeat of ‘Myles Jack wasn’t down’. It simply needed to make New England pay whenever an opportunity presented itself. It did exactly that. The first opportunity arrived late in the opening quarter, when Maye lost the football attempting to throw. Hamilton recovered at the Jacksonville 38, and the Jaguars turned the turnover into seven points. That was the first of three takeaways, and each one helped Jacksonville take control of the game. The most spectacular came from Travis Hunter. With New England driving before halftime and looking for a way back into the game, Hunter intercepted Maye in the end zone with 1:02 remaining. It was Hunter’s first career interception and, more importantly, it erased New England’s best opportunity to turn the momentum before the break. Instead of potentially entering halftime with Jacksonville’s lead under pressure, the Jaguars walked into the locker room up 14-3. Hunter’s usage has been the subject of much debate in Duval County; a timely big play from a player the Jags invested a lot of draft capital into will do wonders for the second-year star’s confidence. Then, just when the Patriots needed to respond in the second half, Jacksonville delivered another knockout blow. Washington’s touchdown gave the Jaguars a 21-3 lead, and on the very next New England snap, Jarrian Jones intercepted Maye and returned it 32 yards. Fifty seconds later, Chris Rodriguez Jr. was in the end zone from five yards out. That’s how a 21-3 lead became 28-3 in the space of 18 seconds of game clock. There was substance behind the opportunism, too. Jacksonville recorded three sacks, with Ruke Orhorhoro getting home in the second quarter and rookie Bryan Thomas Jr. sharing a third-quarter sack with DaVon Hamilton. Maye finished 14-of-25 for 199 yards, no touchdowns and two interceptions, while his lost fumble directly produced Jacksonville’s opening touchdown. The Jaguars didn’t merely stop New England. They punished every mistake the Patriots gave them, and that is how a close game becomes a blowout. Bhayshul Tuten has taken ownership of the backfield Bhayshul Tuten runs it in for SIX! @NEvsJAX on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/O7aXXws1Rp — NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026 There was a legitimate question hanging over Jacksonville’s running game entering the season. Travis Etienne was gone, and the Jaguars needed someone to turn a committee into a functioning backfield. Through three weeks, Bhayshul Tuten is making a very convincing case that he should be that someone. Tuten carried 28 times for 131 yards through the opening two games, and against a Patriots defense that had not allowed a 100-yard rusher during the first two weeks of the season, he continued to get the work. He finished Sunday with 15 carries for 73 yards and a touchdown, averaging 4.9 yards per carry. Make the SB Nation app part of Jaguars game day! New to Big Cat Country? It’s SB Nation’s home for Jaguars fans. Use the app’s NEW game chat to discuss every big play with fans across Duval. Fewer ads Faster commenting and posting Easy access to communities and conversations Download on iOS or Android . The important part wasn’t simply the production. It was the way Jacksonville used the run to control the game once it had established the lead. Tuten repeatedly kept the offense ahead of the chains, allowing Coen to stay patient rather than asking Lawrence to win every possession through the air. That became particularly valuable in the second half. Jacksonville’s 15-play touchdown drive was not built around one explosive play. It was a sustained march that ate more than eight minutes from the clock and ended with Washington’s touchdown. When New England eventually got the ball back, the game was already beginning to disappear. And then, with the Patriots having finally managed to cut the deficit from 28-3 to 28-6, Tuten put the final punctuation mark on the afternoon. He took the ball in from one yard out with 8:02 remaining, pushing Jacksonville’s advantage back to 35-6 and removing any remaining doubt about the outcome. Tuten wasn’t the only Jacksonville back to contribute — Chris Rodriguez also scored — but the distribution of the workload…

title: Jaguars Hand Patriots Its Worst Loss Since 2024
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars had something to prove following their Week 2 road loss to the Denver Broncos. They did that and then some, proving they belong with a dominant, 29-point blowout of the reigning AFC Super Bowl runner-up, the New England Patriots. Trevor Lawrence had an efficient day, spreading the ball to nine different pass […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - SEPTEMBER 27: Trevor Lawrence #16 of the Jacksonville Jaguars throws a pass during the game between the Jacksonville Jaguars and the New England Patriots on September 27, 2026 at EverBank Stadium in Jacksonville, Fl. (Photo by David Rosenblum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Jacksonville Jaguars had something to prove following their Week 2 road loss to the Denver Broncos. They did that and then some, proving they belong with a dominant, 29-point blowout of the reigning AFC Super Bowl runner-up, the New England Patriots. Trevor Lawrence had an efficient day, spreading the ball to nine different pass catchers, while the defense completely shut the Patriots out of the end zone. Here’s everything you need to know from Jacksonville’s Week 3, 35-6 home domination of the New England Patriots. In Case You Missed It After both teams’ early defensive success, which included three consecutive punts, Patriots quarterback Drake Maye made the day’s first mistake. With the Patriots moving down the field into scoring range, Maye turned the ball over, fumbling it back to Jacksonville to end the drive. On 1st and 10 from Jacksonville's 35, Drake May Will Levis's it, fumbling the ball back to Jacksonville while resting in a clean pocket for the game's first turnover pic.twitter.com/IXCsOIYOoO — 𝕋𝕣𝕒𝕧𝕚𝕤 🅓. ℍ𝕠𝕝𝕞𝕖𝕤 (@TravisDHolmes) September 27, 2026 After the turnover, the Jacksonville offense put together the game’s first score on a 10-play, 62-yard, 5:27 drive, highlighted by explosive catches from Parker Washington (18 yards) and Josh Cameron’s 12-yard touchdown catch . However, the first-half turnovers didn’t just belong to Maye, as one series later, Lawrence’s pass to Brenton Strange was dropped/deflected by the tight end and intercepted by New England cornerback Marcus Jones. The turnover in their own end of the field cost Jacksonville just three points, with the defense holding New England to just three yards on the drive, however. Marcus Jones snags the INT for the @Patriots ! @NEvsJAX on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/zqdcfMuhxV — NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026 The Jacksonville offense picked up where it left off before the turnover, putting together a nine-play, 62-yard touchdown drive highlighted by a 23-yard Brenton Strange catch and capped by Jakobi Meyer’s redzone touchdown. What a DOT 🎯 #NEvsJAX on CBS & @paramountplus pic.twitter.com/c4khecQOX1 — Jacksonville Jaguars (@Jaguars) September 27, 2026 New England, driving to the Jacksonville two-yard line, looked ready to cut the Jaguars’ lead to one possession when Maye suffered his second turnover of the first half – this one, a third-down, redzone, attempt directly to cornerback Travis Hunter. This was Hunter’s first career interception, saving a touchdown. Jacksonville was unable to turn the ensuing drive into points, as Cam Little’s 70-yard field goal with time expiring sailed wide right. However, the kick, against the wind, somehow still had the length. QB Trevor Lawrence ended the half 13-for-20 with 111 yards, two touchdowns, and 1 interception (91.9 passer rating). RB Bhayshul Tuten had 8 carries for 48 yards (6.0 per carry). Notable Halftime Stats: Score: 14-3 Jacksonville Third & Fourth Down Offense: 33% Patriots (2/6) vs 50% Jaguars (3/6) Defensive Sacks: 2-0 Jacksonville Turnovers forced: 2-1 Jacksonville Rushing yards: 69 to 54 Jacksonville Passing yards: 111 to 101 Jacksonville Redzone: 100% (2/2) Jacksonville to 0% (0/2) Patriots Points off turnovers: 7-3 Jacksonville Following the half, New England’s day of mistakes continued, to the joy of the Jaguar faithful. After a 10-play, 42-yard drive, Patriots kicker Andy Borregales missed a chip-shot 38-yard kick. The Jaguars’ offense continued their onslaught, compiling a 15-play, 72-yard drive capped by an impossible 17-yard Parker Washington catch while being interfered with. Immediately following the ensuing kickoff, cornerback Jarrian Jones continued the turnover party, securing his first interception of the year. Chris Rodriguez scored on a five-yard rush on the next play. This score resulted in a 28-3 lead and effectively sealed the Jacksonville victory. . @Jaguars with another INT 🔥 @NEvsJAX on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/h2HW8rZ2oZ — NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026 Game balls: Special Teams: WR Josh Cameron: 42-yard kick return, plus a kickoff coverage tackle one play after his receiving touchdown Defense: DT Davon Hamilton: 5 tackles, 3 solo, 1 sack, 1 fumble forced, 1 fumble recovery while helping the defense hold Treveyon Henderson and Rhamondre Stevenson to 2.9 and 3.1 yards per carry. Offense: QB Trevor Lawrence: 19/29 for 182 yards, 6.3 average, 3 touchdowns, 1 interception, 102.9 passer rating. As efficient as he could be, this was essentially a four-touchdown day, as Lawrence purposefully stopped short of scoring in the fourth quarter. Tuten scored on the following snap. Post-game notables: 1. Dominant in Duval While Sunday’s matchup may not have been perfect, it would be hard to identify a more dominant Week 3 performance on the scoreboard, as the Jacksonville defense consistently gave New England quarterback Drake Maye fits in the secondary. While the pass rush occasionally gave Maye slightly more time to scan the field when rushing four, the back end forced two interceptions, with Maye surrendering a third unforced turnover. Offensively, Jacksonville did what good teams do, capitalizing on a struggling opponent’s mistakes. The Jaguars won the turnover battle while also winning in points off turnovers, 14-3. 2. BTJ Moving Down The Depth Chart? Rookie receiver Josh Cameron notably received many of the opening-half third-receiver snaps over third-year, 2024 rookie-of-the-year finalist Brian Thomas Jr. following a rough Week 2 performance featuring two dropped passes. Meanwhile, Cameron secured his second career red zone touchdown against the Patriots, entrenching himself as a bona fide red zone target for this offense. Meanwhile, Thomas received just one target against New England, an eight-yard catch. 3. Hunter makes his mark Travis Hunter’s day started off rough with the second-year dual-threat athlete surrendering an opening-drive 21-yard catch to Patriots receiver Mack Hollins. However, on a day when he noticeably played more snaps than in prior weeks on defense, he also secured his first career interception. title: Andy Reid points out Chiefs’ offense didn’t have a ton of plays in Miami
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs’ offense was clicking on all cylinders against the Miami Dolphins, averaging over seven yards per play for most of the game and opening things up for quarterback Patrick Mahomes to deliver an incredibly efficient performance. The performance may have been masked by the 24 points on Kansas City’s side of the […]
full_text: (Photo by Chris Arjoon/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images). | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs ’ offense was clicking on all cylinders against the Miami Dolphins , averaging over seven yards per play for most of the game and opening things up for quarterback Patrick Mahomes to deliver an incredibly efficient performance. Patrick Mahomes had an 83.3% completion percentage against the Dolphins in Week 3 His 20/24 performance is his highest single game completion percentage since Week 15 of 2022, per @SumerSports — Shawn Syed (@SyedSchemes) September 27, 2026 The performance may have been masked by the 24 points on Kansas City’s side of the scoreboard, an underwhelming total considering how easy things looked for the Chiefs’ offense at times. On Monday, head coach Andy Reid answered questions from reporters on a video conference call. He shared a reason Kansas City couldn’t match the scoring outputs of Weeks 1 and 2. “I thought we handled the pass game pretty well,” Reid said. “We didn’t have a ton of plays; we were in the 40s on that, and normally you’re up a little higher in the 60 or 70 area.” Time of possession was key for the underdog Dolphins to stay in the fight. Miami had nearly 10 more minutes with the ball. Still, the Chiefs’ offense finished enough of the opportunities given to win by two touchdowns. “I thought the way it balanced out… [Kenneth Walker] was still able to have a productive day in the run game and the pass game,” Reid continued. “But it opened up some things in the pass game that we were able to take advantage of with some bigger plays.” Reid shared a note on the team’s top two wideouts by snap count: Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy. The former had a game-high seven catches for 88 yards with 55 coming after the catch. “It was good to see him get a couple of catches in there that were physical, good, strong catches,” Reid said about Rice. “He is so good with the ball after he gets it and so physical… It’s almost like having a running back at a wide receiver spot where, when he gets it, he’s going to bring it, and that’s always good.” Worthy, leading the team in snaps for the second consecutive week, had just one highlight: a 17-yard completion on the sideline. “He had one that was sort of an intermediate throw there, and he did a nice job with it,” Reid reflected. “We’ll just see how it all works out for him as we go forward. He’s busting his tail, and I think, every week, he’s feeling better with the shoulder issue and doing a good job there.” Speaking of feeling better, it’s hard to imagine Mahomes is yet after a penalty for roughing the passer was called on Dolphins edge rusher Chop Robinson for an obliteration of a hit. The quarterback is likely sore today, but it didn’t seem to slow him down for long on Sunday. “It was more than a chiropractor could do,” Reid joked. “I think every bone in his body cracked on that one, but he got back up and kept firing.”

title: Chiefs Week 3 snap count analysis: L’Jarius Sneed, the blitzer
summary: Welcome to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis! So let’s see what we can figure out about the Kansas City Chiefs when taking a closer look at playing time during the 24-10 win over the Miami Dolphins in Week 3. The starting lineups are courtesy of NFL Game Stats and Information, and the snap-count data comes […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis! So let’s see what we can figure out about the Kansas City Chiefs when taking a closer look at playing time during the 24-10 win over the Miami Dolphins in Week 3. The starting lineups are courtesy of NFL Game Stats and Information, and the snap-count data comes from Pro Football Focus’ premium stats. Starters (offensive): LT Kahlil Benson, LG Kingsley Suamataia, C Creed Humphrey, RG Trey Smith, RT Jaylon Moore, QB Patrick Mahomes, WR Tyquan Thornton, RB Kenneth Walker, TE Travis Kelce, TE Noah Gray and TE Jake Briningstool. Starters (defensive): DE George Karlaftis, DT Chris Jones, DT Khyiris Tonga, DE Felix Anudike-Uzomah, LB Nick Bolton, LB Drue Tranquill, LB Jack Cochrane, CB Mansoor Delane, CB L’Jarius Sneed, S Alohi Gilman and S Jaden Hicks Did not play: CB Kristian Fulton, QB Justin Fields Inactive: TE Jared Wiley, QB Garrett Nussmeier (Emergency third QB), S Chamarri Conner (Knee), DE Jack Pyburn, DE Tyreke Smith, OT Diego Pounds, LT Josh Simmons (Back) The big takeaway: L’Jarius Sneed’s playmaking utilized The Chiefs’ main trio of cornerbacks in Miami featured rookie Mansoor Delane, Nohl Williams and L’Jarius Sneed. 33 of Sneed’s 53 snaps were aligned in the slot. On seven plays, Sneed was sent after the quarterback as a blitzer, according to Pro Football Focus . NFL Next Gen Stats credited Sneed with five quarterback pressures, a career-high mark for the seventh-year defensive back. He also caused a turnover that was pivotal in the Chiefs securing victory on Sunday in Miami. Defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo wants Sneed on the field for a reason, and it mostly has to do with his playmaking around the ball. The Offensive takeaway: (Some of) The Auxiliary receivers step up Tight end Noah Gray played the fewest offensive snaps (33) he has in any game this season against the Dolphins, but he saw the second-most catches (3) on the team, including a 24-yard reception on the sideline that put the Chiefs in the red zone late in the contest. His young teammate at the position, second-year tight end Jake Briningstool, earned his first career start by taking the field on the first play of the game. Kansas City presented a 13-personnel set that featured Kelce, Gray and Briningstool on the field at the same time, setting up a play-action pass to Kelce. He played six snaps. Second-year wide receiver Jalen Royals made his season debut last week against the Indianapolis Colts and played two more snaps than he did in Miami (10), but Royals recorded a catch for 11 yards that moved the chains for the Chiefs in the second half. It was good to see the offense get impactful plays from the pass catchers below quarterback Patrick Mahomes’ top shelf of playmakers. However, rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allen recorded one snap; he has played just five snaps for Kansas City’s offense this season. The Defensive takeaway: Peter Woods outsnaps Khyiris Tonga Up front on defense, the Chiefs’ youth movement is taking over more and more with each game. Nose tackle Khyiris Tonga (30 snaps) started on Sunday, but rookie defensive tackle Peter Woods out-snapped the veteran by five. On 23 of Woods’ 35 plays on the field, the Dolphins ran a pass play; on one of those snaps, Woods dropped into coverage. Edge rusher R Mason Thomas also wasn’t the “starter”; fourth-year defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah began the game on the field, but the rookie from Oklahoma played 41 snaps compared to Anudike-Uzomah’s 31. Rookie defensive tackle Bryson Eason also made his Chiefs debut in Miami, playing seven snaps. Offensive Snaps Defensive Snaps Special teams snaps

title: 5 things we learned from the Chiefs’ Week 3 victory in Miami
summary: Was it the cleanest game the Kansas City Chiefs ever played? No. Did they play down to their competition a little bit? Perhaps. Should they have won by more than they did? Maybe. But at the end of the day, the Chiefs are 3-0 and coming off a double-digit road win, beating the Miami Dolphins […]
full_text: (Photo by Chris Arjoon/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images). | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Was it the cleanest game the Kansas City Chiefs ever played? No. Did they play down to their competition a little bit? Perhaps. Should they have won by more than they did? Maybe. But at the end of the day, the Chiefs are 3-0 and coming off a double-digit road win, beating the Miami Dolphins 24-10 . In the NFL, that’s nothing to scoff at, no matter who you’re playing. Because at the end of the day, the Dolphins roster is still full of guys good enough to be in the NFL. Here are five things we learned from the Chiefs remaining unbeaten. 1. Pass rush still looks like an issue This is a topic I feel like we have beaten to death in recent years. The Chiefs can’t get pressure without blitzing. Defensive end George Karlaftis is near the top of the league in pressures but struggles to get home. We need more from the young players we drafted. Defensive tackle Chris Jones looks like his best days could be behind him. And when you add it all up, it makes for a defense that does not rush the passer nearly as well as their investment in picks would suggest. This is the same argument we’ve been having for years now. And the fact we’re still having it, and the Chiefs struggled to get to the quarterback against a team that had allowed nine sacks coming into this game, speaks louder than anything else I could say on this subject. George Karlaftis Takes The Tipped Ball From Chris Jones And PICKS IT OFF! That Ball Felt Like It Was In The Air For A Whole Minute. 😂 pic.twitter.com/s9AurpfAFc — SM Highlights (@SMHighlights1) September 27, 2026 That being said, there are ways to affect the passing game as a rusher aside from sacks. For example, Jones batting a pass late in the fourth quarter and Karlaftis intercepting it. And while this play was truly awesome, they are still too few and far between. 2. The tackles are playing fine… Kahlil Benson and Jaylon Moore are doing a fine job at playing offensive tackle for this team. And that could be the problem. When your entire franchise is wrapped up in a No. 15 jersey, you want better than fine play from them. Because fine is okay until it’s not. And fine is good enough 85% of the snaps, but the other 15% is Mahomes being driven into the turf in the end zone, getting rolled up high and low, or taking helmet-to-helmet contact. Fine is fine, as long as you’re playing the Dolphins. But fine becomes a whole lot less fine when you’re facing off against Las Vegas Raiders defensive end Maxx Crosby. Week Three Patrick Mahomes Passing TD (7) to Travis Kelce (2) pic.twitter.com/TO2WKggU8h — NFL TD Videos (@NFLTDVids) September 27, 2026 It’s officially Raider week, and you know those dirty son-of-a-cusses are going to be gunning for Mahomes. This is the week that we see if our tackles are fine enough, or if they will be an issue moving forward. 3. Does Harrison Butker lose focus? This is the second straight week that Harrison Butker has missed a field goal. We’ve also seen him struggle with making PATs at times in the past. And maybe it’s unfair to hold against him his 51-yard miss from last week, and this week’s miss was from 50 yards, which is also not a chip shot by any means. Butker has been, in my opinion, one of the most clutch kickers in NFL history. When the game is on the line and you need somebody to drill a 56-yarder to win, I don’t think anyone is better, but when you’re up by two scores on the road, I’m not sure I can say the same thing. And Sunday’smiss didn’t matter because there was only a minute left on the clock, but you want your guys to take care of business when they are up, just like they do when the game is on the line. 4. Mansoor Delane will have his rookie moments, but… Dang, he is just a good football player. I feel like it took Delane a couple of drives to really get his feet wet and get into the rhythm, but once he did, he was a difference-maker on this defense. When you combine him and Nohl Williams on the outside, it’s going to be hard for opposing perimeter wide receivers to have much success against the Chiefs. That being said, the safeties on this roster left something to be desired in this game. They seemed a step late to the ball on many plays that could have turned into gains if someone other than Malik Willis had been lofting the ball in the air. Still, as my caveat at the top of this story said, the defense and secondary held an NFL offense to 10 points on a day when the other team was trying to pull out all the stops to beat Kansas City. 5. A win is a win It’s like a wise friend of mine once said, “Do you know what they call a person who graduated medical school with a C average?” “No”, I replied. “A doctor.” The Chiefs are 3-0 and heading into Raiders week, where they will face off on the road against a nasty bunch of mouth-breathing knuckle-draggers to see who will sit alone atop the AFC West. The Chiefs needed to win this game to move ahead, to destroy the Raiders. They did that.

title: Chiefs News: Spags pulled aside defense after opening drive in Miami

It worked | The Kansas City Star “Spags pulled us aside as a defense,” defensive end George Karlaftis said after the game. “(He) said we’ve got to tighten up on our details to a man and just finish and play to the best of our abilities and execute our responsibilities and our assignment on each play.” Based on several players’ accounts, it seemed the defensive coordinator could see the Chiefs letting a single bad play affect the next one, and he wanted to stop that trend in its tracks. “It’s all about the next play,” defensive tackle Chris Jones said. “And the first quarter was very up and down on our end as a defense, and he kind of pulled us together and let us know, don’t let a good play or a bad play affect the next play.” Chiefs struggle to finish off Dolphins, exposing areas of concern despite 3-0 start | The Athletic The Chiefs still have plenty to work on if they want to again be among the AFC’s elite. The top worry has to be left tackle, as undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson has filled in admirably for injured Josh Simmons through three weeks, but he was beaten often in the second half as Miami edge rushers frequently went right around him for quick pressure on Mahomes. “There’s a lot of things I can clean up, but I’m gonna make sure I clean it up in the film room,” Benson told The Athletic after the game. “As a rookie, I’m going to keep listening to my vets, listening to my coaches and make sure I clean up the right things that I need to clean up so we can go back and play better next week.” Patrick Mahomes matches Tom Brady, makes NFL history in Kansas City Chiefs’ 24-10 victory | HITC The win against the Dolphins was Mahomes’ 150th NFL start including the regular season and the postseason. In those 150 games, the Chiefs have tasted victory 115 times. That is the exact number that Brady achieved in his first 150 starts, too. In tying the GOAT, Mahomes has made NFL history himself. Chiefs QB Patrick Mahomes stays in same room he did for Super Bowl LIV in return to Miami | KSHB 41 “That team bonding, you’ll never forget that,” Mahomes said. Those moments flooded back to Mahomes when he returned to the Turnberry ahead of Sunday’s 24-10 win against the Miami Dolphins. “Same hotel room, same room number — everything,” Mahomes said. “It was cool. I didn’t even feel the nostalgia until I got there and you see the room. I was taking pictures and sending it (the photo) to teammates.” Chiefs remain unbeaten: 9 things that stood out in win over Dolphins | KMBC 9 Mahomes spread it around Rice was Mahomes’ favorite target, but he wasn’t the only player involved. Rice led the way with seven catches for 88 yards, while Travis Kelce, Noah Gray, Tyquan Thornton and Xavier Worthy each had at least 20 receiving yards. Mahomes finished 20-of-24 for 246 yards and found two different players for touchdowns. Around the NFL Raiders stay perfect in comeback win over Saints. Time to start taking Las Vegas seriously? | The Athletic How did Bowers’ return from injury impact the offense? It gave Cousins his top target back. Bowers paced the Raiders’ passing attack from all over the field, catching balls after lining up in the slot and on the outside. The tight end was a major boost in critical situations, converting five third downs. His last was his biggest: a 4-yard touchdown that proved to be the game-winning score. Bowers’ presence didn’t remedy all of the Raiders’ offensive issues. Running back Ashton Jeanty had another quiet game after his Week 1 explosion, running for just 56 yards on 2.9 yards per carry. And while the receivers stepped up last week, they didn’t do much until late in New Orleans. title: 6 Winners and 4 Losers from the Chiefs’ Week 3 win in Miami
summary: You may hear a lot of doom and gloom this week about how the Kansas City Chiefs defense struggled to get off the field (they did), or how the team had too many costly penalties (they did). You’ll hear talk about receivers, offensive linemen, linebackers, and pass rushers (see below). But, at the end of […]
full_text: (Photo by Carmen Mandato/Getty Images) | Getty Images You may hear a lot of doom and gloom this week about how the Kansas City Chiefs defense struggled to get off the field (they did), or how the team had too many costly penalties (they did). You’ll hear talk about receivers, offensive linemen, linebackers, and pass rushers (see below). But, at the end of the day, your Chiefs did what they were supposed to do– flew home from a road game against the Miami Dolphins with a 3-0 record. The better team should prevail, even when they make mistakes. Six weeks from now, what will we remember: the ugliness or the win? But alas, this is winners/losers, so we’ll dig a bit deeper and highlight a few who stood out this week. 6 Winners Quarterback Patrick Mahomes: Wins may or may not be a “QB stat”, but it’s no coincidence that Mahomes just passed Tom Brady on the wins-in-first-decade charts. Mahomes was deadly efficient in this game, with the only blip being a fluke interception off of Rashee Rice’s hands. Tight end Travis Kelce : Seriously, what is Taylor’s Personal Chef feeding this guy? The Dolphins forgot to cover the nearly 37-year-old, and 48 yards later, Kelce helped set up the offense for an opening-drive touchdown. We thought Kelce’s role would evolve this season, but who could have predicted it would be into the NFL’s best big-play receiver? Defensive end George Karlaftis: Relentless effort pays off eventually. A tipped pass, a QB hit, a tackle-for-loss, and a couple of pressures weren’t enough for Furious George. No, he had to take it upon himself to basically end the game on his first career interception– a deflection from Chris Jones. Running back Kenneth Walker III: For the first time in his Chiefs career, he didn’t cross 100 yards from scrimmage. He had to fight for every yard and was stopped on some critical short-yardage plays. But Walker also scored two touchdowns– one running nearly untouched, one on a shovel pass. Those two touchdowns were the only thing that came easy for the Chiefs’ featured back, but they were the difference-maker. Tight end Noah Gray: It was Kelce’s day again, but Noah Gray also delivered for Patrick Mahomes when called upon. Three big catches, including a tough back shoulder play while blanketed downfield. Hopefully, he can build upon this performance. Cornerback Mansoor Delane : The rookie returned on Sunday and made his presence felt. The shoulder didn’t seem to be on his mind, as Delane was aggressive as ever. In the second quarter alone, Mansoor Delane ended two drives with a 4th-down pass breakup and a 3rd-down tackle-for-loss. 4 Losers Note: Applying the labels “losers” is not intended to be a judgment on the talent or character of any of these individuals. It’s just a simple way to grade their job performance in a single game. No disrespect should be inferred. Defensive back L’Jarius Snead: He made what should have been one of the biggest plays of the game, forcing and recovering a Malik Willis fumble– and it’s not his fault the offense gave the ball right back. But, like the aforementioned linebackers, Snead was a popular target when in coverage. He’s a Spagnuolo favorite, an effective blitzer, and one of the league’s worst corners in pass coverage. It’s a conundrum in the slot. Linebackers Jack Cochrane and Nick Bolton: The Dolphins saw something they could exploit, and it was these two guys in coverage. Bolton did rack up eleven tackles, but most will remember him getting juked in the backfield on a drive-extending run. The linebacker film room won’t be fun this week. Wide receiver Xavier Worthy: The good news is that Worthy made a play– a 17-yard catch. The bad news is that Worthy only made that one significant play all afternoon. The Chiefs need more out of number one.
author: Matt Stagner

title: Play-action passing a strength from Chiefs’ win against Dolphins
summary: Although the Kansas City Chiefs defeated the Miami Dolphins 24-10 on Sunday to secure a 3-0 start, the game left much to be desired in terms of execution. Against a Miami squad thought to be among the league’s worst, very little seemed to go smoothly for Kansas City, whether on offense, defense, or special teams. One […]
full_text: (Photo by Carmen Mandato/Getty Images) | Getty Images Although the Kansas City Chiefs defeated the Miami Dolphins 24-10 on Sunday to secure a 3-0 start, the game left much to be desired in terms of execution. Against a Miami squad thought to be among the league’s worst, very little seemed to go smoothly for Kansas City, whether on offense, defense, or special teams. One area for the Chiefs to build on will be quarterback Patrick Mahomes’ success on play-action as running back Kenneth Walker demands more defensive attention. Next Gen Stats showed Mahomes averaging 15.3 yards per pass attempt on play-action on Sunday. Patrick Mahomes averaged 15.3 yards per attempt on play-action passes in Miami (11 of 12 for 183 yards) @NextGenStats Eight of the completions from under center — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) September 27, 2026 After the game, Mahomes was predictably down on the team’s tougher-than-expected offensive performance. He has no doubt, however, that Walker and rookie running back Emmett Johnson are making his job easier. “It’s helping out a ton,” Mahomes remarked. “I think people look at the stats, and they see the touchdowns that Kenneth has and that Emmett’s been able to run the ball and the run game that we’re doing. But I don’t think they really understand how the play-action and the movements and stuff like that have really opened up in our offense. “That’s a credit to them. That’s a credit to the offensive line firing off the ball on run and pass. That’s something we have to continue to get better at marrying as the year goes on. I thought we did a great job with that today — being better at the drop back passing game…It’s just about finishing drives and not making those little mistakes.”

title: Patrick Mahomes reminds young Chiefs team they can’t relax
summary: The first road trip of the 2026 regular season was an interesting one for the Kansas City Chiefs. The offense came out firing with two touchdowns in two drives, and tight end Travis Kelce put the game on ice with a highlight-reel touchdown catch in traffic. Everything in between the strong start and the strong […]
full_text: (Photo by Carmen Mandato/Getty Images) | Getty Images The first road trip of the 2026 regular season was an interesting one for the Kansas City Chiefs . The offense came out firing with two touchdowns in two drives, and tight end Travis Kelce put the game on ice with a highlight-reel touchdown catch in traffic. Everything in between the strong start and the strong finish was touch and go. The Miami Dolphins ’ offense kept the pressure on the Chiefs all game by staying on the field and winning the battle for time of possession (34:21 to 25:39). The Chiefs prevailed 24-10 , but the team’s leader on the field knows it could have been a more comfortable victory. Quarterback Patrick Mahomes talked about the 14-point victory after the game at the podium. “Obviously, we didn’t play to our standard that we would hold for ourselves, especially in that middle part offensively in the game,” Mahomes told reporters. “But we found a way to come together at the end of the game; we had two great drives at the beginning of the game, and now it’s about learning the in-between. “It will be a learning experience for us to know that we have to come with our A-game every single time in order to win.“ Sandwiched between the successful opening drives and Kelce’s game-sealing score, the Chiefs’ offense scored just three points over five possessions. While Kansas City’s offense struggled, the defense failed to get off the field. Mahomes pointed to the game’s location and start time as things affecting the NFL’s third-youngest roster as of Week 1. “We’re young, we’re a young football team,” Mahomes reminded the media. “So guys have to learn that. There will be learning experiences throughout the season; luckily enough for us, we still won the football game. “You have to continue to press that this is a long season,” Mahomes continued. “Just because we had the first two weeks, good weeks against two really good opponents doesn’t mean you can relax when you’re playing a 12 o’clock game. A lot of these guys, [it was] their first 12 o’clock game, first time traveling and having that experience in the NFL, so for them, learn how to get themselves ready to go faster we can go out there and play better football.” For most of the game, Mahomes captained an offense that averaged over seven yards per play. He averaged over 10 yards per pass. The numbers — tagged with a first-half interception thrown behind wide receiver Rashee Rice — made the 24-point output feel underwhelming. “At the end of the day, we left a lot out there,” Mahomes said. “We’re not going to be mad about winning. We won the football game. You think about last year, we were losing some of these games… we’re going to look at the tape hard and find ways to get better for next week.” Patrick Mahomes to the podium: pic.twitter.com/gTKlmTFjnl — Vahe Gregorian (@vgregorian) September 27, 2026 “I wouldn’t say I feel disappointed; I’m happy for the win,” Mahomes said later. “I think last year taught me that you can’t be disappointed when you win football games… but I know we can be better. I know we can get better, and that’s going to take watching the tape, going out and having a better week of practice, communicating throughout the entire offense and the entire team. We’re going to enjoy this victory, but if we want to get to where we want to go, we have to continue to get better and better, and so we’ll do that.” As Kansas City learns from the third consecutive win to begin this season, Mahomes reflected on the benefits of a training camp run by head coach Andy Reid. “We had such a great training camp, but it wasn’t always pretty,” Mahomes remembered. “We have a lot of young guys, and we’re all building chemistry together. It wasn’t always the prettiest, but guys pushed through. I think that built that up for games like this. It wasn’t always pretty on both sides of the ball… we have a lot of stuff to clean up, but I was proud of how our guys finished the game.”
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Chiefs-Dolphins: 3 instant takeaways from Chiefs’ win in Miami
summary: After two games that showed a reinvented self against two AFC contenders, the Kansas City Chiefs fell back to earth and looked more like the frustrating team we saw for much of the 2025 season, still winning 24-10 over the Miami Dolphins in Week 3. The Chiefs’ offense was efficient, quarterback Patrick Mahomes was nonchalantly […]
full_text: (Photo by Chris Arjoon/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images). | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After two games that showed a reinvented self against two AFC contenders, the Kansas City Chiefs fell back to earth and looked more like the frustrating team we saw for much of the 2025 season, still winning 24-10 over the Miami Dolphins in Week 3. The Chiefs’ offense was efficient, quarterback Patrick Mahomes was nonchalantly dealing, and things were still tight until late in the fourth quarter. Here are three trends from the game that mirrored last year’s disappointing performances… until they didn’t! 1. Not getting off the field on third down The Dolphins’ offense converted eight of 16 third downs against the Chiefs, but Miami’s ease in converting third-and-longs really brought up the frustration of the 2025 campaign. Miami converted multiple third downs by throwing short of the sticks or handing off to a running back. On two third-and-longs in the same drive, both from inside Kansas City’s 25-yard line, the Chiefs couldn’t generate pressure or make an aggressive play on the ball after the snap. The team’s second and third-level players lacked playmaking throughout the afternoon, especially safety Alohi Gilman. Safety Jaden Hicks struggled to keep up with tight end Greg Dulcich, and cornerback Mansoor Delane didn’t look as sound in coverage as he did in the short sample size we got from Week 1. However, Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis wasn’t sacked and rarely saw pressure from the Kansas City pass rush. That made it easier to challenge a Chiefs secondary that wasn’t up for matching it. The Chiefs generated just one quarterback hit on Willis, who threw 36 passes. With Miami needing a quick score, down by 14 points late, defensive tackle Chris Jones made his presence felt by batting a pass up into the air, giving defensive end George Karlaftis a chance to secure it. Karlaftis was also the only Chiefs pass rusher to hit Willis. 2. Situational struggles Early on, Kansas City’s offense gave spectators the impression it would light up the scoreboard. The team scored touchdowns on its first two drives by driving inside the 10-yard line and finishing them off from there. The Chiefs scored just three points after that until the final minutes. In the second quarter, Kansas City worked inside the 15-yard line to third-and-one. Both plays were inside handoffs, and Miami’s defense stuffed both for no gain. The empty red-zone trip kept the score within one game. The Chiefs’ next three drives stalled. Kansas City would reach the red zone again in the fourth quarter after a strong catch by tight end Noah Gray over linebacker Willie Gay Jr. on the sideline. However, Kansas City — from the eight-yard line — lost eight yards over the next three plays, failing to secure a two-score lead in order to take any pressure off the defense. With another chance to put the game away late, a possession deep in Miami territory was backed up by a penalty on center Creed Humphrey. Fortunately, two chunk plays redeemed the offense; tight end Travis Kelce went up for a pass in the end zone, secured it, and put the game away late. The Chiefs’ offense finished with just three third-down conversions on seven attempts; the team also missed its only fourth-down attempt, as noted above. 3. Leaky pass protection If the Dolphins have a strength on defense, it was certainly up front, and they played into it well. Edge rusher Chop Robinson was a problem throughout the game, and not just when he obliterated Mahomes and had the two-time MVP holding his back and moving gingerly for a few moments afterward. Fortunately for the Chiefs, Robinson drew a roughing-the-passer penalty, but he and other Miami defensive linemen were terrorizing Kansas City’s front five. Mahomes was not sacked, but he was hit five times. Former Chiefs edge rusher Josh Uche recorded two, including a late pressure that drove left tackle Kahlil Benson to the ground. This is likely the only reason Mahomes didn’t have a nuclear-level performance against an inexperienced Dolphins secondary. He finished with 246 yards on 20 of 24 passing attempts (10.3 yards per attempt) and a passer rating of 119.8.
