title: Drake Maye looks broken. That doesn’t mean he can’t be fixed.
summary: Their 2023 season was one of the most frustrating in recent New England Patriots memory. It was not just that they won only four games all year, but that they were seemingly out of answers throughout. No matter what button head coach Bill Belichick pushed, the team and its third-year quarterback, who had shown promise […]
full_text: Their 2023 season was one of the most frustrating in recent New England Patriots memory. It was not just that they won only four games all year, but that they were seemingly out of answers throughout. No matter what button head coach Bill Belichick pushed, the team and its third-year quarterback, who had shown promise earlier in his career, kept spiraling as the losses continued to pile up. The Patriots of 2026 are not at that point. Their season is only three weeks old and their own third-year QB has shown that he can play the position at a significantly higher level than his predecessor, Mac Jones, ever had. And yet, the frustration and helplessness are starting to feel similar. And just like it was back then, it all starts at quarterback. Back in 2025, Drake Maye looked like one of the best QBs in football. Heck, he was one of the best QBs in football. He completed 72% of his passes during the regular season for 4,394 yards, 31 touchdowns and just eight interceptions. His 0.313 EPA per play among qualifying passers was the highest in the league, and he only narrowly missed out on the league MVP award while leading a team that had gone 4-13 in back-to-back seasons to division title and 14-3 record. It was impressive, but it also was a mirage — at least to a degree. The playoffs, after all, were a different story for the Patriots and their quarterback in particular. Maye’s regular season swagger seemed gone, and the success followed suit: his EPA per play dropped to -0.148, as his completion percentage tanked and turnover rate increased. Of course, it wasn’t all his fault. The offensive line, starting two rookies on the left side, felt apart; the receivers were unable to generate consistent separation; and the unit ran into four of the best six defenses in the league en route to the Super Bowl. Three games into the 2026 season, however, Maye again seems all out of sorts. Yes, the offensive line continues to have some problems — it’s the right side now — and the offseason changes at wide receiver have not yet paid the proper dividends. However, the problems seem to run deeper than that. Maye himself looks broken, and Sunday’s 35-6 loss in Jacksonville made this dramatically clear. In a way, it was a greatest hits collection of bad football from the MVP runner-up. He had a bizarre fumble in the first quarter (and another later in the game that he recovered). He gave away points when he forced a pass and threw an interception at the Jaguars goal line. He had another pick when he couldn’t connect with wide receiver Kyle Williams on a backside curl. Ultimately, he had to watch backup Tommy DeVito finish the game in his place . It was a low point both this season and in what had been a quite promising career up until last year’s playoffs. Now, the Patriots and Maye are faced with an uncomfortable truth: if they don’t transform it from a low to a turning point, their season could be over before it even began. Last year and under different circumstances the Patriots managed to do so. And even though they are dealing with a more daunting challenge this time around, they can do so again. The first step is identifying what the hell is even going on. For head coach Mike Vrabel, it seems the issue is not so much a physical but a mental one. Appearing on WEEI on Monday, he used golf as an analogy. “We really want to make a good score. Sometimes, we’re so focused on it that we try to choke the life out of the golf club, and we’re squeezing it so damn tight that the ball has no choice but to go sideways,” he said. “We need to stop trying to choke the life out of every single play. We need to relax. We need to settle in, and go play football, and not try to force things that aren’t there.” Three games into his third season, forcing things has been one of Maye’s biggest problems. He forced passes in the season opener against the Seahawks, single-handedly costing his team the game and later admitting he simply ran out of patience. He made another questionable decision in Week 2 versus Pittsburgh, and then again on the aforementioned goal-line pick versus the Jaguars. Just like that 2023 season we mentioned earlier, the issues have put the young quarterback in a dangerous downwards spiral. He knows it himself. “I think the ball starts rolling like that, we can’t get out of our own way — can’t get out of my own way, personally,” Maye said after the Jaguars game . “I have to look myself in the mirror and take this as a turning point. It’s Week 3, and at the same time we have to get some fuel and realize that what we’re doing out there offensively is unacceptable. It’s been unacceptable for three weeks. So, I have to start with myself and then lead these guys, and we have to get back after it.” Maye does seem to find some solace in the fact that the Patriots bounced back from a 1-2 start last season as well, but his head coach sang a different tune on Monday. “We’re not focused on last year. Each situation and each play is different,” said Mike Vrabel. For the Patriots, the situation is clear as day: if they can’t fix their quarterback, it’s game over for at least 2026. That fixing will not be easy, but also not impossible. As a starter, the Patriots have to get his confidence back up. Naturally, that is easier said than done, but amid all the disappointment through Week 3 there also have been glimpses. On Sunday, for example, Maye did throw some good passes. The drive that ended with his first interception down at the goal line? It was set up by a well-executed 38-yard pass connection with DeMario Douglas that was nearly followed up with another big gain out of a no-huddle look on the very first snap; Maye overshot Douglas — whether faulty ball placement or an imprecise route is to blame cannot be said at this point — but the play was there to be had. And maybe that is something the Patriots can use to get Maye back on track: no huddle. They did not use any up-tempo snaps in Weeks 1 and 2, partially due to game situation. Against Jacksonville, that incompletion was one of two no-huddle plays; the other being a 34-yard pass to Kyle Williams that could have become a 50-yard touchdown had the second-year wideout not stepped out of bounds. Ultimately, none of those moments helped tip the scales in New England’s favor versus the Jaguars. Neither did a 21-yard Maye touchdown run being brought back by penalty or the defense failing to get a single red zone stop. What those moments and multiple others throughout this so-far underwhelming season show, however, is that there is hope. Unlike 2023, when it became obvious that Mac Jones and Bailey Zappe were a lost cause in New England, Maye continues to have his moments of brilliance. The problem is that they are overshadowed by head-scratching decisions and insufficient ball security. But, and here is the glass-half-full-perspective, those issues can be fixed. Just ask the man himself. “It’s not that I feel like these mistakes that I’m making personally are really them beating us. I think it’s beating myself,” he said. “You have to flip to the next play and realize that this league will humble you quick. Just finding ways for me to step up when I feel like I’m not playing my best and still lead the team. I think that’s what this position is about, and that’s what as the quarterback of this football team is my obligation.” Drake Maye looks broken right now and the buttons he is pushing are not functioning properly, there is no sugar-coating it. However, he also is not beyond salvaging either.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Mike Vrabel voices ‘very high concern’ after Patriots loss to Jaguars
summary: After a Marcus Jones interception early in the second quarter awarded the New England Patriots a new set of downs at the Jacksonville Jaguars’ 21-yard line, trailing 7-0, the Patriots offense unraveled before they could run a full play. On first down, right tackle Morgan Moses was called for a holding penalty that wiped out […]
full_text: After a Marcus Jones interception early in the second quarter awarded the New England Patriots a new set of downs at the Jacksonville Jaguars’ 21-yard line, trailing 7-0, the Patriots offense unraveled before they could run a full play. On first down, right tackle Morgan Moses was called for a holding penalty that wiped out a Drake Maye scrambling touchdown. Then, a Romeo Doubs offensive pass interference call quickly followed that mishap, pushing New England back to a 1st-and-30 possession and forcing the offense to settle for a field goal. That sequence was an early glimpse of the sloppy, undisciplined football on Sunday afternoon that plagued the Patriots in their dismal 35-6 road loss to the Jaguars. “My concern level is very high for this football team,” head coach Mike Vrabel said after the contest. “When you come off a game like that, you just want to get back to work … We have to fix a lot of things.” New England committed nine penalties throughout the matchup. While Jacksonville wasn’t far behind with seven of its own, the Patriots repeatedly made mistakes that prevented them from capitalizing on the Jaguars’ shortcomings. Trailing just before halftime, but with a larger disparity at 14-3, Maye and his unit had an opportunity to at least cut the game to one score with a third-and-goal snap two yards out from the end zone. However, instead of settling for another three points, the quarterback forced a throw to a smothered Efton Chism III in the back of the painted area, allowing Jacksonville cornerback Travis Hunter to intercept the pass. Maye was responsible for all three of New England’s turnovers stemming from poor decision-making when dropping back to pass and a jarring fumble that slipped from his hand on a pass attempt. Still, Vrabel believes that resolving those mistakes begins with himself. “We haven’t made good decisions with the football,” Vrabel added. “We have to get it fixed. We have to practice. We have to work and get it corrected. And everybody else has to do much better, and it starts with me. That’s how it goes … I need to get guys in there to do the things the way that we need them done. “There are going to be mistakes, but there are too many things that get us beat: turnovers and not taking advantage of [Jacksonville’s] turnover opportunities.” Following Maye’s final interception in the third frame, the team’s body language noticeably shifted, with the defense losing its physicality as the game progressed and the offense continuously failing to score. That body language was evident at all three levels. After the Jaguars extended their lead to 28-3, Kyle Williams, instead of letting the ball roll out of bounds on the ensuing kickoff to accept a penalty, caught the kick, pinning the Patriots at their own nine. “I think it’s one day at a time,” Vrabel said. “It’s about what we can do to get healthy and improve individually and as a football team. That’s all we can do. It’s going to start with me and my ability to teach and get the guys in the right spots.” New England, dropping to 1-2 on the season, will travel to Buffalo next week to face the undefeated Bills in a crucial divisional game.
author: Andrew Guindon

title: 10 things we learned from Patriots vs. Jaguars
summary: The New England Patriots got embarrassed in Jacksonville on Sunday. The offense struggled, the defense struggled, special teams struggled. It looked like the 2024 season all over again, as there was almost nothing positives to take away from the game. Let’s get into our lessons learned from the 35-6 blowout loss that dropped New England […]
full_text: The New England Patriots got embarrassed in Jacksonville on Sunday. The offense struggled, the defense struggled, special teams struggled. It looked like the 2024 season all over again, as there was almost nothing positives to take away from the game. Let’s get into our lessons learned from the 35-6 blowout loss that dropped New England to 1-2 on the year. Drake Maye is playing like a bottom-5 QB Drake Maye was a finalist for MVP last season, and we all expected him to take another leap forward this year and put a firm claim in that he is a top-5 quarterback in the NFL. So far, he is trending in the complete opposite direction: he is playing like a bottom-5 QB at the moment. Not only has he looked bad, but the lengths of bad he has been is downright impressive. He dropped the ball as he was trying to make a throw on Sunday; he threw another horrendous interception in the end zone; he fumbled a few other times, but recovered twice or was already down before the ball came out. Maye doesn’t just look bad right now, he looks like one of the worst quarterbacks in the NFL through three weeks and it is costing the Patriots. The offseason moves haven’t worked out Last offseason, the Patriots hit on almost every single one of their free agency moves. This season, not so much. Kevin Byard has been a non-factor on a defense that got gashed on Sunday; Romeo Doubs has been, to put it nicely, underwhelming; A.J. Brown was hurt in Week 1 and might be out through October as well; Alijah Vera-Tucker has been fine but not 11th-highest-paid-left-guard-in-football great; Dre’Mont Jones is currently hurt, and Reggie Gilliam has had almost zero impact on an offense that cannot consistently run the ball. The switch from Kayshon Boutte and Stefon Diggs to Brown and Doubs in particular, while good on paper, has not paid any dividends so far and the rest of the offense has taken a turn for the worse because of it. It’s still early, but, after seemingly making all of the right moves last year, the Patriots appear to have made all of the wrong ones this year. Coaching concerns are real Multiple pre-snap penalties on the defense, some baffling decisions on both offense and defense, and being clearly outplayed on special teams leaves but one conclusion: the Patriots didn’t look ready to go on Sunday. The execution obviously hasn’t been good, but the coaching staff has not been up to the task either. It feels like the defense overthought this game; after playing a ton of man defense, the Patriots played a ton of zone, and it was not effective at all, partly because the Patriots simply don’t play zone on quite the same level well given the personnel they have. We won’t speculate whether or not some of Mike Vrabel’s extra curricular activities have had an impact on the team, but the fact is he needs to be the one to start righting the ship — and quickly. Carlton Davis competed well in his return Starting cornerback Carlton Davis missed last week’s game against the Steelers, but played physical in his return this week in Jacksonville. Multiple times, he blew up plays with his quick click-and-close abilities, almost intercepting one pass along the way. The Patriots have a shutdown corner on one side with Christian Gonzalez, and if Davis can play consistently well on the other side, it could be a big boost for the Patriots defense (especially if Zak Kuhr starts leaning into their man-cover abilities more). Elijah Ponder and Gabe Jacas look like solid players There are not many positive things to discuss from a 29-point defeat that was very much over by the third quarter, but two of them have to be the Patriots’ young edge defenders, Elijah Ponder and Gabe Jacas. It was far from perfect from them, but they both have multiple plays every game where they stick out due to their effort and ability to generate pressure. The defense wasn’t close to good enough on Sunday, including Ponder and Jacas, but there are some positive signs from the youth on the Patriots defense. Marcus Jones always plays hard No matter what is going on, you always know that one guy is going to be busting his butt out there, and that’s Marcus Jones. He got his first interception of the season on Sunday, and had a solid return after as well. His competitive spirits always run hot, even though he did get beat for a touchdown on back-to-back plays (the first of which didn’t count due to an offensive penalty). I would classify those as very good plays by Jaguars wideout Parker Washington instead of bad plays by Jones, but it deserved to be mentioned nonetheless. Morgan Moses is struggling The Patriots picking a developmental offensive tackle in the first round this year in hopes of having him replace an established starter no sooner than a year from now drew some criticism after the NFL Draft. However, it seems that they might be needing Caleb Lomu sooner rather than later. Morgan Moses, after all, has been subpar in almost every regard this year. Against the Jaguars, for example, he was flagged for holding to negate what would have been a game-tying 21-yard touchdown on the very next play after Marcus Jones’ second-quarter pick. The Patriots need him to play well, especially with Mike Onwenu missing extended time, and possibly the rest of the season, at right guard. On Sunday, Lomu went in and replaced him at the end of the game but the team gave up a safety off the right side on the first play he was in there. It remains to be seen how much he can and will contribute in the near future, but until the youngster is fully prepared to take over, Moses simply needs to play at a higher level. It’s awfully hard to trust Kyle Williams right now The Patriots need as much help on offense as they can get right now, but I don’t know how the team could trust second-year receiver Kyle Williams. He struggles to get open on anything but deep go routes, and Drake Maye was picked trying hit him on a hitch where he had zero separation and didn’t fight back to the ball, even if it wasn’t a good throw. The real issue to me, however, is his game readiness. He caught a kickoff on the sideline — he literally had to toe-tap to catch the ball — pinning the Patriots inside in the 10 instead of letting it get out of bounds to allow his team to start at the 40 instead of the 9. Then, when he finally did make a catch, he stepped out of bounds when running towards the end zone. For a team like the Patriots whose margin of error is slim right now, missed opportunities such as these simply cannot happen. And with Williams missing two of those in limited action, I don’t know how the team could possibly trust him moving forward. More injury questions arise The Patriots have already placed 16 players on injured reserve this season, so their depth, which wasn’t all that good to begin with, has already been tested significantly. On Sunday, the Patriots lost Greg Van Roten, who was in for the injured Mike Onwenu at right guard, and he was replaced by Walter Rouse. The depth is a serious concern. We will see how long Van Roten is out, but they can’t afford to lose many more guys to still have a chance to compete. A potentially season-defining game awaits The Patriots are teetering, and they have to go into Buffalo next week and try to take down the Bills, who have looked very good, at least when Josh Allen isn’t turning the ball over. Even when he does, though, their offense is good enough to keep scoring anyway. The Patriots have a chance to fight back and show that they can still be a serious contender this season, and that their first three games have been an aberration. On the other hand, they could continue to struggle and look nothing like a team capable of retaining its division crown. Unfortunately, it’s hard to watch a game like the one against the Jaguars and not prepare for the latter.

title: 6 winners and losers from Patriots loss to Jaguars
summary: The New England Patriots came out on the wrong side of a 35-6 blowout against the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday, falling to 1-2 on the year. Here is who caught our eye for better or worse upon live-viewing the Patriots’ Week 3 contest. Winners WR Mack Hollins: The veteran did have a poor and unnecessary […]
full_text: The New England Patriots came out on the wrong side of a 35-6 blowout against the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday, falling to 1-2 on the year. Here is who caught our eye for better or worse upon live-viewing the Patriots’ Week 3 contest. Winners WR Mack Hollins: The veteran did have a poor and unnecessary taunting penalty , but it was apparent again that Drake Maye has the most trust and confidence in throwing to him. Hollins led the team in catches (6), targets (9), and receiving yards (87) as he was their only consistent source of offense in Jacksonville. CB Christian Gonzalez: New England ditched their man-to-man coverage usage on Sunday leaning into a near 70% zone coverage rate. Trevor Lawrence shredded the Patriots zone looks throughout the day, but star cornerback Christian Gonzalez was his usual self along the outside. Gonzalez allowed just one catch on three targets in his direction with a pass breakup. Losers QB Drake Maye: It was another unacceptable performance from Drake Maye, as the quarterback acknowledged himself postgame. Maye threw a pair of interceptions and lost a fumble while completing just 14 of 25 passes for 199 yards. While the turnovers remain a major problem, Maye also continues to look indecisive with his decision-making and hesitant to rip throws into his receivers. Those mental issues appear to be the biggest concern from this point of view. Now, it’s up to the 24-year-old and the Patriots’ coaching staff to snap him out of it. RT Morgan Moses: The Patriots entire offensive line largely struggled on Sunday as Maye was pressure on 48.8% of his drop backs while the run game generated little movement. Starting right tackle Morgan Moses allowed three pressures while a holding call negated a 21-yard touchdown run by Maye. Elsewhere up front, the Patriots are down to their third string right guard after Greg Van Roten left the game early. He was replaced by Walter Rouse, who allowed a team-high four pressures. Red zone defense: The Jaguars offense won the situational football battle against the Patriots’ defense, specifically in the red zone where they scored on all five of their trips. Much of that success came from Trevor Lawrence attacking New England’s split-safety zones over the middle of the field for all three of his touchdown passes — while wide receiver Parker Washington also had an acrobatic catch with Marcus Jones tight in coverage. Jacksonville also finished the day 8-for-12 on third down. Mike Vrabel: Beyond the turnovers and red-zone woes, the self-inflicted wounds piled up for the Patriots. They were flagged nine times in total, including another delay-of-game penalty on Drake Maye and back-to-back penalties on Morgan Moses and Romeo Doubs following Marcus Jones’ interception. Mike Vrabel’s team lacked discipline Sunday, while the Patriots also continue to struggle in end-of-half situations to start the season. On their final possession of the first half, the Patriots ran the ball twice inside the five-yard line, appearing more focused on forcing the Jaguars to burn their timeouts than attacking the end zone. Honorable mentions It continues to be a slow start for Romeo Doubs, who had just one catch for eight yards until garbage time. DeMario Douglas was open downfield several times and Maye sailed a potential touchdown pass over his head on one instance. Kyle Williams showed his speed on a 34-yard catch-and-run but stepped out of bounds en route to the end zone. He also fielded a kickoff that appeared to be heading out of bounds at the 9-yard line. Another strong game from Alijah Vera-Tucker with zero pressures allowed across 39 pass blocking snaps. Milton Williams was held without a pressure on Sunday as his quiet start to the season continues. Teams have been sending extra attention in Williams’ direction early on, but it was disappointing he could not make more of an impact against a weak Jaguars’ interior. New England’s entire defensive front lost the line of scrimmage as Bhaysul Tuten averaged 4.9 yards per carry as their rushing attack as a whole generated a 53% success rate. Elijah Ponder (4) and Gabe Jacas (3) led the team in pressures and also combined for a sack. Carlton Davis blew up a pair of perimeter screens. Marcus Jones had an interception on a deflected pass and nearly had another one later in the game. Another missed field goal from Andy Borregales, this one coming from just 38 yards out. The second-year kicker is now 4-for-6 on the year.
author: Brian Hines

title: Patriots captain invokes Bill Belichick after Jaguars loss
summary: Coming out of their 35-6 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars, the New England Patriots know they need all the help they can get. Well, maybe some of the old Bill Belichick magic can do the trick. While the Patriots’ longtime head coach will not be walking through the door, Patriots captain Kevin Byard cited one […]
full_text: Coming out of their 35-6 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars , the New England Patriots know they need all the help they can get. Well, maybe some of the old Bill Belichick magic can do the trick. While the Patriots’ longtime head coach will not be walking through the door, Patriots captain Kevin Byard cited one of his legendary sayings after Sunday’s loss in Jacksonville. “As Bill Belichick used to always say, just do your job, and I think we’ll be fine,” said Byard during his postgame press conference. “For me, just being a leader and just being one of 11, I have to make sure that I’m playing at my highest level. Whatever I need to do to go out there, trying to go make a play to spark this team, that’s what I need to do and that’s what I’m focused on throughout this week. And I think that’s what everybody will be focused on, bringing the right attitude, bringing the right energy every single day, and just being one of 11 doing our job.” While the offense and quarterback Drake Maye in particular are the story of the game for the Patriots, the team’s defense also was not able to play to its typical standard. The 35 points given up are tied for the worst ever under head coach Mike Vrabel — a distinction shared with a loss to Buffalo last December — while the unit allowed Jacksonville to score five touchdowns on five red zone trips. For Byard, that second part was especially problematic coming out of the game. It is also why he pointed to the defense before placing any blame on Maye and company. “We’re not pointing the finger at one side of the ball or anything like that. We have to go out there no matter where they put the ball down,” he said. “As a defense, we have to go out there and line up, and we didn’t get a stop at all. They had the ball in the red zone five times and they scored five times. That is inexcusable on our part.” Byard, who referred to the loss as an “old-fashioned ass-whopping,” has come out on the wrong end of multiple disappointing games through his 11-year career in the NFL. Naturally, he knows what it takes for a quick turnaround. And considering what comes next for the Patriots — a trip to Buffalo to play the Bills — such a quick turnaround is paramount. “We have to come together. We understand what’s ahead of us,” he said. “We’ll have to hear all the noise or whatever it may be, but I think the main thing for us as a team is that we will have to ignore all that noise and get back to work. That’s the only way we can improve.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Drake Maye searching for answers after Jaguars loss
summary: Unacceptable. That was the word quarterback Drake Maye used to describe the Patriots’ offensive performance in a 35-6 blowout loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday. “It’s disappointing,” Maye said. “The ball starts rolling like that and we can’t get out of our way, I can’t get out of my own way, personally. So I’ve […]
full_text: Unacceptable. That was the word quarterback Drake Maye used to describe the Patriots’ offensive performance in a 35-6 blowout loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday. “It’s disappointing,” Maye said. “The ball starts rolling like that and we can’t get out of our way, I can’t get out of my own way, personally. So I’ve got to look at myself in the mirror and take this as a turning point.” Entering Week 3 with four turnovers, Maye gave the football away three more times on Sunday. It started in the second quarter when the ball slipped out of his hands in the middle of his throwing motion. “Jared [Wilson] happened to be bleeding on his hand. Got the football and was trying to put one to Kyle [Williams]. Slipped out of my hand,” Maye said. “I have to hold on to the football.” Later in the quarter, Maye threw an interception in the end zone when forcing a ball to Efton Chism III. His second interception came in the following half when he threw a late pass to Kyle Williams along the sideline. “Second one down there, just forcing it. Trying to give Chiz a chance to score and get some momentum going into halftime,” Maye said. “Then, had a one-on-one matchup outside. Shouldn’t have thrown it.” After throwing eight interceptions all of last season, Maye has now thrown six in his first three games. The third-year quarterback has looked uncomfortable and indecisive to start the season as the Patriots offense has struggled to find any consistency. “I think he knows what to do,” head coach Mike Vrabel said. “I think we have to do it better. We all want to make plays. We just have to make them good ones. And if it’s not there, we have to make a great decision. And I think sometimes you can want it too badly and we can’t force anything.” “I wouldn’t say hesitant,” Maye added. “I think I’m back there seeing it and we just got to make plays. I got to make throws.” Maye downplayed whether the struggles had to do with any lingering effects of the right throwing shoulder he suffered in last year’s AFC Championship Game. While the quarterback noted everyone is “a little” banged up, he added: “I wouldn’t say there’s a problem with my shoulder.” The quarterback is also adjusting to new personnel around him. The Patriots are without No. 1 wide receiver A.J. Brown, while free-agent addition Romeo Doubs has gotten off to a slow start. At 1-2, Maye and the Patriots are in familiar territory. They also started last season 1-2 before rattling off 10 straight wins. But if they’re going to start another streak next week against the Buffalo Bills, they’ll need a much better version of Maye. “We got a chance to earlier in the season, to put our head down and work,” Maye said. “Know that this is opportunity to band together and realize that the best football that we play is together and realizing that that’s going to start with me protecting the football and protecting this team, because that’s my job and I’ve been failing to do that.”
author: Brian Hines

title: Instant analysis from Patriots’ 35-6 loss to Jaguars
summary: The nor’easter would not be escaped on a sunny Sunday in Florida. The Jacksonville Jaguars made sure of it with a 35-6 runaway win over the New England Patriots at EverBank Stadium. Here’s a glance back on the 1 p.m. ET kickoff as the visitors head back into the elements with a 1-2 record. Maye […]
full_text: The nor’easter would not be escaped on a sunny Sunday in Florida. The Jacksonville Jaguars made sure of it with a 35-6 runaway win over the New England Patriots at EverBank Stadium. Here’s a glance back on the 1 p.m. ET kickoff as the visitors head back into the elements with a 1-2 record. Maye unravels with fifth, sixth and seventh turnovers Four turnovers had been tallied through two games. The 2025 NFL MVP runner-up tacked on more against the Jaguars. Drake Maye completed 14-of-25 passes for 199 yards on Sunday. The Patriots quarterback found no touchdowns, two interceptions and one lost fumble along the way. Taking the field in “21” personnel, the opening drive brought a 21-yard comeback route to move the chains. But things soon gave way to a punt under pressure. Any semblance of a fast start stayed at bay on the second drive, as well. That was the case as Maye, looking deep, saw the football slip out of his right hand while stepping up in a clean pocket. A fumble recovery by defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton was the result on the way to a 7-0 New England deficit. A three-and-out sack followed before the Patriots got on the board with a field goal off a takeaway of their own. But by halftime, New England’s QB stood with a can’t-have-it interception at the goal line to go with the fumble. Travis Hunter was there waiting on third down in the back of the end zone as the seconds ticked down versus Efton Chism III. No throwaway. No points. And the first career pick for the former Heisman Trophy winner. The erratic play did not depart at the half. Maye was intercepted again with 1:03 left in the third quarter as corner Jarrian Jones blanketed his man. Thrown late and inside, a 28-3 game it became on the subsequent snap. And a 35-6 game it would be by the time backup quarterback Tommy DeVito took over midway through the fourth quarter. Hollins draws nine targets, taunting The wide receiver depth chart had been carried by Romeo Doubs in the first game following A.J. Brown’s high ankle sprain. The former Green Bay Packer accounted for 96 of the position’s 131 receiving yards last week against the Pittsburgh Steelers. But at EverBank Stadium, Mack Hollins led the undisciplined offense with nine targets, six catches and 87 yards. The eldest statesman was penalized for taunting down by 25 points. Before then, he had picked up a back-shoulder pass for a first down as well as a stiff-arming gain of 21 on third down. Behind him, Doubs, who was flagged for offensive pass interference, caught three passes for 49 yards. The rest of the room was buoyed by a DeMario Douglas 38-yard gain and a Kyle Williams 34-yard gain. Backfield rotation rushes for long of seven After losing his 10th career fumble last week in Foxborough, Rhamondre Stevenson knew his grip would be tested in Jacksonville. The starter hung on for 22 yards across seven carries and 16 yards across three catches. A downhill conversion on fourth-and-inches was among them. TreVeyon Henderson got his share, too, after sprinting into the backfield for a 39-yard touchdown in his September debut. The No. 38 overall pick in the 2025 NFL draft was involved by the offense’s second snap and finished with 29 scrimmage yards through nine touches on Sunday. New England’s running back rotation managed to rush for a long of seven yards. Corey Kiner, acquired at the 53-man roster deadline, was the one to get it in the closing stages. 147-game veteran checks out at right guard A broken right ankle sent Mike Onwenu to injured reserve after the home opener at Gillette Stadium. And in the absence of an offensive lineman whose tenure dates back to the 2020 draft class, an August signing was turned to on the road. Sunday would be the 147th game and 106th start in Greg Van Roten’s NFL career. But the 36-year-old CFL alum was announced as questionable to return before halftime due to a thigh injury. Walter Rouse replaced him at right guard for his first offensive snaps of September. That was the move next to right tackle Morgan Moses, who had given up an early pressure and was penalized for holding as a 21-yard touchdown scramble disappeared. The rest of the starting unit went forward with center Jared Wilson, left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker and left tackle Will Campbell. Two sacks were in the cards for Jacksonville’s pass rush. No. 28 overall pick Caleb Lomu reported as a jumbo tight end for New England before taking over at right tackle in the fourth quarter. Patriots fans, join the game-day huddle! Follow every snap and discuss every decision with fellow fans on the SB Nation app. Connect through our live game chat Browse with fewer ads Seamlessly move between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Lawrence delivers three touchdowns, one pick “I think he is just much more decisive and comfortable. I think you could always count on some turnovers, maybe three or four years ago. I don’t think that is necessarily the case now.” Trevor Lawrence lived up to what Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel told reporters during his midweek press conference . The Jaguars quarterback completed 19-of-29 passes for 182 yards with three touchdowns and one turnover on Sunday before backup Quinn Ewers took the keys. Jacksonville got the afternoon underway with penalty flags and two quick punts. The third drive stayed alive with conversions on third down, however, and ended with a 12-yard touchdown over the middle to wide receiver Josh Cameron. Marcus Jones was in position to respond. He turned a tipped ball from a trade pickup ’s coverage into an interception at the 11:13 mark in the second quarter. But the Jaguars answered right back with old friend Jakobi Meyers slicing through zone coverage for a 10-yard touchdown. By halftime, the offense stood 3-of-6 on third down and 2-of-2 in the red zone while averaging 5.5 yards per play. And the Patriots captain and nickelback who picked off a pass before intermission was tried on back-to-back throws in the red zone after it. Favorite target Parker Washington capitalized on the size advantage with a 17-yard touchdown as Jacksonville’s lead extended to 21-3 and then some. Veteran Carlton Davis III made his return opposite All-Pro Christian Gonzalez and had a hand in one tackle for loss and one pass breakup on screens. Safeties Jaylen Reed and Kevin Byard III accompanied the cornerbacks with Craig Woodson on the wrong side of questionable due to a shoulder injury and Dell Pettus on injured reserve . Amid the attrition in the secondary, Mike Brown got the call as a standard elevation from the practice squad. Young edge rushers split New England’s lone sack The Patriots ruled out veteran Dre’Mont Jones on the final injury report and placed rookie Quintayvious Hutchins on IR soon after. But the outside linebacker room traveled to Duval County with what it had. It had a Cal Poly product who arrived as an undrafted free agent in 2025 and an Illinois product who arrived at No. 55 overall in 2026. Elijah Ponder started on Sunday. Gabe Jacas rotated in. The young tandem entered the afternoon having already combined for two sacks, one interception, one fumble recovery and one touchdown in September. Both were flagged for neutral zone infractions during an afternoon in which the Patriots collectively racked up nine penalties. But both split the defense’s only sack in bending fashion, as well, at the 3:02 mark in the third quarter. Rounding out the edge department, New England recently promoted Jose Ramirez from the practice squad to the active roster and he notched the game’s initial tackle in kickoff coverage. The starting base front on Sunday included Milton Williams, Cory Durden and elevation Jeremiah Pharms Jr. in the middle of things. The defensive linemen were joined off the ball by the blitzing Robert Spillane, Christian Elliss as well as waiver claim Darius Muasau. Jacksonville’s two-headed backfield of Bhayshul Tuten and Chris Rodriguez Jr. finished the…

title: Game Recap: Saints host Raiders in home opener
summary: The New Orleans Saints at last played their home opener when they hosted the Las Vegas Raiders in the late window on Sunday afternoon. Here’s a look back at all that went down in the Caesars Superdome. First Quarter The hosts received the opening kickoff but went three-and-out. The Raiders, meanwhile, found instant momentum as […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - SEPTEMBER 27: Chris Olave #12 of the New Orleans Saints stretches for a first down as Isaiah Pola-Mao #20 of the Las Vegas Raiders makes the tackle during the fourth quarter at Caesars Superdome on September 27, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints at last played their home opener when they hosted the Las Vegas Raiders in the late window on Sunday afternoon. Here’s a look back at all that went down in the Caesars Superdome. First Quarter The hosts received the opening kickoff but went three-and-out. The Raiders, meanwhile, found instant momentum as Kirk Cousins completed his first four throws for 53 yards, including three receptions by tight end Brock Bowers who was suiting up for the first time this season. But after an offensive holding and a sack by Chase Young, the defense was able to hold Vegas to a field goal attempt. Matt Gay converted from 41 yards. The Saints faced another quick three-and-out as they began their ensuing series, but a huge 3rd down scramble from Tyler Shough for 36 yards kicked the offense into life. Travis Etienne Jr had some work on the ground, and Shough found Devaughn Vele and Chris Olave for double-digit gains as the Saints entered the red zone. CJ Donaldson would then run for 5 yards to set up a 2-yard touchdown throw from Shough to Juwan Johnson. Daniel Carlson’s extra point was blocked by his former team, so the score remained 6-3. Second Quarter The Raiders began their next drive at the 40 after the kickoff fell short of the landing zone. They drove past midfield with a run from Mike Washington, before Cousins found Michael Mayer for 18 yards. An offside penalty helped the defensive effort as the Saints were able to force another field goal attempt, which Gay converted from 37 yards to tie the game at 6-6. New Orleans then went three-and-out, and punted to the visitors who began the ensuing possession at midfield. The Raiders took full advantage, with Cousins continuing to find Mayer and Bowers as they entered the red zone. The Saints thought they’d done enough to keep Vegas out of the end zone again, but a roughing the passer penalty against Danny Stutsman for what looked like a perfect hit on the quarterback gave the Raiders 1st-and-goal. Cousins found Mayer for the 3-yard score, and the visitors took a 13-6 lead. Etienne had a few short gains on the ground to begin the Saints’ next possession, before Shough found Olave twice in a row for a total of 29 yards. He then found his tight ends Noah Fant and Johnson, before another short run from Etienne put the ball at the 3-yard line. Shough found Fant in the end zone for the score, and Carlson’s extra point levelled the game at 13-13. Cousins ran a successful two-minute drill before the half, helped by another pair of big gains through Bowers. A 25-yard field goal from Gay gave Vegas a 16-13 lead as time expired. Third Quarter The Raiders went three-and-out to begin the second half. Shough continued to have success moving the football as he returned to the field, with passes to Vele and Etienne alongside runs from Alvin Kamara moving the black and gold past midfield. Shough continued to sling it, connecting with Johnson, Vele, and Olave to move the hosts to the 1-yard line. It was Johnson again who caught another touchdown pass, continuing the game of the tight-ends. Trailing 20-16, the Raiders return-man Dylan Laube then fumbled the kickoff return. The Saints recovered, and took instant advantage. Etienne broke out a 16-yard run before Shough threw to Fant for a 16-yard touchdown pass, and just like that the hosts were up 27-16. But the Raiders did well to respond, as Bowers continued his dominant display with a 20-yard catch to move the drive past midfield. Before long, Washington ran in a 36-yard touchdown to cut into the lead. After an unsuccessful 2-point conversion attempt, the score remained 27-22. The team exchanged quick punts after that, before an 11-yard pass from Shough to Olave on 3rd down extended the ensuing series for the black and gold and put them into Vegas territory. Fourth Quarter Shough converted another 3rd down to Olave a few plays later. But with the Saints on the edge of field goal range, Shough was sacked and stripped by Malcolm Koonce as he intended to throw, in the same fashion that Chase Young got to Jared Goff in Week 1. The fumble was recovered by the defense, but this time, the ruling on the field stood and Vegas would take over. Cousins found Ashton Jeanty for 22 yards to begin the drive, before connecting with Tre Tucker for 15 yards a few plays later. Cody White would catch the short touchdown to restore the lead for the visitors. After another failed 2-point conversion, they led just 28-27. But the Saints’ woes would then continue as Shough’s pass for Bryce Lance was picked off by Hezekiah Masses. Masses then fumbled himself, but the Raiders fell on it again and had 1st-and-goal from the 4-yard line. The Saints stopped Jeanty twice before on 3rd down Cousins connected with Bowers in the end zone, and the Raiders went up 35-27. Still just a one-score game, the Saints did promptly enter the red zone helped by runs from Kamara and a 22-yard throw to Johnson. But Shough fumbled as he was sacked again, with Maxx Crosby forcing the ball out. The defense forced the Raiders into a quick punt to keep hopes alive. But in the two-minute drill, Johnson fumbled after a catch near midfield as turnovers continued to mount for the black and gold. The Raiders jumped on it, and knelt out the clock from there to secure a 35-27 win. The Saints’ focus now turns to Monday Night Football when they host the Atlanta Falcons in a week’s time.
author: Sam Mackenzie

title: Ups and downs from Saints vs. Raiders
summary: The New Orleans Saints fell to 1-2 after a fourth-quarter meltdown to the Las Vegas Raiders, allowing 19 unanswered points. While the Saints looked to have finally fixed their slow starts, other problems arose, and there are more questions than answers. Up: RB Travis Etienne Jr. Through the first two weeks of the regular season, […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - SEPTEMBER 27: Ashton Jeanty #2 of the Las Vegas Raiders is tackled by Kool-Aid McKinstry #1 of the New Orleans Saints during the second quarter at Caesars Superdome on September 27, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Morgan Simmons/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints fell to 1-2 after a fourth-quarter meltdown to the Las Vegas Raiders, allowing 19 unanswered points. While the Saints looked to have finally fixed their slow starts, other problems arose, and there are more questions than answers. Up: RB Travis Etienne Jr. Through the first two weeks of the regular season, the Saints haven’t seen the production match the large contract they gave running back Travis Etienne Jr. The fifth-year running back signed a $48 million deal in the offseason and headlined the New Orleans’ expensive running game rebuild. Fortunately for the Saints, Etienne finally started to find consistency as a runner during their home opener against the Raiders. Unfortunately for New Orleans, Etienne would leave the game in the third quarter and not return. Etienne ended the day with 13 carries for 57 yards, averaging 4.4 yards per carry. The Saints entered the day with a clear game plan: get Etienne involved. He was a valuable part of the team’s first-half scoring drives and was on his way to having his best day as a Saint. But after Etienne left, the wind was taken out of the Saints’ sails, and it was clear he was pivotal to their game plan. Up: DE Chase Young Defensive end Chase Young continues his strong season, following his 1.5-sack game with 2 sacks on Sunday. Young ended the day with 2 tackles, 2 sacks, and 2 tackles for loss. Young is a game wrecker. Opposing offenses are accounting for him on every down, and he creates chaos when rushing the passer. The eighth-year pass rusher is finally blossoming into the star he was projected to be when he was drafted second overall, and you can look for him to make a play when the Saints need him the most. While the rest of the Saints’ defense struggled during Sunday’s loss, Young came out with a strong showing. Down: Magical Fourth Quarter We’ve spent all week analyzing the Saints’ slow starts and monster fourth quarters, exclaiming, “If only they could play in the first half how they play in the fourth quarter.” Well, we finally saw the Saints’ start significantly quicker, finding the end zone twice and scoring 13 points in the first half, compared to just 6 over their first two games. While the Saints finally found the answers to scoring in the first half, they suffered a complete meltdown in the fourth quarter, turning the ball over four times and allowing 13 points. The Saints’ monster fourth quarters weren’t going to last forever, but the meltdown was a complete counter to the strong showings we’ve seen in the past weeks. Simply put, if New Orleans was even 20% as good as they’ve been in the fourth quarter this season on Sunday, they would’ve come out with the win. The loss falls mainly on the offenses’ inability to protect the ball and run the clock. Down: Defense By far the biggest standout from Sunday’s loss was the defense’s inability to stop the Raiders from scoring. Las Vegas started the game scoring on each of their first four drives, and scored on 7 of their 11 offensive drives. The Raiders established early on that they wanted to get superstar tight end Brock Bowers the ball, and the Saints failed to successfully counter it. New Orleans even assigned their best cornerback, Kool-Aid McKinstry, to mirror Bowers, but he still came away with 10 receptions for 116 yards and a touchdown. It also appeared the Saints defense was too content after going up 27-16, with the following drive being too easy and efficient for the Raiders offense. After New Orleans scored a touchdown to go up 11, the defense allowed a five-play, 71-yard drive. The Saints defense was the backbone of the team during their rebuilding season last year, with defensive coordinator Brandon Staley’s name lingering around a possible head coaching return. But over the first three weeks of the season, New Orleans is allowing 27 points per game.

full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - JANUARY 04: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints rushes against Kaden Elliss #55 of the Atlanta Falcons during the second half of the game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints are now 1-2 after falling to the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday night at the Caesars Superdome in a game that featured what was another very controversial call by the officials. The call came in the fourth quarter when Raiders defensive end Malcolm Koonce hit Tyler Shough as he attempted to throw. The officials ruled that Shough lost control of the ball before his hand began moving forward, making it a fumble rather than an incomplete pass. The ruling was upheld after review, giving Las Vegas possession and adding another frustrating chapter in the book of discrepancies from NFL officiating. Unfortunately, that fumble became the turning point of the game as the Saints were leading 27-22 and we’re at Raiders’ 30-yard line with a chance to extend their lead when Shough lost the ball. Instead, the Raiders were given possession and scored shortly after to take a 28-27 lead. The turnover resulted in a complete shift in momentum for the Saints, becoming the first of four straight possessions to end in turnovers as the Raiders scored the final 19 points of the game. The Saints will look to bounce back this week in what will be an emotional matchup against the Atlanta Falcons. The game will recognize the 20th anniversary of the historic “Domecoming” game, when New Orleans returned to the Superdome for the first time following the devastation of Hurricane Katrina. With one of the NFL’s biggest rivalries taking center stage, there is certainly no love lost between these two teams. Under the bright lights of Monday Night Football, with a national audience watching, both teams will have plenty to prove as they write the next chapter in their heated NFC South feud. According to FanDuel, the Saints are currently 2.5-point favorites against the Falcons, with an over/under of 48.5 points. However, those odds could move as kickoff approaches. title: J.J. McCarthy trade: NY Giants acquire quarterback from Minnesota Vikings
summary: The New York Giants are acquiring quarterback J.J. McCarthy from the Minnesota Vikings, per a report from NFL insider Ian Rapoport. Per Jordan Schultz, the Giants are sending a 2027 fifth-round pick to the Vikings for McCarthy. The Vikings have confirmed the trade. The Giants, of course, lost starting quarterback Jaxson Dart for the season […]
full_text: J.J. McCarthy | Getty Images The New York Giants are acquiring quarterback J.J. McCarthy from the Minnesota Vikings , per a report from NFL insider Ian Rapoport. Per Jordan Schultz , the Giants are sending a 2027 fifth-round pick to the Vikings for McCarthy. The Vikings have confirmed the trade . The Giants, of course, lost starting quarterback Jaxson Dart for the season with a knee injury during their Week 2 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. Jameis Winston’s play since has been uninspiring, and the only other quarterback on the roster was journeyman Jake Haener. The Giants had an opportunity to draft the 23-year-old McCarthy out of Michigan with the sixth overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft. They passed on McCarthy, as well as Bo Nix and Michael Penix, to select wide receiver Malik Nabers. The Vikings took McCarthy No. 10 overall. That, of course, worked out well for the Giants. Nabers had a sensational rookie season, and the Giants were able to move up in the 2025 NFL Draft to select Dart as their quarterback of the future. Things did not go well for McCarthy in Minnesota. McCarthy missed all of his rookie season with a torn meniscus in his right knee. He started 10 games for the Vikings last season, compiling a 6-4 record. He completed 140 of 243 passes (jusy 57.6%) for 1,623 yards with 11 touchdowns, 12 interceptions and a 72.6 passer rating. This offseason, the Vikings signed veteran Kyler Murray as a free agent. McCarthy not only lost a competition with Murray for the starting job, but ended up as the No. 3 quarterback in Minnesota behind Murray and Carson Wentz. Now, he will join the Giants. In his recently-launched Substack, ‘The Sweep’, NFL insider Tom Pelissero said this about why the Giants made the deal: The Giants extensively scouted McCarthy (and the rest of the 2024 quarterback class) before deciding to wait and taking Dart in 2025. McCarthy’s athletic ability and play style is a fit for the offense that OC Matt Nagy and company built for Dart, and he should be capable of running many of the QB movement concepts that figure to be dormant as long as Winston, a pocket passer, is in the lineup. At age 23, McCarthy is less than four months older than Dart. He’s 6-4 as an NFL starter. He’s cost-controlled for 2027. And in the event McCarthy takes over and flourishes down the stretch this season, the Giants have the right to exercise his fifth-year option for 2028. The Giants are now spending a healthy amount of money on quarterbacks who will be backups to Dart after this season. The financials for the #Giants : Just under $1m for McCarthy this season. Next year, they’re on the hook for $3.775m fully guaranteed. They owe Jameis Winston just over $6m fully guaranteed in 2027 as part of his new deal. https://t.co/zV8V3ZmFap — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) September 28, 2026 Valentine’s View While I figured the Giants were going to be aggressive in the quarterback market after McCarthy’s injury, this is not a move I expected them to make. The Giants spent a massive amount of time with McCarthy prior to the 2024 draft, concluding in the end that he was not the right quarterback for them. Maybe the Dart injury, and what they saw on the market made them view McCarthy differently. Maybe John Harbaugh had a different impression of McCarthy than Joe Schoen and the Giants’ scouts when the Ravens studied him in 2024. Maybe Harbaugh’s brother, Jim, gave his brother a glowing recommendation of McCarthy. Jay Glazer is reporting that John Harbaugh did speak to his brother about McCarthy before the Giants made the deal. Maybe the idea of adding another 23-year-old quarterback with NFL experience and upside was too good for the Giants to pass up. Both as a hedge against Winston’s ups and downs, and perhaps as a long-term option if Dart doesn’t become what the Giants believe he will. I have mixed feelings about the trade. If McCarthy couldn’t handle Minnesota or succeed with quarterback guru Kevin O’Connell as his coach, what makes the Giants believe he can succeed in New York? Does this open them to questions about whether they full believe in Dart’s future? I can’t blame them for taking a big swing and getting the best quarterback they could get. And, I certainly think this is a better swing than Justin Fields or Gardner Minshew. It just comes with a lot of questions. Vote in the poll and let us know what you think of the move, Giants fans.

title: Giants-Titans: 5 plays that led to the Giants’ Week 3 victory
summary: The New York Giants improved to 2-1 after their 12-7 victory in the rainy conditions at MetLife Stadium on Sunday. The Giants’ special teams helped secure the win, with Jordan Stout averaging 53 yards on five punts and rookie kicker Dominic Zvada booting all four of his attempts for the 12 points the Jameis Winston-led […]
full_text: The New York Giants improved to 2-1 after their 12-7 victory in the rainy conditions at MetLife Stadium on Sunday. The Giants’ special teams helped secure the win, with Jordan Stout averaging 53 yards on five punts and rookie kicker Dominic Zvada booting all four of his attempts for the 12 points the Jameis Winston-led offense scored. Winston didn’t prove he should be the Giants’ quarterback for the rest of the season, but he did enough to secure the win. The Giants possessed the football for nine more minutes than the Titans, and the Giants were penalized ten times for 88 yards. The Titans ended up outgaining the Giants 262 yards to 238. Both offenses were inefficient on third down; the Giants went 4 of 13 and the Titans 5 of 13 — all five in the second half. Arvell Reese led the Giants with 12 tackles, with Dru Phillips recording 11 and Tremaine Edmunds recording 10. However, the vaunted Giants’ pass rush lost Brian Burns midway through the game to a right knee injury, and the Giants did not sack Ward once in the game. The defense bent badly in the second half after a hot start. It’s something to monitor moving forward. The Giants were lucky enough to escape with a win against the Titans, and here are five plays that were crucial for one reason or another. Play 1: Jevon Holland! Holland has an interception in each game so far this season — none bigger than this game-sealing pick: JEVON HOLLAND CALLS GAME @TENvsNYG on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/ECvOY9ckOt — NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026 Holland’s patience and vision were exceptional on this play against the second-year signal caller. Holland started to close width on Ward, who was scrambling to the boundary, but the safety read the quarterback’s eyes and sank underneath the route breaking behind him. Holland intercepted the pass and secured the Giants’ second win of the season. Holland is having a fantastic season for the Giants. Play(s) 2: FIVE three-and-outs to start Brian Daboll’s return did not go as planned in the rainy, windy conditions of East Rutherford, N.J. New York’s defense shut down Tennessee’s rushing attack, holding them to 13 first-half rushing yards, an average of 2.2 yards per carry. The first Tennessee drives resulted in three-and-outs, resulting in 32 total yards. Wan’Dale Robinson failed to secure two catchable passes, and the offense struggled to do anything against the Giants until the two-minute drill. The Titans did respond well in the second half. Brian Daboll started attacking the Giants on quick out routes, which allowed Cam Ward to get into a rhythm. The Titans finished the day with a twelve-play drive and two thirteen-play drives. Unfortunately, for Tennessee, it resulted in just one touchdown and the aformentioned Jevon Holland — game-sealing — interception. Play 3: 59-yard field goal try Tennessee drove the football to the Giants’ 41-yard line, and Robert Saleh opted to kick a 59-yard field goal, down 6-0. Joey Slye missed the kick, and the Giants took over with 41 seconds left in the first half. Jameis Winston threw two incompletions and then found Malik Nabers on a quick slant that converted the third-and-10. He then found Darnell Mooney for 7yards to help set up Dominic Zvada’s third field goal, a 39-yarder that gave the Giants a two-possession lead. Play(s) 4: Fourth-down stop The Giants with a big third quarter fourth down stop against the Titans, who remain scoreless. pic.twitter.com/yPcuwexLfx — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) September 27, 2026 The Titans had a 12-play, 62-yard drive that yielded zero points after Cam Ward sailed this ball incomplete. The Giants’ defense bent through the drive, surrendered a 20-yard completion to Carnell Tate and a 12-yard run by Tony Pollard. Still, the Giants defense clamped down with deceptive pressure looks in the red area that resulted in two incomplete passes. Ward missed an open Tate in the end zone on the third-and-goal play. Play 5: Cam Skattebo the receiver The Jameis of all Jameis plays. pic.twitter.com/ImklXwdBv8 — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) September 27, 2026 Points were hard to come by in this sloppy, weathered game, but the Giants broke the 0-0 tie after this third-and-seven conversion by Jameis Winston to running back Cam Skattebo. Matt Nagy called a familiar 3×1 look with the pivot/corner to the three-receiver side and the running back releasing toward the lone receiver side; Skattebo does a great job extending his route downfield, and Winston took a SHOT as he released to the open back. In patented fashion, Skattebo finishes the play with tenacity.
author: Nick Falato

title: ‘Things I think’: The Giants won, but to keep doing that they must get better
summary: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — To win a decent number of football games this season, the New York Giants are going to have to be better — much better — than they were Sunday against the Tennessee Titans. They survived the Titans — a bad 0-3 football team — on Sunday, thanks to a brilliant game-saving […]
full_text: Jevon Holland makes the game-saving interception on Sunday. | Getty Images EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — To win a decent number of football games this season, the New York Giants are going to have to be better — much better — than they were Sunday against the Tennessee Titans. They survived the Titans — a bad 0-3 football team — on Sunday, thanks to a brilliant game-saving interception in the end zone by the suddenly ball-hawking Jevon Holland. Until the Holland play, the second half had all the earmarks of the kind of fourth-quarter collapse the Giants suffered five times last season en route to a miserable 4-13 record. The kind of fourth-quarter collapse the Giants hope will become a rarity rather than a rule with the highly-successful John Harbaugh now installed as head coach. A win is a win is a win. The Giants are 2-1, and no one is going to apologize for how they got there. “That’s just how it is. I told them that’s really how it works most of the time.,” Harbaugh said after the game. ‘I mean, there’s very few wins where you walk in and you’re really happy with everything. Where you feel like you played this great, amazing game. And even when you did, even the few times you have those games, you go back, you look at tape and you’re disappointed by a bunch of stuff. “Football is really – it’s crazy. It’s crazy out there. So, that’s what it’s all about. It’s finding a way to win a rough game. It’s just – they’re never pretty. They’re never perfect. But they need to be us doing what we need to do to win games. Find a way to win games in those kinds of moments.” Thanks to Holland, the Giants did that. They can also thank rookie placekicker Dominic Zvada for going 4 of 4 on field goals, punter Jordan Stout for constantly backing the Titans up, a running game that did just enough, and quarterback Jameis Winston for avoiding a fatal mistake that would have doomed the Giants to a loss they couldn’t have afforded. “There’s plenty of times we could have put this game away. We should have put this game away. We’re going to look at our red zone offense and be really, really unhappy about the penalties. I mean, you get the ball down there inside the 5, inside the 10, and we penalize ourselves out of scoring position. That’s going to be, obviously, a major point of emphasis. So, to your point – but then our kicker – our kicker comes in there, our rookie kicker, in these kind of conditions, and kicks all those field goals. I’m really proud of him for that.” The Giants won the game. That’s important. Winning is the bottom line. How doesn’t really matter. Well, in this case, maybe it does. This is a game the Giants almost certainly would have lost a year ago, when they blew five fourth-quarter leads. It is a game they looked like they would lose until Holland read Ward’s intent to throw rather than run, sat in the end zone, and made a play when Ward threw the ball low enough that he could get his hands on it. Veteran tight end Chris Manhertz lived through all of those losses last season. He admitted thinking about them from the sideline as he watched Tennessee’s final drive, helped by an Elijah Campbell kick catch interference penalty and a fourth-and-1 encroachment penalty on Tremaine Edmunds, unfold. “It definitely did,” Manhertz said. “I do question last year if we would have been able to pull that one out. I think it’s a testament to the players we hsve, the leaders we have, and just having a mentality of finding a way to win. “It’s not going to be pretty, but players make plays. Jevon made a helluva play, and we go home in peace tonight.” Andrew Thomas, who has lived through a lot of difficult losses in six-plus seasons with the Giants, said he was focusing on “the task at hand” rather than the past. “It’s the National Football League, so whenever you get a win, it takes great players to make great plays and we have the safety that made a play a game to win it,” Thomas said. “To win in this league, it’s not an easy thing to do. So for us to do it, I’m proud of the guys. Obviously, there’s things that we can clean up, even going back to the Dallas game. “When you play well and you win a game and you feel like you play well, there’s things to clean up. So that’s the approach you have regardless. But like I said, we’re happy to have the win.” The Giants have a lot to clean up Let’s be honest. The Giants were fortunate on Sunday to be playing the Titans. As I said above, a win is a win. There are not, though, a lot of teams the Giants would have beaten on Sunday. They were fortunate that Holland made a phenomenal play to prevent a devastating loss. They were fortunate that Ward somehow sailed a pass over the head of a wide open Carnell Tate on third-and-5 from the Giants 7-yard line, leading to a turnover on downs. The Giants committed 10 penalties for 88 yards. Some of those limited the number of points the Giants had the opportunity to score. Two of them helped Tennessee on its final drive. The Giants passed for only 118 yards. To be fair, the conditions were miserable and the Giants’ biggest ask of Jameis Winston on Sunday was to not screw the game up. The pass rush was, again, non-existent. Improving that is not going to be easy now that it appears Brian Burns is lost for the season with a torn ACL. Keeping Kayvon proves prescient Remember all that chatter about trading Kayvon Thibodeaux? Well, the Giants certainly have to be happy that they didn’t do what it seemed everyone tried to get them to do and move on from him. Thibodeaux will now return to being a full-time starter, and a massively important player for the remainder of the season. If he plays well, Thibodeaux can help the Giants immensely the rest of the season, and set himself up for a massive payday in the offseason. The biggest decision comes at quarterback The Giants will add at least one quarterback to their roster, perhaps as early as Monday morning. Winston, though, is going to be the quarterback this Sunday against the Arizona Cardinals. No matter who the Giants sign or trade for, it is going to take that quarterback time to learn the system. Winston is going to be the quarterback, at least for a while. For better or worse. Winston said his job Sunday was to “do what’s required” to win. “Focus on protecting football, being efficient on first and second down. And eliminating negative plays,” he said. “Every quarterback is really judged off if they won or lost the game. So, I’m grateful that I get to be judged off of [a win], not a loss. And I’ve had games where I’ve thrown for 500 yards, right, and the game didn’t turn out the way I wanted it to be. And anytime, any day, I would rather win.” The Giants, without Jaxson Dart and now Burns for the season, are clearly not tossing in the towel on a season that has 14 games remaining. They will eventually find themselves needing to decide whether or not Winston is the quarterback who gives them the best chance to win games. Facing that decision so soon after giving Winston a two-year, $13 million contract extension makes it fair to wonder what the Giants were thinking when they gave Winston that deal. For now, though, the Giants are 2-1. That is a lot better place than they could have been this morning. As Manhertz said, they are “at peace.” They need to get better. Much better. Still, it is better to know that and be 2-1 than 1-2 or 0-3.
author: Ed Valentine

title: Brian Burns injury: NY Giants’ star suffered season-ending torn ACL, per report
summary: New York Giants star pass rusher Brian Burns suffered a torn right ACL on Sunday against the Tennessee Titans, per a report from Ian Rapoport. The injury didn’t look good in the moment, with Burns holding his knee on the ground in obvious pain and pounding the turf in frustration. Despite that, Giants’ head coach […]
full_text: New York Giants pass rusher Brian Burns on the ground Sunday after injuring his knee. | Getty Images New York Giants star pass rusher Brian Burns suffered a torn right ACL on Sunday against the Tennessee Titans, per a report from Ian Rapoport . The injury didn’t look good in the moment, with Burns holding his knee on the ground in obvious pain and pounding the turf in frustration. Despite that, Giants’ head coach John Harbaugh said after the game that there was “some hope” regarding Burns’ injury. That hope, it appears, was in vain as Burns’ season is over. This is the Giants’ second season-ending knee injury to a star player in as many weeks, with quarterback Jaxson Dart suffering a knee injury against the Los Angeles Rams. Burns was playing through an ankle sprain he suffered at the end of the Giants’ loss to the Rams last week. It was a surprise that he even took the field against the Titans, given the sloppy, rainy conditions and the fact that Burns didn’t practice at all during the week. Burns’ presence on the field against Tennessee is a testament to his toughness, but that won’t get him back on the field in 2026. Instead, he’ll be relying on that toughness to push through his eventual rehab for a return in 2027. The Giants will now rely on Abdul Carter and Kayvon Thibodeaux as their starting edge defenders. The team came into the season with just three dedicated outside linebackers, though they can also use Chauncey Golston and rookie Arvell Reese in that role on occasion. The Giants also have Trace Ford, who had a promising preseason, on their practice squad. Even so, this is a significant loss for a Giants’ defense that has been very uneven through the first three games of the season.
author: Chris Pflum

title: NY Giants vs. Arizona Cardinals odds: Opening lines for Week 4 matchup
summary: The New York Giants open Week 4 as scant 1.5-point favorites against the Arizona Cardinals, per FandDuel Sportsbook. The Giants escaped a rainy, windy Week 3 game against the Tennessee Titans with a win. It wasn’t pretty, and the Giants desperately needed Jevon Holland to continue to rack up turnovers, but New York came away […]
full_text: The New York Giants open Week 4 as scant 1.5-point favorites against the Arizona Cardinals, per FandDuel Sportsbook . The Giants escaped a rainy, windy Week 3 game against the Tennessee Titans with a win. It wasn’t pretty, and the Giants desperately needed Jevon Holland to continue to rack up turnovers, but New York came away with a 12-7 victory and is now 2-1 on the season. It was an ugly performance by the offense, with Najee Harris, Cam Skattebo, and Malik Nabers doing just enough to put Dominic Zvada in position to kick four field goals. The Giants defense, meanwhile, played great in the first half, but was a sieve in the second — and lost star pass rusher Brian Burns to a potentially serious knee injury in the process. Burns’ status is unknown as of this writing. The Giants will finally have a normal week of preparation. Will that be enough for the Giants to field a functional offense with Jameis Winston at quarterback? Whether they win or lose will likely depend on whether the offense can find traction against the Cardinals’ unconventional defensive scheme. Giants fans: Make your pick in the SB Nation app!
