title: Mike McCarthy’s proactive approach was key component in Steelers Week 3 win
summary: The first two weeks of the season proved to become a showcase of low-quality offensive line play for the Pittsburgh Steelers. Over those first two games, Aaron Rodgers was pressured 37 times – the fourth-most in the NFL. Mike McCarthy clearly saw enough of that and made sweeping changes up front by pulling Spencer Anderson […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 27: Head coach Mike McCarthy of the Pittsburgh Steelers looks on during the second quarter against the Cincinnati Bengals at Acrisure Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images The first two weeks of the season proved to become a showcase of low-quality offensive line play for the Pittsburgh Steelers. Over those first two games, Aaron Rodgers was pressured 37 times – the fourth-most in the NFL. Mike McCarthy clearly saw enough of that and made sweeping changes up front by pulling Spencer Anderson and Dylan Cook in favor of Brock Hoffman and rookie Max Iheanachor. The early results? Rodgers had an average of 3.19 seconds to throw – his highest mark as a Steeler, per Ben Solak of ESPN . Additionally, the extra time allowed Rodgers to launch 15 passes of 10+ yards downfield, the most he’s ever had in a Steelers uniform, as well, as Pittsburgh defeated the Cincinnati Bengals 30-27. In recent years, this wouldn’t have happened. The Steelers would have trudged through mud for at least the first month of the season, trying to solve problems with the same solutions and wondering why things wouldn’t get better while the offense continued to struggle. Mike McCarthy is showing he is not Mike Tomlin, though, and became proactive, making changes when it was clear they needed to be made. On top of Rodgers having an efficient day, the Steelers finally found some semblance of a rushing attack. After a combined 149 rushing yards over the first two games, Pittsburgh rushed for 138 against the Bengals, including 127 from Jaylen Warren. The Steelers entered Week 3 ranking 27th in EPA per rush and 31st in rush success rate, per Sumer Sports. In Week 3 thus far, however, Pittsburgh ranks fourth in EPA per rush and jumped up to 11th in success rate. Had an 87-yard carry not been wiped out by a questionable holding call, those numbers would be even higher. And when Warren rushed to the right side, he totaled 39 yards on eight carries – just shy of five yards a pop. It wasn’t just offensive changes that were made, either. As Chris Carter of the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette pointed out, the Steelers took Samuel off the field in favor of rookie third-round pick Daylen Everette after Samuel was struggling to slow down Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins. It's possible the #Steelers benched Asante Samuel Jr. because of the size mismatch against Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins. Both were out-physicaling him. Daylen Everette is bigger and might hold up there better. — Christopher Carter (@CarterCritiques) September 27, 2026 Would we have seen a veteran benched mid-game for a rookie under the previous regime? It’s hard to remember many examples of that taking place. Credit to McCarthy for a high-quality coaching job in Week 3. He could have sat on his hands and continued throwing the same thing at the wall, hoping it stuck. Instead, he got rid of what wasn’t working and tried something new. It could have failed, but what they were doing was already failing, and he knew that. His decision-making was the difference in Pittsburgh being 2-1 rather than 1-2. Now, they have a chance to leave Week 4 at 3-1 and in sole possession of first place in the AFC North. Let us know what you think in the comments . title: Steelers stock report after upset win over Bengals
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers offense came alive in their 30-27 win over the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 3. Pittsburgh’s offense racked up 411 yards as their offense finally looks to be on track, and they head into Week 4 with a 2-1 record. As always, here is this week’s stock report after the Steelers’ thrilling victory. […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 27: Ben Skowronek #15 of the Pittsburgh Steelers celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Cincinnati Bengals during an NFL football game at Acrisure Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers offense came alive in their 30-27 win over the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 3. Pittsburgh’s offense racked up 411 yards as their offense finally looks to be on track, and they head into Week 4 with a 2-1 record. As always, here is this week’s stock report after the Steelers’ thrilling victory. Stock Up Offensive Line The Steelers shifted around their offensive line today, giving rookie first-rounder Max Iheanachor the nod at right tackle, and giving veteran Brock Hoffman the start at right guard. Things looked much better for the Steelers offensively today, as they totaled 430 yards of total offense. The running game was much improved, and despite a few drops from the receivers, Rodgers threw for three touchdowns. All of that starts with the revamped offensive line, which could very well be the key to unlocking the Steelers’ offense. WR Ben Skowronek What a game for Pittsburgh’s do-it-all guy. Skowronek doesn’t get many reps as a receiver, but made the most of his time on the field in the first quarter as he hauled in a 22-yard touchdown from Aaron Rodgers. Skowronek also recovered a muffed punt in the fourth quarter, allowing the Steelers to tie the game at 27. It was a huge day for the special teams ace who continues to make an impact wherever he is needed. RB Jaylen Warren Jaylen Warren fully deserves to be the Steelers’ bell cow back moving forward. With fellow running back Rico Dowdle inactive, it was Warren’s first chance this season to get the majority of the touches. It’s safe to say he made the most of his opportunity. Warren turned 17 carries into 175 yards, good for 7.5 yards per carry. Warren also added 49 yards on three catches. The back was the heart and soul of the Steelers offense today and was a large part of the offense’s success today. DT Derrick Harmon Harmon made the play of the day with the strip sack of Joe Burrow, as Sebastian Joseph-Day recovered. The bull rush of Harmon moved the Steelers to 2-1 on the season. The defensive lineman continues to make strides in his second season. Stock Down WR Roman Wilson Wilson’s day started strong, as he caught two balls on the team’s opening drive. However, Wilson had a ball bounce off his hands that led to an interception in the second quarter. After that, it was rookie second-round pick Germie Bernard who was on the field for the majority of the second half. I thought I was going to be putting Wilson in the “stock up” category today, but the inconsistencies continue to haunt Wilson and cost him opportunities in the Steelers offense. Offensive Execution If you are going to complain about the Steelers offense at all today, you can reasonably be disappointed in how many times they were forced to use timeouts because they were simply not ready to snap the ball in time. The CBS broadcast even commented on how unusual it is for people who have worked together for so long like Rodgers and McCarthy, to have so many problems snapping the ball in time. Pittsburgh used all three of their timeouts in the first half within the first 22 minutes of game time due to problems either getting the play in or set. Although it was not as prevalent in the second half, the Steelers were forced to use at least one timeout because of similar issues. Today was a great step forward for the offense, but small things like snapping the ball in time and not wasting timeouts can certainly be cleaned up. Let us know what you think in the comments . title: Steelers offense comes to life in Week 3 win over Bengals
summary: After scoring just 16 points in the first two weeks of the season, the Pittsburgh Steelers’ offense erupted for 411 yards in a 30-27 win over the Cincinnati Bengals. The Steelers began the game with the ball and a new-look offensive line. Out were Spencer Anderson and Dylan Cook and in came Brock Hoffman and […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 27: Ben Skowronek #15 celebrates his touchdown with Aaron Rodgers #8 of the Pittsburgh Steelers during the first quarter against the Cincinnati Bengals at Acrisure Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images After scoring just 16 points in the first two weeks of the season, the Pittsburgh Steelers’ offense erupted for 411 yards in a 30-27 win over the Cincinnati Bengals. The Steelers began the game with the ball and a new-look offensive line. Out were Spencer Anderson and Dylan Cook and in came Brock Hoffman and Max Iheanachor. The Steelers offense looked terrific out of the gate and made it clear that Sunday would be the Jaylen Warren show. The dual-threat back caught a 30-yard pass on the first play of the game. Four plays later, Aaron Rodgers launched a 38-yard touchdown to Roman Wilson to give the Steelers a 7-0 lead. Cincinnati would answer back with an 11-play drive that ended with a Ja’Marr Chase touchdown. The Steelers, though, showed this would be a shootout early, as they responded with an 11-play touchdown drive of their own with Rodgers connecting with Ben Skowronek on a beautiful play design. The Steelers’ receiver came in motion and ran through the B gap as if he was going to lead block on a run. Instead, it was a play action pass and Rodgers hit Skowronek for a 23-yard touchdown. Rodgers had himself a vintage performance, going 19-of-34 for 292 yards, three touchdowns and one interception. His third touchdown pass came in the third quarter, as DK Metcalf and Michael Pittman ran overlapping crossers that caused a collision between a pair of Bengals defenders and left Metcalf wide open. The two plays that ended up deciding the game both came on Steelers punts. Cam Johnston was hit in the knee in the third quarter, which causes a roughing the kicker to be called. The Steelers kept the ball, which resulted in the Metcalf touchdown. Then, in the fourth quarter after the Bengals had taken a 27-24 lead, a muffed punt recovered by Skowronek set up the Steelers for a game-tying field goal. Pittsburgh’s defense held the Bengals to a three-and out, and the offense then drove 77 yards in eight plays to take a 30-27 lead on a Chris Boswell field goal. That still left Joe Burrow and the Bengals with just over two minutes to put together a potential game-winning drive – Derrick Harmon had other plans, though. On first down inside Steelers territory, the rising star defensive linemen busted through the Bengals’ offensive line, sacked Burrow, and forced a fumble that was recovered by Sebastian Joseph-Day, sealing the win and a 2-1 start for the Steelers. As mentioned earlier, the Steelers leaned on Jaylen Warren, who finished the day with 127 yards on the ground and 49 yards receiving. Pittsburgh’s ground game finally came to life, finishing the day with 138 yards after totaling less than 100 in each of the first two weeks. The offense as a whole nearly doubled its season total, overcoming a slow start in Weeks 1 and 2. The Steelers will now take their 2-1 record into Week 4, where they will kickoff the week on Thursday night on the road against the fellow 2-1 Cleveland Browns with a chance to take sole possession of the division lead. full_text: The Pittsburgh Steelers will feature an entirely new right side of their offensive line this week, according to NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport . First-round rookie Max Iheanachor is set to make his debut as a starter at right tackle, while Brock Hoffman will take over at right guard. Iheanachor has been pushing for an opportunity after showing promise during the preseason, while Dylan Cook had struggled to consistently secure the right tackle spot. Spencer Anderson started the first two games at right guard, but he’ll now take a seat in favor of the veteran Hoffman, who McCarthy is familiar with from their time in Dallas. With Aaron Rodgers at quarterback, protecting the pocket will always be a major priority. The Steelers will now turn to two new starters on the right side as they look to establish more stability up front. Let us know what you think in the comments . full_text: LANDOVER, MD - SEPTEMBER 27: Seahawks wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba (11) celebrates after his second touchdown catch of the game during the Seattle Seahawks versus Washington Commanders National Football League game at Northwest Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Landover, MD. For Smith-Njigba, it was more of the same — and kept him on a historic path to begin the 2026 season. 2ND OF THE DAY 😮‍💨 IT'S A TOUCHDOWN @jaxon_smith1 📺: @NFLonFOX pic.twitter.com/t4uZvbSJ23 — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) September 27, 2026 According to Seahawks PR , Smith-Njigba became the fourth player in the Super Bowl era with six touchdowns across the first three games of a season, after Calvin Johnson (2011), Marvin Harrison (1999), and Daryl Turner (1985). Smith Njigba’s consistency has him in incredible company, too. Mariota didn’t have to do a whole lot, but he made timely, accurate throws (including a couple of passes that were nearly caught […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks lost to the Marcus Mariota-led Washington Commanders on Sunday . While it’s one of the biggest upset losses the Seahawks have suffered in years, maybe we should’ve seen it coming. Mariota didn’t have to do a whole lot, but he made timely, accurate throws (including a couple of passes that were nearly caught or caught but marginally out of bounds), and cemented the game with a read-option keeper on a 3rd and long. Three touchdowns, no turnovers, and only one pass that was ever in serious jeopardy of being intercepted. And now, for your double depressing stat of the day, Mariota owns Seattle football teams. He’s had three cracks apiece against the Seahawks and Huskies and come out a winner every single time. Marcus Mariota has never lost to a team from Seattle 3-0 against the Seahawks and 3-0 against the Huskies — Curtis Rogers (@AKidFromKent) September 27, 2026 Marcus Mariota vs. Seattle 2012 (Oregon) : W 52-21 vs. Washington 2013 (Oregon) : W 45-24 at Washington 2014 (Oregon) : W 45-20 vs. Washington 2017 (Tennessee Titans) : W 33-27 vs. Seahawks 2022 (Atlanta Falcons) : W 27-23 at Seahawks 2026 (Washington Commanders) : W 33-31 vs. Seahawks It wasn’t like Mariota was a passenger in any of those games. He had 10 total touchdowns and just one interception against the Huskies, while his three separate starts versus the Seahawks saw him get seven touchdowns (six passing, one rushing) and only two turnovers (both with the Falcons). This is definitely not like when known Seahawks nemesis, Colt McCoy, had modest stats in two of his three winning starts but the games were low-scoring and McCoy could win a game 6-3 or 17-12. McCoy never even played the Huskies when he was at Texas. Mariota has owned Seattle’s two big football teams for almost 15 years. You know what? Tip of the cap. Hopefully the Seahawks never have to play him again.

title: Seahawks vs. Chargers odds: Opening lines for Week 4 matchup
summary: Despite a shocking 33-31 upset loss to the shorthanded Washington Commanders on Sunday, the Seattle Seahawks still open up as heavy favourites against the winless Los Angeles Chargers in Week 4. Seattle opened the season 2-0 and even after dropping an extremely winnable game, Sam Darnold and the offense strung together 437 total yards, leaving […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 10: George Holani #36 of the Seattle Seahawks scores a touchdown against the Los Angeles Chargers in the first half during a preseason game at SoFi Stadium on August 10, 2024 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Ronald Martinez/Getty Images) | Getty Images Despite a shocking 33-31 upset loss to the shorthanded Washington Commanders on Sunday , the Seattle Seahawks still open up as heavy favourites against the winless Los Angeles Chargers in Week 4. Seattle opened the season 2-0 and even after dropping an extremely winnable game, Sam Darnold and the offense strung together 437 total yards, leaving little concern about the team’s production moving forward. According to the current lines at FanDuel Sportsbook , the Seahawks are a 6.5-point favourite (-118) , with their money line set at -335 and Los Angeles’ at +270 . The line for total points is 44.5 , seemingly predicting a higher scoring affair but not quite a shootout Although the Chargers sit at 0-3 with losses to the Arizona Cardinals, Las Vegas Raiders, and Buffalo Bills, they’re still not a team who should be taken lightly. While the offense has struggled to move the ball under new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, they’re led by a proven veteran in Justin Herbert and have a strong supporting cast, consisting of Omarion Hampton, Ladd McConkey and Oronde Gadsden II. Defensively, they picked off superstar quarterback Josh Allen twice in their Week 3 loss to the Buffalo Bills and held the dual threat signal caller to 22 rushing yards—even though he found the endzone twice. Regardless, the odds don’t necessarily justify how strong of a team Los Angeles can be. But they’ll have to contain a dangerous Seahawks attack, led by Jaxon Smith-Nijgba, who’s totaled an unworldly 405 receiving yards and six touchdowns across the team’s first three games. The real concern comes with their defense, who just allowed 33 points to a Marcus Mariota led Commanders team. Normally, it’s far from the issue but their secondary took a hit with safeties Julian Love (calf) and Ty Okada (hamstring) sidelined. It’ll be worth monitoring their status’ as the week progresses to see if either are healthy enough to suit up, but given Okada’s been completely sidelined so far this season and head coach Mike Macdonald hasn’t provided an update, they appear on track to be missing at least one of the two starters. The line of 44.5 for total points seems to align with one of two returning and Seattle’s defense improving, especially when taking into consideration they allowed just 17 points across their first two games with Love on the field. The Seahawks loss to Washington is eerily similar to Week 5 of last season, when they dropped a 38-35 offensive thriller to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers while missing several key defensive pieces. title: Seahawks-Commanders review: A win in horseshoes, but that’s not what they were playing
summary: The invincible Seattle Seahawks, literal champions of the world, found the losing column. A fate which was unavoidable, probably, given the sport they play and the league they play in. What would’ve been nice to avoid is losing the same way they’re accustomed to winning. On a wet afternoon more suited for a Pacific Northwest […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 27: Terry McLaurin #17 of the Washington Commanders reacts after play against the Seattle Seahawks during the fourth quarter at Northwest Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The invincible Seattle Seahawks, literal champions of the world, found the losing column. A fate which was unavoidable, probably, given the sport they play and the league they play in. What would’ve been nice to avoid is losing the same way they’re accustomed to winning. On a wet afternoon more suited for a Pacific Northwest fall weekend, the team used to delivering sound beatings with a specific duplicatable formula got upended by another team using the same formula. Take care of the ball, pounce on errors, run when you need it, hunt explosives without being risky, and come up clutch in high-leverage moments. You can win so many games that way! Well. You don’t have to tell the Washington Commanders twice. They snagged three takeaways. They pounced on too many errors. They eschewed risk but got enough explosives to move the ball. They ran when they really needed it. And when the leverage was highest, their execution and planning were at their best. Or at least better than Seattle’s, which is all that counts. About the only things Washington didn’t do right for this game were use legal offensive formations consistently, and draft Jaxon Smith-Njigba in 2024. With each passing day, the legend of JSN, demigod, grows. 2ND OF THE DAY 😮‍💨 IT'S A TOUCHDOWN @jaxon_smith1 📺: @NFLonFOX pic.twitter.com/t4uZvbSJ23 — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) September 27, 2026 Back to the sad trombone. While the Seahawks lost a game they were heavily favored to win, they didn’t lose because of those dang late third-down mess-ups. Or just because of the (extremely) questionable flag on AJ Finley. Or because of Jadarian Price’s fumble, which is inexcusable and alarming. Even, and this may be hard for the Drew Lock-pologists to accept, Seattle didn’t lose just because of Sam’s turrbl throw that went for six the wrong way. The Seahawks didn’t even lose because they let Kenneth Walker go in free agency but dang, it sure would be nice to have that dude toting the rock 20 times a game; no, the Seahawks lost chiefly because of three turnovers in general, and not one in isolation. Washington scored 21 points off the guests’ thoughtful housewarming gifts and that’s that, with the that as inescapable a that as you’ll ever find in football. Show some ball security, run it slightly better and instead of talking about a narrow defeat, people are wondering low long the defending Super Bowl champs might run the table. Be less careless, and you’re flying home with the kind of comfortable victory the 2025 team trained us to enjoy and expect. In one way, the semi-surprise loss confirms our best thoughts about the Seahawks: they’re really hard for anyone to outscore unless X, Y and Z all happen in the same artificial 60-minute period. In another way, screw that, moral victory is just an elaborate way to spell the word “defeat.” Still, it is fall, and as fall reminds us, everything dies. 16-2 on the road isn’t sustainable. Having a non-explosive run game and still winning has a very short shelf life. Losing the turnover battle by three and still prevailing won’t ever last. Like, don’t give them a red zone fumble, a pick six and a helmet-carom interception. And, yet. Somehow, someway. And. Yet. Despite cooking with all the toxic ingredients necessary for an embarrassing setback, the Seahawks defense was one stop away from sending the ball back to their offensive teammates at the end, with plenty of time, down two, on a day Jason Myers had already connected from 57 yards out. They were gonna claim redemption. They didn’t. Rachaad White scampered to the outside when the defense sold out for a run to the left or up the middle. Leonard Williams, he of the otherwise enormous game, discarded his blocker only to see White kick it east-west and outrace Drake Thomas to the yellow line. Three plays later, Marcus Mariota hopped in a time machine and came out an Oregon Duck again, faking the handoff and running the freakin’ quarterback option for the clinching first down. Marcus Mariota just called game! @SEAvsWAS on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus — NFL (@nflbot.bsky.social) 2026-09-27T20:27:13.000Z To the Commanders’ credit , they took the Seahawks’ best punch — two late TDs, including six points in 66 seconds, and came out the other end winners. To the Seahawks’ credit, sort of, they tied one hand behind their backs by running as ineffectively as you can, and it almost didn’t matter. The champs very nearly went unpunished after: Managing just 44 total rushing yards Going 17-33-0 after Price’s opening-play burst. Less than two yards per carry. Fumbling in their own red zone Converting only two first downs on the ground with running backs. It’s okay to recognize they miss Walker, they would’ve won in Week 3 with him, and still shouldn’t have paid him what the Chiefs did. It’s okay despite K9’s production in KC. (Look it up at your own risk.) But the Seahawks missed him, undeniably, for the second time in three games. To the recap! Q1: Commanders 7, Seahawks 0 Predator : DeMarcus Lawrence on Washington’s fourth drive Prey : either side of the O-line, names don’t matter, irrelevant How : Tank simply did not allow the Commanders to block him. Any age or motivation concerns around the 34-year-old should probably be shelved. Sandwiched around their disallowed touchdown, Lawrence provided a pressure that set up 3rd and forever, only to see Josh Jobe get flagged for DPI. His second one forced an incompletion. They're not blocking D-Law and that's fine with me — John Fraley (@johndavidfraley.bsky.social) 2026-09-27T17:39:37.412Z Who are opponents supposed to double-team across that D-line? There’s a reason Big Cat has three sacks, Byron Murphy looks like a Pro Bowler at minimum, Derick Hall keeps running free in those monster wheels he calls thighs, and Uchenna Nwosu is having a career revival. So, early on, with Darnold back after less than two full games missed, fans were likely looking for signs he’d be okay. After a handoff that would prove to be the zenith of Seattle’s rushing attack — 11 yards, all at once, in this economy? — the Hawks starter was forced into a scramble that tested his lateral movement. Check. A Price rushing fail got us to third down, where Sam zipped a third-down torpedo to Shaheed. Check. No conversion, but two checks. Alles glute, meine Freunde. When the Commanders followed suit by going three-and-out on their opening drive, the usual optimism about our road Seahawks surfaced. For exactly one play. On a very benign-looking tackle from Amik Robertson, Price put the ball on the ground for the second time in three appearances. Given a short field, the hosts leaned on three successful run plays from Jacory Croskey-Merritt — nine on first down, easy conversion, and six more bunnies right after — to knock on the door. One knock was sufficient to open the scoring, as Mariota threaded the needle to White in the end zone, inches past the outstretched hand of a diving Drake Thomas. Tellingly, Mike Macdonald called on Emanuel Wilson and George Holani for his offense’s next drive, which went nowhere. Arguments accepted, but Price is probably one more giveaway from losing his role as feature back altogether. And it’ll hard to blame anyone but the rookie. Following the drive where Lawrence asserted his will and the Commanders shot themselves in the foot with two pre-snap penalties, a lightbulb went off on the Seattle sideline. It was the JSN lightbulb, which burns brighter than even the oncoming LED headlights of any new car. (Elect me. My entire platform is banning them.) This newfound knowledge that football’s most dominant offensive player wears a Seattle uniform changed everything. JSN for 11 right out of the gate. Another…

HOUSE CALL. 📺: @SNFonNBC pic.twitter.com/rvtzMZwzoT — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) September 28, 2026 HUF CALLED GAME. 📺: @SNFonNBC pic.twitter.com/HwTg0LzAXx — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) September 28, 2026 It’s the first 16-point comeback the Rams have been on the wrong end of since, well, you know… NFC West standings San Francisco 49ers (3-0, 2-0 NFCW) Seattle Seahawks (2-1, 1-0 NFCW) Los Angeles Rams (1-2, 0-1 NFCW) Arizona Cardinals (1-2, 0-2 NFCW) NFC West Week 4 schedule San Francisco 49ers vs. Denver Broncos Seattle Seahawks vs. Los Angeles Chargers Los Angeles Rams at Philadelphia Eagles Arizona Cardinals at New York Giants This was arguably a blown opportunity by Seattle to get some early separation on the Rams, but there’s still a chance to get a two-game lead next week with a win over the Chargers and an Eagles win over LA. title: Jadarian Price has a fumbling problem until he doesn’t
summary: The Seattle Seahawks have been blessed with tremendous ball security from their main running backs over the past few seasons. Kenneth Walker III never lost a fumble with the Seahawks and only had one career fumble on an actual run play, while Zach Charbonnet’s next fumble will be his first. Walker is on another team […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks have been blessed with tremendous ball security from their main running backs over the past few seasons. Kenneth Walker III never lost a fumble with the Seahawks and only had one career fumble on an actual run play, while Zach Charbonnet’s next fumble will be his first. Walker is on another team (and looking like a viable Offensive Player of the Year candidate) while Charbonnet isn’t back for at least another two weeks. The Seahawks are relying on Jadarian Price to be an immediate contributor as a first-round pick. He’s shown some flashes of explosive runs and an ability to be a receiving threat out of the backfield, so there’s been a good helping of promising plays. He’s also put the ball on the ground twice in as many weeks. . @ZavenCollins liked what he saw 😳 #SEAvsAZ | 📺 FOX pic.twitter.com/QHufimdBab — Arizona Cardinals (@AZCardinals) September 20, 2026 FUMBLE 🚨 @SEAvsWAS on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/RNgk2tQRjX — NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026 The second fumble was enough for the Seahawks to bench him until late in the first half of their 33-31 loss to the Washington Commanders . It might seem like tough love, but Price is a rookie and he doesn’t have the same leeway as more established running backs. “I think just as a team, if we turn the ball over, it’s not good business,” Mike Macdonald said after the game. “So, when you come back after the initial fumble, we decide to calm it down and bring it back after the half. He’s gonna be fine. He’s gonna figure it out, he’ll be fine.” “I made a mistake,” Price said . “Just got to deal with the consequences.” Price only carried the ball two more times and had just six total touches for 21 yards. It was a day in which the Seahawks generated almost nothing on the ground, so it wasn’t like Emanuel Wilson or George Holani were significantly better. But the fumbling for Price is not a new issue. It was brought up in his final season at Notre Dame, in which he fumbled three times (losing two) on just 113 carries. All of his fumbles last year were inside the opposition 10, with C.J. Carr preventing a hat trick of red zone turnovers. That may or may not be why Seattle has been hesitant to give him the ball in goal-to-go situations. pic.twitter.com/lEz2G3xKln — Mookie Alexander (@mookiealexander) September 28, 2026 Adding his 12 games in his final Notre Dame season, Price has five fumbles in 15 games. That’s five fumbles over 141 carries, or one on every 28 attempts. In effect, that’s two games worth of carries for Price. James Cook of the Buffalo Bills led all running backs in the NFL with six fumbles last season, except that’s on 309 carries and he did a little thing called leading the league in rushing yards. Price hasn’t quite built up that sort of equity to where the fumbles are a minor story due to terrific productivity. This is not an indictment of the pick or an indication that this is who Price will always be. But for someone who was not the primary back at Notre Dame and hasn’t even had the bulk of the carries as a pro, this is a legitimate concern until he fixes it. I trust that Price will be able to work on this as he develops, but it’s a weakness in his game that opposition defenses are going to relentlessly attack. And this, never mind any pass protection concerns, might affect his workload until he earns the trust of the coaching staff.
author: Mookie Alexander

title: Seahawks Droppings: Everyone is to blame for Seahawks stinker against Commanders
summary: It’s been a long time since we had to feel the sting of a Seattle Seahawks loss, going way back to November 2025. Yeah, it still sucks. Have you ever woken up in a bad mood for no reason? That was me this morning. The Seahawks had a chance to flip my mood around with […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 27: Marcus Mariota #8 of the Washington Commanders runs with the ball during the fourth quarter of an NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Northwest Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s been a long time since we had to feel the sting of a Seattle Seahawks loss, going way back to November 2025. Yeah, it still sucks. Have you ever woken up in a bad mood for no reason? That was me this morning. The Seahawks had a chance to flip my mood around with an early game against a (seemingly) outmatched Washington Commanders team. However, no one accounted for the fact that Marcus Mariota is undefeated as a starter against Seattle. That statistical anomaly continued today as he led the Commanders to a stunning 33-31 win over the Seahawks. Obviously, my mood got worse. For as perturbed as I’m feeling as I write this, it doesn’t hold a candle to just how horribly the Seahawks played for much of the game today. The offense couldn’t move the ball on the ground and turned the ball over three times. On defense, the Dark Side bent and broke, giving up three TDs and key third down conversions with the game on the line. Special teams isn’t getting off the hook, as Jason Myers kicked the ball out of bounds directly after Seattle tied the game, immediately setting Washington up near FG range. Seahawks Droppings For his first game back, Sam Darnold played well…except for one throw. Driving for the potential leading score, Darnold threw a late game pick-six. During the winning streak, he largely avoided those throws. I see that INT throw off the helmet as mostly just bad luck. The one over the middle was much more egregious. Jadarian Price was put on a very short leash after his early fumble, the second for him in three games. The conditions were crappy, but that’s not an excuse. As awesome as I think Price will be, he won’t be able to show it if they can’t trust him to hold on to the ball. Jaxon Smith-Njigba is amazing, but even he had an easy drop of a potential first down today . Still, he kept dragging the Seahawks back into the game and continues to show why he’s arguably the best WR in the NFL. The thin depth at safety is starting to show . No offense to AJ Finley, but he’s a quantum leap below Julian Love. Part of the defense’s struggles are related to being short-handed. That’s not an excuse, it’s just a fact. The guys playing meaningful snaps in this game aren’t nearly as experienced nor talented as Love. Hopefully his calf injury is a short term thing. Mike Macdonald won’t be very happy with his defense today. Seattle couldn’t get a turnover against the Mariota-led Commanders, and gave up key third-down conversions leading to both the FG to go down 27-24 and allowing the Commanders to run out the clock. The fact that those last two conversions were running plays on third and long really stand out. Washington was almost conceding the play to keep the clock running, and the Seahawks couldn’t stop them. Penalties were an issue again today, much like the preseason . Just before Darnold’s pick-six, Seattle had an illegal formation penalty that dropped them back to 1st and 15 when they were already almost in FG range, basically taking the run game completely out of that decision. The AJ Finley penalty was a huge call at a pivotal point. Seattle had stopped Washington on 3rd down and would’ve gotten the ball back with the game tied 24-24. Instead, the Commanders would go on to get a FG. I really don’t know how you coach Finley to play that any differently. The guy lowered his head into Finley, and he did nothing wrong. Don’t misunderstand me, the refs were not the reason the Seahawks lost this game. Seattle did that to themselves. Ultimately, I’m annoyed, but I believe the Seahawks will be fine. This game feels eerily similar to all three of the Seahawks losses last season particularly the Tampa Bay Buccaneers game. They were undermanned in the secondary, played like crap on defense, turned the ball over, and were still in position to potentially win the game. Same thing against the Commanders. The fact that Seattle can play so terribly in all three phases and still have a chance at the end just goes to show that they’re a really, really good team. I hope this pisses them off and sends them on another (at least) 12 game winning streak.

title: Winners and Losers from a disappointing Seahawks loss to the Commanders
summary: Well, the Seattle Seahawks weren’t going to win every game. They were also going to inevitably lose to a bad team, and to suggest Mike Macdonald would be immune to this would smack of arrogance. Almost every contending team, including teams coached by all-time greats over the years, manage to throw up a clunker at […]
full_text: Well, the Seattle Seahawks weren’t going to win every game. They were also going to inevitably lose to a bad team, and to suggest Mike Macdonald would be immune to this would smack of arrogance. Almost every contending team, including teams coached by all-time greats over the years, manage to throw up a clunker at least once in a season. We accept this in every other sport but football. With that said, I did not think they would lose this game to the Washington Commanders. It was a deceptive 33-31 shootout loss given how many short drives the Commanders scored, but it’s still a loss that is about as disappointing as any I can recall in the Mike Macdonald era. Alright, it’s been a minute since we’ve had to do a negative Winners and Losers column. I gotta dust off the cobwebs for this one! Seattle Seahawks Winners Jaxon Smith-Njigba is a dual threat So much for JSN being done throwing passes. He is 1/1 for 14 yards on the season after the double pass to George Holani. But the main thing he’s paid for? He’s still great at that. Another 10 catches for 128 yards and a couple of touchdowns. There were a couple of false starts and a drop by JSN, but he produces at such a comically high level that those negative moments are a blip on the radar. Of all the players he might be competing against for OPOY, it might be… Kenneth Walker? Just saying. Tory Horton and Cooper Kupp come alive The Seahawks got their non-JSN targets involved a lot more than in the previous two weeks. Horton had three grabs for 48 yards and Kupp had four for 46 and a touchdown. Seattle has to have a passing offense that does not live and die off of JSN’s production, and while the Commanders pass defense is not very good, this was very welcome to see. Brian Fleury unleashes A.J. Barner as a pass-catcher Do the Seahawks have a screen game now? A.J. Barner had five catches for 69 yards and had his best game of the young season. Brian Fleury got his main tight end involved heavily and it worked out. Elijah Arroyo’s continued non-involvement is a tiny bit bothersome. Sam Darnold’s pick 6 was costly, but he still played a great game I cannot justify or defend the pick-six that Darnold threw. Bad read, bad decision, pretty much a back-breaker. But on a day when he’s coming back from injury and had no run game to support him, he carried the load on offense. He finished 31/45 for 379 yards and four touchdowns, albeit with one more interception on a tip-drill. Darnold avoided pressure expertly and did not get sacked, making some excellent throws throughout the afternoon. Even acknowledging the picks, his performance provided some relief in terms of his mobility and what the passing offense could look like for the rest of the season. Welcome back to the end zone, Eric Saubert! Saubert’s previous end zone trip as a Seahawk was the most important two-point conversion in franchise history. His first actual touchdown as a Seahawk is, for now, a receiving touchdown. I do wonder if there is a stat correction coming if he did fumble before crossing the plane. It could be an “other” touchdown in the form of a rare offensive fumble recovery, but we’ll see. Leonard Williams is still dominant He had one of Seattle’s two sacks, three tackles for losses, and three QB hits. Big Cat has not missed a beat entering 2026. Jason Myers’ kicking struggles are behind him Making a 57-yarder in wet conditions is big-time. He hasn’t missed a kick yet this regular season. Seattle Seahawks Losers Jadarian Price’s ball security is a real concern Two weeks in a row with a lost fumble. He didn’t have a high volume of carries at Notre Dame but the ball security question marks were brought up back then. I have no issue with his benching; he’s a rookie and you hope he gets better and learns some lessons. The cost is any sort of speed and elusiveness in Seattle’s backfield. If he can’t figure this out then he won’t get a heavy workload any time soon. The Rashid Shaheed contract is looking shaky I’ve given it another week, there’s still a lot of time left in the season, but Shaheed finished another game without a big return and he had just two catches for 14 yards. There’s just not been enough out of him in this offense to start the year, and it looks more glaring when Tory Horton immediately outperformed him when he got extended snaps for the first time this season. At $17 million/year this is not the productivity Seattle should be getting. It makes you wonder if Horton having a healthy 2025 would’ve influenced the Shaheed decision. Sloppy penalties are not stopping The Seahawks had eight accepted penalties against them, including multiple pre-snap penalties on Jaxon Smith-Njigba and a false start on A.J. Barner. There are some real procedural problems that are hurting them on offense, and they’ve shown themselves to be undisciplined and a little disorganized in the early portion of this season. The run blocking, as a whole, was abysmal The Seahawks miss Anthony Bradford, perhaps? I don’t know yet, because the Commanders run D has actually been good for two straight games and the Seahawks ran over the Arizona Cardinals last week without Bradford. But they are struggling in short-yardage in the low red zone, and are not resetting the line of scrimmage in their favor. I’ve said it for two straight weeks, but I am concerned about Abe Lucas’ ability to anchor and move laterally. The worst runs seem to come on the right side of the field. Emanuel Wilson and George Holani didn’t offer up anything more than Price on the ground, and Wilson’s plodding style is more exposed when he can’t immediately go north-south. A grand total of 39 yards on 17 carries from the running backs. That ain’t going to get it done. A.J. Finley’s first start will probably he his last Tough ask to be thrust into the starting lineup after a mid-week calf injury for Julian Love. It’s a nice reminder that not every preseason star translates into regular season action. Finley was picked on all game and was spared bigger plays against him thanks to an illegal formation penalty taking away a 48-yard touchdown run, as well as expedited review wiping out a long Dyami Brown catch. The penalty he got for roughness was complete junk, so I have to defend him there. But he was brutal and Seattle needs one of Love or Ty Okada back next week. Bare minimum, D’Anthony Bell should be elevated next week. The edge rushers don’t get home Derick Hall recorded a sack but wasn’t noticeable in getting after Mariota. DeMarcus Lawrence at least had three QB hits, but it was otherwise a game in which neither Uchenna Nwosu nor Dante Fowler Jr made much of an impact. Leonard Williams was his usual excellent self, but Seattle needs more from its edges and not just the interior. Michael Dickson might have had one of his worst games ever Dickson had a touchback (his first of the season) on his first punt. His final three punts traveled 44, 38, and 40 yards while inside his own half of the field. It was a breezy day but he did nothing to flip the field, and that’s part of why the Seahawks kept gifting the Commanders favorable field position. For what it’s worth, Seattle’s kick coverage has not impressed throughout the season and seems to default give returners the ball at the 30 or better. That’s why the defense was deceptively worse than it actually was (258 yards allowed, 3/13 on third down, four yards per play). Commanders starting field position: WSH 20 (punt) SEA 21 (TD) WSH 28 (punt) WSH 44 (punt) WSH 40 (TD) WSH 2 (punt) WSH 35 (FG, two-min drill) WSH 34 (punt) SEA 43 (TD) WSH 26 (punt) WSH 44 (punt) WSH 40 (FG) WSH 33 (EOG) Only 4 of their 13 drives were inside their own 30. Bad. — Mookie Alexander (@mookiealexander) September 27, 2026 Seattle’s special teams losses through free agency and injury are being felt here. Final Notes Josh Jobe did get picked on a bit and even beaten for a touchdown by Terry McLaurin but sometimes it’s just better offense beating good defense. McLaurin is one…

title: Seahawks-Commanders score: Turnover woes doom Seahawks to stunning loss
summary: The Seattle Seahawks (2-1), for whatever reason, cannot solve Marcus Mariota regardless of which team he’s playing for. Mariota is now 3-0 lifetime as a starter against Seattle, with his other wins coming as a member of the Tennessee Titans and Atlanta Falcons. In the most disappointing loss arguably of the entire Mike Macdonald era, […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks (2-1), for whatever reason, cannot solve Marcus Mariota regardless of which team he’s playing for. Mariota is now 3-0 lifetime as a starter against Seattle, with his other wins coming as a member of the Tennessee Titans and Atlanta Falcons. In the most disappointing loss arguably of the entire Mike Macdonald era, three turnovers led to 21 Washington Commanders points, and Dan Quinn was able to get the better of his former team in a 33-31 upset victory. Sam Darnold threw four touchdown passes in his return to action, but also had a costly pick-six that put the Seahawks down nine late in the fourth quarter. Seattle’s winning streak is over at 12, and the champs have some issues to figure out as far as the run game and the low red zone. The defense actually held Washington to only 258 yards and four yards per play, but even elite defenses (especially without two starting safeties) will struggle when the average starting field position is repeatedly favorable for the other team. Seahawks vs. Commanders 1st half recap The Seahawks started on offense and gained a first down through Jadarian Price, but that’s all. Sam Darnold was nearly picked on his first pass but completed his second to Rashid Shaheed for 10 yards. Michael Dickson had his first touchback of the season on a 4th-and-4 punt. Washington punted it right back after a 3-and-out. Jadarian Price lost a fumble last week and lost one on the first play of Seattle’s second series. Can’t have that happening whether it’s a rainy day or not. The Commanders recovered just outside the red zone. Three plays later, Rachaad White made a good catch past a diving Drake Thomas for the game’s first touchdown. 7-0 Commanders. FUMBLE 🚨 @SEAvsWAS on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/RNgk2tQRjX — NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026 . @Chaad_1 FOR 6️⃣ 📺 #SEAvsWAS FOX pic.twitter.com/mRvAhZEZ6d — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) September 27, 2026 The Seahawks struggles continued on offense with a three-and-out, but the league’s best defense was having some major troubles. A 3rd and 11 was converted to Terry McLaurin on a rare coverage bust. Mariota audibled to a Bill Croskey-Merritt handoff, and the second-year back took it 48 yards for the score. An illegal formation, however, nullified the TD. Dyami Brown had a 23-yard catch on the ensuing play, only for that to be nullified by expedited review when his second foot was found to be out of bounds. Seattle got the ball back and finally got to work. Who do you think they went to? Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who caught three passes for 32 yards and drew a pass interference penalty. Seattle’s 90-yard touchdown drive was capped off by a JSN TD at the 1-yard line. Hat tips to A.J. Barner and Brady Russell for their own explosive plays in the pass game. 7-7. JSN takes it to the end zone 🔥 @jaxon_smith1 📺: @NFLonFOX pic.twitter.com/sWal2PwFKm — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) September 27, 2026 After the two teams traded punts, the Commanders retook the lead off of yet another short field. Uchenna Nwosu nearly picked off Mariota when he dropped into coverage, and that dropped pick proved costly. Jaylin Lane took a screen pass 21 yards for the first explosive pass allowed by Seattle all season. Treylon Burks beat A.J. Finley for the go-ahead touchdown. 14-7 Commanders . Sam Darnold was dealing to Cooper Kupp, A.J. Barner, and Tory Horton for big gains. The Seahawks once again had a goal-to-go situation and again struggled to finish off the job. Three straight passes at the two-yard line all fell incomplete for a turnover on downs. Washington actually had a -1 yard drive while backed up and had to punt it back to Seattle. Darnold couldn’t do a whole lot (in large part due to the excellent play by Amik Robertson), but there was enough for Myers to hit a 57-yard field goal. 14-10 Commanders . Good from distance 😮‍💨 @JayMy_31 with the 57-yard field goal. 📺: @NFLonFOX pic.twitter.com/Kd62bk319a — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) September 27, 2026 A touchback gave the Commanders the ball at their 35, and Mariota hit an open Terry McLaurin for 18 yards. Another short throw put Washington in field goal range, and rookie Drew Stevens matched Myers with his own 57-yarder to end the half. 17-10 Commanders . Seahawks vs. Commanders 2nd half recap Marcus Mariota could’ve hit a huge play to rookie Antonio Williams deep down the field. Ernest Jones IV was in coverage and stayed in phase with Williams, who got his hands on the ball but dropped it. Big stop and a three-and-out by the Commanders offense to start the half. Disaster struck on Seattle’s opening drive, as Sam Darnold’s pass hit the helmet of Tim Settle and settled (heh heh, get it?) into the arms of the outstanding rookie Sonny Styles. SONNY STYLES INTERCEPTION 📺 #SEAvsWAS FOX pic.twitter.com/iv9cWR33Es — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) September 27, 2026 Another costly turnover led to another Commanders touchdown. Terry McLaurin beat Josh Jobe on a typically brilliant McLaurin catch. 24-10 Commanders. WENT UP AND GOT IT. TERRY TOUCHDOWN 🙌 📺 #SEAvsWAS FOX pic.twitter.com/CLDeeVJobP — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) September 27, 2026 Sam Darnold went 5/5 on what was essentially a must-score drive for the reigning Super Bowl champions. Eric Saubert, for the time being, has a receiving touchdown. This might get overturned into a fumble recovery TD after the ball was ripped away from him at the goal line. He recovered it so it’s a score either way, but it’s Saubert’s first touchdown since 2024. 24-17 Commanders. Saubert takes it in 😤 📺: @NFLonFOX pic.twitter.com/BbVgIVhUjE — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) September 27, 2026 It was another exchange of punts and sloppy penalties through the end of the third quarter. Seattle struggled to gain any traction in the run game. They could sure as hell throw the ball, and Sam Darnold was in a zone. He was escaping pressure in the pocket and his best play was arguably an incomplete pass, as he avoided a sack and scrambled to find Rashid Shaheed, who was whacked for a roughness penalty. Shaheed didn’t catch the ball on review but the penalty was upheld. After Smith-Njigba hit a double pass to George Holani on a trick play, Darnold took over the normal quarterback duties. Normal service resumed when it’s Sam to JSN for a tying touchdown! 2ND OF THE DAY 😮‍💨 IT'S A TOUCHDOWN @jaxon_smith1 📺: @NFLonFOX pic.twitter.com/t4uZvbSJ23 — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) September 27, 2026 A kickoff short of the landing zone resulted in another short-ish field for Washington. Terry McLaurin was unable to bring in a catch on third down, but A.J. Finley was tagged for a very harsh personal foul penalty for a helmet shot. McLaurin lowered his helmet and Finley didn’t initiate any contact. McLaurin would feature on a 4th and 1 conversion on a perfect Mariota pass. Ernest Jones made a critical, possible touchdown-saving tackle on Mariota on the red zone to set up a Drew Stevens field goal. The rookie converted to make it 27-24 Commanders with 4:34 to go . Welp. Sam Darnold nearly threw a pick on a double coverage shot to Rashid Shaheed. He threw a pick-six to Kain Medrano, who replaced the injured Leo Chanal in the first half. The celebration penalty led to a longer PAT and a miss, but it’s still 33-24 Commanders . OWEH WITH THE PRESSURE….KAIN TO THE HOUSE!!!!! 📺 #SEAvsWAS FOX pic.twitter.com/7jfhys1A4q — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) September 27, 2026 Some horrendous defense and dominant play by Jaxon Smith-Njigba meant that the Commanders allowed Seattle free access to the end zone in next to no time. Cooper Kupp was wide open for his first touchdown of the season. 33-31 Commanders with only 2:51 to go. And just like that… TOUCHDOWN! @CooperKupp 📺: @NFLonFOX pic.twitter.com/d4SAXW9Vam — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) September 27, 2026 A second down incomplete pass gave Seattle a chance to get the ball back quickly and maybe burn one timeout at most. Rachaad White beat Drake Thomas to…

title: 49ers grades vs. Cardinals: The offensive line is officially a strength
summary: If the San Francisco 49ers make the playoffs, nobody will look back and say, “Well, they almost lost in Week 3!” You can’t say the same about the other two playoff contenders in the division. Winning is all that matters. Here’s how the 49ers got there. Let’s hand out some positional grades. Quarterback: A If […]
full_text: (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images If the San Francisco 49ers make the playoffs, nobody will look back and say, “Well, they almost lost in Week 3!” You can’t say the same about the other two playoff contenders in the division . Winning is all that matters. Here’s how the 49ers got there. Let’s hand out some positional grades. Quarterback: A If you didn’t watch the game, you’d look at Brock Purdy’s 55.6% completion percentage and think he played poorly. After all, he only completed 15 of his 27 passes. But 14 of those went for first downs. Another four went for touchdowns. Winners and Losers mentioned it , but it’s always a great sign when Purdy throws the ball away. No quarterback had a higher throwaway percentage in Week 3 than Purdy. The Cardinals did everything they could to condense the middle of the field. Over 40% of Purdy’s attempts came outside of the numbers. That’s not where the 49ers generally operate. Winners and Losers also highlighted how Brock Purdy passes Lamar Jackson for the all-time record for the most games in a career with at least a 130 passer rating. In Week 3, Lamar’s EPA per pass was 0.51, an excellent number and second-best in the league that week. Purdy’s was 0.81. A number you’d be hard-pressed to accomplish in Madden. Nearly every time Purdy dropped back, he added a point to the scoreboard. Purdy gets an A because the Cardinals were down multiple members in their secondary, and it’s the Cardinals. Plus, he wasn’t perfect. There were at least two throws he’d want back. And if we’re going to judge him like the MVP candidate he is, then he should be graded on an MVP scale. Purdy’s been in complete control through three games. His EPA per pass was higher in Week 2 (the 11th-best mark for any quarterback since 2022). You love to see Purdy pick and choose when to scramble. Purdy became the first quarterback since 2022 to post an EPA per pass of 0.8 or higher in back-to-back weeks. He was great, and the 49ers need him to be. Running back: A Last week in this piece, we mentioned how Kaelon Black left some yards on the field. He’s a rookie. There will be games like that. So it’s no surprise to see Christian McCaffrey get the lion’s share of carries in a divisional game. Purdy being awesome will overshadow how well McCaffrey played. It shouldn’t. McCaffrey forced four missed tackles, averaged 2.6 yards after contact, and five yards per carry. When the 49ers ran the clock out toward the end of the game, McCaffrey chewed up much-needed yardage and time, keeping the defense off the field. McCaffrey picked up three first downs as a receiver. He gained 24 yards after the catch on 41 receptions. He’s still one of the most dangerous receivers out of the backfield, despite the declining speed. McCaffrey played 41 snaps compared to Black’s 8. Wide receiver: C+ The wide receiver group wasn’t bad, but most of the production came from the quarterback or the scheme. Was it cool to see Jordan Watkins catch passes? Of course. Making plays in your first regular-season game could be exactly what Watkins needs to build confidence moving forward. He was wide open on both receptions. On the play before the half, he was the only player in the picture. Deebo Samuel didn’t have a reception. He showed he can still run, but he had zero targets across 22 routes. Jacob Cowing was targeted twice across 14 routes. Losing Mike Evans changed everything. He ran only 12 routes but was targeted on six of them. KhaDarel Hodge played the second-most snaps behind Deebo, but that’s because of what he can do in the run game. It’s evident that Purdy really only trusts Evans. Maybe a better way to phrase it is that Purdy might be most comfortable throwing to Evans. If Evans is out for multiple weeks, which it seems like that’s where we’re headed, this group faces an uphill battle, going against two of the best secondaries in the NFL in the next two weeks. Tight end: B+ If Luke Farrell stays in-bounds on his one target and George Kittle doesn’t egregiously hold on Purdy’s touchdown run, then this is an A. Farrell is so much better as a run blocker than he was a year ago. His blocking prowess lets the team let Kittle run routes. A novel concept, isn’t it? Purdy’s success rate targeting Kittle was 85.7%. Kittle caught his lone contested catch, forced a missed tackle, picked up 30 yards after the catch, caught a couple of touchdowns, and reached 17.06 miles per hour, which is crazy when you consider he’s basically been playing football for a month after a torn Achilles. Offensive line: A- Jake Brendel was the only player to keep a clean sheet in pass protection, but if you allow two pressures — which a few of the linemen did — on 28 pass-blocking snaps, in no way is that a bad game. In what field is being successful 92% of the time considered bad? None that I’m aware of. Through three weeks, the #49ers have two of the top 6 and three of the top 13 offensive linemen in the league in pressure rate allowed, per Next Gen Stats: No. 1 — C Jake Brendel – 0% T-No. 6 — RG Dominick Puni – 2.2% No. 13 — LT Trent Williams – 3.7% — Nick Wagoner (@nwagoner) September 28, 2026 For the season, the line has allowed 12 pressures in true pass sets. They are winning almost every rep. A neck stinger for Trent Williams meant Vederian Lowe would finish the final 19 snaps at left tackle. He held up well. Per Sumer Sports, each lineman recorded impact plays, with Dominick Puni leading the way with three. Brendel and Colton McKivitz each had two apiece. McCaffrey averaged 2.6 yards before contact on his attempts. That’s incredible. There were two to three series that felt like the Cardinals got the best of the line, but across 50 plays, the Niners won the battle and did so convincingly. There’s no need to sugarcoat it: the offensive line is a strength for the 49ers, and pretending otherwise is either being purposely obtuse or you’re living off plays from past years. The real test happens over the next two games. Defensive line: B- Since we are humans, we don’t have to trash a defensive line whose longest-tenured player is Keion White: The 49ers defensive line yesterday: Player they traded for last October Player they signed on August 6 Player they signed on August 24 Player they signed on September 4 Player they traded for on March 11 Player they drafted in the 4th round of '26 Practice squad player making… — Kyle Posey (@KP_Show) September 28, 2026 You cannot have high expectations when you enter a game with two defensive tackles who were on the roster entering training camp, and one of those gets hurt halfway through the game. Khalid Kareem played 51 snaps. He was a last-minute add ahead of Week 1. Raheem Morris did everything in his power to increase the variance. He blitzed Jacoby Brissett on 50% of his dropbacks. In a way, it worked. Ogbo Okoronkwo and Keion White had a sack. Okoronkwo managed a 15.2% pressure rate. Newcomer Viliami Fehoko won a couple of his pass rushes and turned them into pressures. White has been closer to good than average through three weeks. His pass rush win percentage was 15.9%. The problem is when you ask role players, in this case pass rush first players, to play the run, they wear down, and you get the second half against the Cardinals. Fehoko was the only edge rusher to make a run stop. Jeremiyah Love averaged 1.81 yards before contact on 21 attempts. Sebastian Valdez had two run stops, and Naquan Jones added a run stuff. Those two held up well against the run but offered little in the pass-rush department. Kevin Givens flashed. Osa Odighizuwa made an impact rushing the passer. Gracen Halton was headed for another strong performance before an injury. But after he left, Odighizuwa couldn’t leave the field, Givens was stretched to the max, and the lack of bodies up front really hurt the defensive line’s effectiveness. Linebackers: C+ Early on, I thought Dre Greenlaw played his best football to date this season. He lived in the backfield, whether as a…

title: One potential Mac Jones suitor is off the board after trading for J.J. McCarthy
summary: The Ringer’s Tom Pelissero broke the news that the New York Giants are trading for Minnesota Vikings backup J.J. McCarthy. Reports surfaced on Sunday that the Giants were interested in San Francisco 49ers quarterback Mac Jones, but there were three other quarterbacks: McCarthy, Jones, Jimmy Garoppolo, Justin Fields, and Gardner Minshew. The Giants’ offensive coordinator, […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 21: Head Coach John Harbaugh of the New York Giants walks the field prior to the game against the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium on September 21, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Ringer’s Tom Pelissero broke the news that the New York Giants are trading for Minnesota Vikings backup J.J. McCarthy. Reports surfaced on Sunday that the Giants were interested in San Francisco 49ers quarterback Mac Jones, but there were three other quarterbacks: McCarthy, Jones, Jimmy Garoppolo, Justin Fields, and Gardner Minshew. The Giants’ offensive coordinator, Matt Nagy, had a chance to select Jones in 2021 while coaching the Chicago Bears, but passed. He passed again on Jones, this time for another first-rounder who should never have been selected that high to begin with. The Giants gave up a fifth-round pick for McCarthy, who was drafted in 2024. We’ll never know what the 49ers’ asking price is for Jones when he was on the hypothetical trade block last year, but we may find out if there are any other QB-needy teams during the next month and a half. It’ll likely take an injury at the position, or a team that wasn’t a contender emerges. Until then, Jones remains on the 49ers’ roster.
